California Masonic Memorial Temple-San Francisco

ANTHONY P. WORDLOW

Grand Master 1997-1998
Grand Master, Anthony P. "Tony" Wordlow, was born in Sheridan,
Wyoming, on July 16, 1936. When he was very young, the family moved to
California, finally settling in Rio Linda. He attended public schools, graduated
from Grant Union High School and continued his education at Grant Technical
College. He excelled in his favorite sport, swimming.
In 1959, Most Worshipful Brother Wordlow became a Master Mason in
Tehama Lodge No. 3 in Sacramento and quickly began his labors in the vineyards
of Freemasonry. He has served Tehama Lodge No. 3 on numerous committees
and in each line office beginning with Junior Steward. He was Master in 1970,
serving with distinction and honor. He was the recipient of the Hiram Award in
1994. Representing Tehama on the Sacramento Masonic Temple Board, he was
president 12 years. He sat on the Sacramento Masonic Cemetery Association
Board.
His Grand Lodge committee assignments have included Memorial
Service, Leadership Workshop, 1984 Junior Grand Warden Selection Committee,
Temple Properties, Wardens Retreats, Nob Hill Management Board, California
Masonic Memorial Temple Board, and Masonic Homes Board. He was Grand
Marshal in 1985-86 for Most Worshipful Grand Master John Driskell
At the October 1994 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge he was
elected Junior Grand Warden, served in each successive office until his election
October 14, 1997 as Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of California Free and
Accepted Masons.
At the 1998 Conference of Grand Masters of North America, Grand
Master Wordlow was elected to a three year term on the Board of Directors of the
George Washington Masonic National Memorial in Alexandria, Virginia.

ANTHONY P. "TONY" WORDLOW
Grand Master
October 15, 1997 -October 14, 1998
11

An active member of the Sacramento Scottish Rite Bodies since 1961,
He was Venerable Master in 1977 and coronetted with the Thirty-Third Degree in
1987. His achievements in that body are legend. Just to mention a few, he had
been Temple Board President, on the Clinic Board of Governors, the Club
Coordinator, Membership Chairman and a member of the ritual cast for several
degrees. He is proud that several of the programs he introduced to the Sacramento
Scottish Bodies have now become "tradition."
In 1962, he inched his way across the hot sands of Ben Ali Shrine
Temple -serving that body as presiding officer in several clubs and units. 1990
was a grrreat year for Ben Ali when he was Potentate, better known as Tony the
Tiger. He was a member of the East-West Game Executive Committee.
Most Worshipful Brother Tony delights in participating with the
Sacramento Scottish Rite and Ben Ali Shrine Past Masters Third Degree Teams.

iii

As you might expect, he is a member of many other Masonic
organizations, including Sacramento York Rite Bodies; Red Cross of
Constantine; Past Toparch, Sciots Tract Pyramid No. 11, Ancient Egyptian Order
of Sciots; Marysville-Friendship Chapter No. 55, Order of the Eastern Star;
Sacramento Court, Order of the Amaranth; National Sojourners; Royal Order of
Jesters, Court 119; Royal Order of Scotland; The Robert The Bruce Association;
Honorary Member of the Chinese Acacia Club.
Married to Marilyn since 1956; they are the parents of one son, Chris,
who was raised to the Sublime Degree of Master Mason in Western Star Lodge
No. 2, F. & A.M., April 11, 1998, this year. Tony and Marilyn own and operate a
print shop in Sacramento, Deason & Stirn Printing. Tony has served as a printing
industry counselor to the Sacramento Unified School District and Folsom Prison.
He is a member of Sacramento Elks Lodge No. 6. They belong to Westminster
Presbyterian Church in Sacramento; Tony has been a deacon and an elder.
He has enjoyed working with youth groups - Boy Scouts, Little
League, PTA and, of course, Masonic Youth Groups. He is a Member of Honor
of Bethel No. 292, International Order of Job's Daughters, and holds the
DeMolay Honorary Legion of Honor.
His hobbies and interests include golf, traveling, action and science
fiction films, Star Trek and good food!
He has a natural ability to lead, strength of character, is creative,
innovative, thoughtful, considerate, caring, sensitive and blessed with good
humor and an intense joy for life. He is personable and reaches out to people.
Most Worshipful Tony has been aptly called a "Mason's Mason."
He considers his election to serve the Grand Lodge of California, Free
and Accepted Masons, as Grand Master a privilege, honor and pleasure. He
accepted and fulfilled the responsibilities, challenges, excitement and joys of the
office of Grand Master with flair, focus, and determination with the strong
support and assistance from the Past Grand Masters, the 1997-1998 Grand
Lodges Officers, committeemen, the Grand Lodge office staff and, of course, the
grrreat class of 1998 Masters of the constituent lodges of this jurisdiction.
His background of valuable
experience combines with his devotion,
dedication, commitment and love of
Freemasonry to prove his theme for his term
of office: Freemasons United: An Indelible
Impression.

MASONIC HOMES CENTENN IAL CELEBRA TION
Saturday, October 10, 1998

On Saturday morning, October 10, 1998, Grand Master Anthony P.
Wordlow opened the Grand Lodge in due form in the Siminoff Temple Lodge
Room, at the Masonic Home in Union City, California, for the purpose of
rededicating the Masonic Home on the occasion of the 1OOth Anniversary of the
Masonic Homes of California.
Hundreds of Masons, their wives, families and friends were present as the
Grand Master, accompanied by the Grand Lodge Officers, led a procession to the
front steps of the SiminoffT emple. After welcoming remarks by Brother Kelly
Wiest, Administrator of the Union City Masonic Home, Stanley M. Cazneaux,
PGM, President of the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees delivered an address on
the Centennial year's theme of "Building a Future Upon a Century of Caring".
Brother David Francis Philips delighted the guests with several musical numbers,
including a moving presentation of the "Lord's Prayer".
The Grand Master, joined by the Deputy Grand Master, the Senior and
Junior Grand Wardens, the Grand Lecturer, and the Grand Chaplain, rededicated
the Masonic Homes of California in due and ancient form. The ceremonies
concluded with appropriate remarks by the Grand Orator and the Grand Master.
To commemorate the Centennial for future ages, a time capsule was
deposited, containing memorabilia appropriate to the occasion.
Following the Grand Chaplain's Benediction, the Grand Master and the
Grand Officers joined those in attendance for a delicious box lunch. Special tours
of the Masonic Home's modem facilities were conducted for the Masons and their
families visiting the Masonic Home.
The day's festivities concluded with a gala Banquet at the Stanford Court
Hotel in San Francisco, which included a guest list of former Trustees and
Administrators of the Masonic Home, as well as the current Masonic Homes
Endowment Board committee members and the Grand Lodge Officers. The
following is an oration given to those present by Very Worshipful Ralph H. Head,
Past Grand Treasurer, and former Trustee of the Masonic Homes Board of
California:

They arrived safe and sound at San Gabriel and there they would have
to wait
Until a brand new Home at Covina was built and ready to go
Then they moved into beautiful new buildings with acres of grass to
mow.

With the square, the plumb, and level our buildings have won great
awards"
And the Gods of the Operative Masons returned to their drawing
boards.

And the Gods of the Speculative Masons told them, "Read about
science and art
As you go to the public schools at Covina and learn what the teachers
impart."
And the children at the Home at Covina, the best kids we have in mind
Learned many of life's lessons from teachers of the finest kind
And when came the day eventually they were ready to fly on their own
Scholarships cleared the way to college among the very best that were
known.
Graduates have served in the armed forces and then entered life
contemporary
Becoming successful in marriage and business and as citizens we call
exemplary.
Way back when the Decoto Home was building, an idea was born that
would grow
It was properly called the Endowment Fund that all Masons would
come to know.
It started with twelve thousand dollars and its total has continued to
climb
Today it has reached great proportions and its benefits last a lifetime.
No Endowment funds are expended, but its income proceeds to mount
And is spent every month on our elderly and children where its benefits
can really count.

The Homes have many supporters besides many Lodge donations
unrivaled
Now add to these benefactors the names Lorber, Grider, Coil and
MacDonald.
And the Gods of the Speculative Masons said "We always learn from
the past
That the Greatest of These is Charity whose generosity continues to
last."
The Gods of the Operative Masons never wanting to be out done
Said "Look at all the buildings that Masonic Benevolence has done.

7

Then the Gods of the Speculative Masons came back to explain it again
They said "Masonry builds its temples in the hearts and minds of men."
The activities for seniors at Union City can be counted in so many ways
From trips to the local shopping malls to the ballpark of the Oakland
A's
There are arts and crafts for the creative and books with big type to
read
Provided by Lady Tigers who recognized an important need.
For those who want to shape up there's always the Grider Health
Quarter
Where a therapy pool makes it possible for the seniors to walk in water.
As we celebrate the one hundredth birthday of the Masonic Homes we
embrace
We can never pay enough homage to Trustees always hard to replace
There are many among the living but we look tonight at the past
To Brothers Wollenberg, Adams, and Sedam whose memory shall long
Jast.
We have designated buildings in their memory for the devotion and
love they bestowed
Toward the Residents at Union City and their esteem for the Masonic
code.
Our Masonic Homes have had fine leaders who pledged their best to
perform
Their duties as administrators and their work high above the norm
Brothers Brown, David, Ankney, Rose, Wiest, and Blaine
And others devoted to caring and whose commitment in our memory
remains.

I pause here to acknowledge other fine Administrators from the past,
Brothers Hartman, Eubank, Perry, and Herring. The reason I could not include
them in the verses was because I could find no words to rhyme with their names.

And the Gods of the Speculative Masons remind us these men had
strong beliefs
In what they learned in the Masonic teachings of Brotherly Love, Truth
and Relief.

But the Gods of the Speculative Masons and the Gods Operatively
inclined
Will never rest from their labors and their works be unalterably
entwined.

So the Gods of the Operative Masons said "There's always building
emerging"
So they built a new hall named Siminoff and a modem Lorber Skilled
Nursing
Apartments were added at Covina so our seniors could find a new
home
And kinds without home or Masonic relations would no longer have to
roam.

Then only the Great Architect shall praise us and only He shall blame
And no one shall work for money and no one shall work for fame
But each for the joy of working and each on a favorite separate star
With the working tools God gave us, the God of Things as they are.

So one hundred years are completed by our Homes of incomparable
worth
Built and maintained by Masons on the best of California's earth
And the Gods of the Operative Masons are happy to have played their
part
And the Gods of the Speculative Masons said "Charity comes from the
heart."
As Freemasonry in California has for nearly one hundred and fifty
years progressed
Our Masonic Homes have flourished and their goal to serve has never
digressed.

Before I recite the last two verses of this narrative based on a poem by
Rudyard Kipling titled "L'Envoi to the Seven Seas" I want again to acknowledge
the inspiration from his works. I may be preempting the Grand Master but as the
fonner trustee living who served the longest, I want to personally thank the trustees
past and present who have served with diligence, dedication and devotion for so
many years, the men and women who have worked for the Homes and provided
such tender loving care for the residents, and the thousands upon thousands of
Masons who have supported the Homes, morally and finally, for one hundred
years.
When the earth's last picture is painted and the tubes are twisted and
dried
When the oldest colors have faded and the youngest critic has died
We shall rest and, yes, we shall need it, Masons of charity, faith, and
hope
For the work we set out to do is nearly finished and we're now on that
slippery slope.

RESPONSE TO THE WELCOME TO DISTINGUISHED VISITORS

By H.L. Kathleen Kelly, Grand Royal Matron
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Distinguished Members of the Masonic
Family and Brethren of California Freemasonry:
Most Worshipful, on behalf of the distinguished v1s1tors
assembled here this afternoon, it is my great honor and privilege to thank
you for your most gracious and cordial welcome, and for the many
courtesies extended to us. Most Worshipful Tony, we applaud you for
your many efforts on behalf of Masonry this year. The warm personality
of yourself and your Lady Marilyn has won the hearts of the entire
Masonic Family. We are proud to be a part of that Masonic Family and

14

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

appreciate your invitation to attend the Public Opening of the Grand
Lodge of California.
As members of the Masonic Family we share your concern for
the loss of membership in all our orders. I remind the ladies that the
restriction of not asking a man to become a Mason does not apply to us,
and I urge each one of you to seek out those good men, encourage them
to join, and help the Masonic Fraternity rebuild for the future.
Sir Knight and Most Worshipful Tony-I can refer to the Grand
Master as Sir Knight because he became a member of the Order of the
Amaranth last year-we wish for you, and the many California
Freemasons attending this 149th Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge of California, a most hannonious, productive and successful
session.

MASON OF THE YEAR FOR 1998

David Walker, is in Salinas Valley State Prison, serving a nine-year term
on robbery and accessory convictions.

Brother Mike Reynolds
a Member of Las Palmas-Ponderosa Lodge No. 366
by: Vernon L. Gordon, PGM
My Brethren of the Grand Lodge, Members of .o ur Masonic
Family, and our distinguished guests:
Prior to this day, so far as my memory and somewhat limited
research reveals, only six men have been honored by our Grand Lodge
with the rank and title of"Mason of the Year." I have known each man
personally and can say to you that each were or are Masonic giants in our
Fraternity, and each are entitled to be addressed by the most honorable
titles this Fraternity has to offer.
By contrast, the Brother we honor here today has but one
Masonic title, and that is "Master Mason," but in my opinion he is a
Mason who is a giant in our society.
In his private life he is a professional photographer and a deepl_y
devoted family man. He comes from a Masonic family background. His
father was a 33 ° Scottish Rite Mason; his brother John is a Past Master
of Las Palmas-Ponderosa Lodge No. 366, and his mother is a longstanding member of the Order of the Eastern Star.
Our honoree is a member of Las Palmas-Ponderosa Lodge No.
366. He is a Senior DeMolay and has earned the following credits in that
Order: In 1959 he received the York Rite DeMolay Perpetual Trophy
Award· in 1960 the Sciots DeMolay Ritual Award; in 1962 the Scottish
Rite O~tstanding DeMolay A ward; he is the recipient of two Blue Honor
Keys, the Chevalier Degree, and in June of this year he was elect~ to the
DeMolay Legion of Honor, by the International Supreme Council.
Our Brother is not a representative of any legislative body.
However, he has represented the citizens of this State as well as some,
and far better than most.
On June 29, 1992, Kimber Reynolds, a beautiful example of all
about the youth of America, was standing on the sidewalk in
good
is
that
of Fresno, California, when two men tried to steal her
District
the Tower
purse. The first and most natural reaction is to resist. For that instinctive
reaction, Kimber was brutally murdered on the spot.
The trigger man, identified as Michael Davis, 25, was killed a
few days later in a gun battle with the police. The second man, Douglas

During the next few days, following the loss of their youngest

~hild and only daughter, Brother Mike Reynolds and his wife Sharon

retreated to the quiet of their home to try to understand this tremendous
void that had suddenly been cast into their family circle.
Both Mike and Sharon, however, became angered when they
learned that both of the perpetrators had criminal records, with that of the
triggerman being extensive. A month later Brother Mike gathered a few
friends and legal experts around the table and chairs on his patio.
Together they hammered out the "Three Strikes and You're Out" law.
Brother Mike is a strong advocate of recycling the resources of our land;
however, he believes that a certain element of our society cannot be
salvaged by human efforts.
Brother Mike took the draft of his proposed law to the proper
committees of the State Legislature where he found the doors of reason,
concern, and understanding to be shut in his face. Undaunted, Mike took
his cause to the streets of our State, in the form of a voter initiative, and
with much volunteer help and a great deal of his own personal resources
gathered enough signatures to place the issue on the State ballot.
In 1993, the kidnapping and murder of twelve-year old Polly
Klass, in Petaluma, also by a repeat felon, fanned the fires of public
outrage that Mike had created, resulting in the passage of Mike's "Three
Strikes" initiative by an overwhelming majority. By this time the State
Legislature, sensing the mood of the electorate, also passed the measure.
On January 1•1 of this year, Brother Mike's second anti-crime
law, 10-20-Life, also known as "Use a Gun and You're Done" became
law. Essentially this law provides that if you carry a gun during the
commission of a felony it adds l 0 years upon conviction, 20 years if the
gun is fired, and ifthe gunshot kills or seriously injures another person,
the prescribed sentence is life in prison.
There have been many articles in the "Public Speaks" section of
our newspapers praising Mike for his efforts. I share with you just one:
"Mike Reynolds is a man to be admired. He is fighting for the lawabiding citizens with his efforts to get convicted criminals off the streets
of California. He should be commended for all the work he has done to
ensure the safety of the people."
The most effective way to prevent crime is to make the
punishment outweigh the benefits. I hope Reynolds and others will

continue to strengthen the laws. The tougher America gets, the safer
we'll be.

The Grand Master raised the Masons present, and afforded Brother Mike
Reynolds the Public Grand Honors of Masonry, by the battery of three times three.

Have there been critics? Of course! Hundreds of the apologists
for these heartless criminals raised the cry that we need instead to try to
work with them and show them a better way of life. I applaud them for
the thought, and urge them to go into the target crime areas after dark, and
when they see the car with the smoked windows, cruising the street, pull
them over and admonish them that it is naughty to be out so late at night.
Go into the alleys of these target areas and invite whoever you meet to
join you at your house for dinner next Sunday.
Meanwhile, I will stand under the umbrella of Mike Reynolds'
efforts.

The Grand Master then announced that the ceremonies of the Public
Opening of Grand Lodge had been concluded, and he invited the audience to
remain forthe Devotional Service, which would be held in the Auditorium of the
California Masonic Memorial Temple.

What Brother Mike has done is consistent with what Masons
have done for centuries, taking a vigilant stand in the cause of freedom
and safety for our families. The historical records of our Fraternity show
that whenever and wherever societies were being formed, the Masons
were already there. I cite the following examples: When the City of
Fresno was chartered, Fresno Lodge No. 247 was already ten years old.
When the State of California was drafting its charter, this Grand Lodge
was fully-formed, chartered and operational. And when this great Union
was formed, the Masons were there fighting for and participating in the
framing of its Constitution.
In more recent times, in this decade, there was a cry for a
revolution against habitual criminals and their presence among us.
Brother Mike Reynolds, a Master Mason, was there.
We have been accused in some circles of being a cult. If that be
true, then we proudly admit to being an integral part of the greatest cult
the world has ever known, which we are pleased to call the United States
of America.
Most Worshipful, I commend you on your selection of Brother
Mike Reynolds to receive this honor, and for your decision to choose this
Masonic Family forum for the presentation. I also extend my thanks to
you for permitting me to participate in this the weaving of another golden
thread in the fabric of our Fraternal Order.
The Grand Master directed the Grand Marshal to conduct Brother
Reynolds to a place West of the Altar, and joined by the Deputy Grand Master, he
presented Brother Reynolds with a plaque recognizing him as "Mason of the
Year."

27

EULOGY
LESTER STAFFORD MCELWAIN
Grand Master 1971-1972
Born: January 1, 1910
Entered into Rest: September 28, 1998

Lester Stafford McElwain, a Master Mason in the truest and finest sense
of that honored title. He entered this world as a native son in San Mateo on New
Year's Day in 1910, the child of George W. and Ethel Dickson McElwain, and he
entered into rest on September 28, 1998 in Pleasanton, California at the age of
eighty-eight years, eight months and twenty-eight days.
What a full life and wonderful career he has experienced, and how
fortunate the Grand Lodge of California was to have had him serve as our 1061h
Grand Master.
Les well profited from the examples of hard work and industry
demonstrated by his parents, and started his business career as a young boy selling
morning newspapers at the Southern Pacific Railroad depot in San Mateo. He
attended his hometown public schools and spent countless after school and
weekend hours with the Boy Scouts of America learning their important lessons,
including love of family, high moral principles, and patriotism, ultimately
becoming one of the first Eagle Scouts in San Mateo County.
Les Mc'Elwain matriculated to Stanford University and joined the Phi
Sigma Kappa fraternity. This large-framed, six foot two inch, broad-shouldered
young man played on the Stanford Varsity basketball and handball teams, and
graduated with a Bachelor of Arts Degree in economics in 1931. His summers
were spent swinging a twelve pound sledge hammer driving stakes for a Southern
Pacific Company survey party and working with a shovel for a Pacific Gas &
Electric Company labor party while they were building dams to create
hydroelectric power.
Young Les then attended Stanford Law School; became a member of the
Phi Alpha Delta honorary legal fraternity; and graduated with the Degree of Juris
Doctor in 1934. Upon graduation, he was admitted to practice law in California
and joined an Oakland law firm specializing in trial practice. Les became a junior
partner in the firm, and after six years, in December, 1940, with World War II on
the horizon, he volunteered for active duty with the Intelligence Branch of the
United States Navy, in which he served until the war was over, being honorably
discharged with the rank of Commander in December, 1945.
LESTER STAFFORD MCELWAIN
PAST GRAND MASTER

January 1, 1910 - September 28, 1998

I

I

28

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

During the war, Les met and married Margrite Beadle Ludlow, and,
together, they produced three sons, Roderick, Malcolm and Douglas, all of whom
followed in their father's footsteps to become Eagle Scouts.
Les McElwain returned to the practice of law following the war and
became very active in numerous civic and service organizations, including service
as the Vice President of the California Junior Chamber of Commerce and as a
Director of the United States Junior Chamber of Commerce.
Brother McElwain received all three Degrees of Masonry in 1937 in
Yerba Buena Lodge No. 403 of Oakland (now Live Oak Lodge No. 61 ), and in
December of 1950 was elected and installed as its Master. In that same year he
became a member of the Oakland Kiwanis Service Organization where he served
for forty-five years, becoming its President in 1976 and three years later he was
elected a Lieutenant Governor in the International Kiwanis Organization.
Les became the Venerable Master of the Oakland Bodies of the Scottish
Rite in 1966, having been coronetted at the House of the Temple in 1957 as a
Scottish Rite Mason of the 33'd Degree. He later served the Oakland Bodies for
twenty-two years as its Chairman and Personal Representative of the Sovereign
Grand Inspector General in California.
Following his diligent participation as a member of numerous Boards and
Committees of the Grand Lodge, Most Worshipful Brother Lester S. McElwain
was installed as our Grand Master in October of 1971, the 52°d attorney to occupy
that office. His family, Boy Scout, Naval and legal training well prepared him, and
he will be remembered for his dynamic and innovative leadership which reflected
his determination of character, initiative, strength and wisdom, all while displaying
a smile and friendly personal attitude, together with emotional sensitivity
concerning those with whom he had close personal ties.
Past Grand Master Les McElwain left as a legacy his love for the
fraternity and the entire Masonic family. By his Edict on June 23, 1972, he
expressed his beliefthat there was great need for attention to be focused upon our
Country's courageous beginnings, its heritage of Masonic tradition, and the
manifold blessings which resulted, by proclaiming "Patriotism Week" to be
observed by Masons each year following the September 17th Anniversary of the
signing of the United States Constitution.
He urged meaningful support of our Youth Orders, and, as further
evidence of his belief in America, mailed a personal message to each of the
227,000 Masons in his California and Hawaii jurisdiction calling upon them to
participate in community public service.
In 1977 following the termination of his first marriage the previous year,
Les married a long-time family friend, Loretta Barksdale, the widow of Dr. Robert

j

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

29

Barksdale. Lori and Les had a happy nineteen years of marriage travelling
throughout the world and thoroughly enjoying themselves at Masonic, Kiwanis,
Stanford and other functions, and by receiving great pleasure from their respective
children and seven grandchildren. Sadly, Lori preceded Les in death in February
of 1996.
Les McElwainhas been a great benefactorto scholarship funds he created
through the California Masonic Foundation and the Kiwanis Foundation, and he
has been most generous in sharing.his worldly accumulations with the DeMolay
Foundation, the Masonic Homes of California, Stanford University, and numerous
other educational and philanthropic charities.
Most Worshipful Brother McElwain was also a member of the Aahmes
Temple of the Shrine, and as much as we feel the loss of this great man, it is fitting
that he was attending a Shrine Mason meeting when he suffered a massive stroke
which resulted in his death some ten days later.
We shall ever cherish in our hearts the memory of our departed Brother,
and commending his spirit to Almighty God, we trustingly leave him in the hands
of that Beneficent Being who has done all things well; who is glorious in His
Holiness, wondrous in His Power, and boundless in His Goodness; and it should
always be our endeavor so to live that we too may be found worthy to inherit the
kingdom prepared for us from the foundation of the world.

following his Installation were as follows:
It has been said that the more things change, the more they stay
the same. We near the 1501h Anniversary of Freemasonry in California
and over 275 years since modem Freemasonry was instituted in London,
England in 1717, and how so many millions of men have taken our
degrees and shared our camaraderie since that time. How different is the
world in which we now practice our ritual than the one which our brothers
lived at the beginning of the 20th century.
When I was young, and that seems so Jong ago, we were all
familiar with the radio program about a masked man and his Indian
companion who traveled the Southwest helping those in need. Even
without the strains of the William Tell Overture in the background and the
clouds of dust and the hearty "Hi ho Silver", you can all tell me, I am
sure, that I am describing the Lone Ranger, aided by his faithful
companion, Tonto.
Move ahead with me now about 50 years and picture a desolate,
desert landscaf>e and two metallic robots. They Jive in a world where
space travel is commonplace. The movie series Star Wars comes to mind,
doesn't it? Here a young man receives knowledge from an old knight and
goes out to do battle against the forces of evil, armed with a sword which
materializes in a ray of blue light. What do these two entertainments have
to do with Freemasonry in California? Well, it seems to me that that
entertainment is a reflection of what society dreams about. You all know
what happens at the end of the Lone Ranger episode and the end of Star
Wars - the men in the white hats win! Good triumphs over evil and we
all desire to be a part of that scenario. Stop and compare-th e costumes,
the landscape, the weapons, the mode of transportation - have all
changed but the basic plot is still the same.
As I made that comparison in my mind, I thought the characters
in both of those fantasies could surely have been Masons. Brotherly love,
relief and truth are no small part of each of these stories. It would seem
that the unchangeable things in which we believe are still a part of our
everyday world. Masonry tells its story through symbols, and perhaps
that masked man stands for Masonry in a previous time- hidden, at least

46

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

in part, from public view. Do we want to continue to have people ask
"Who is that masked man?" Perhaps the time has come for us to be more
vocal about our Craft, so that men who knock at the door for admission
are more knowledgeableofwha t they can rightfully know before entering
a lodge. Perhaps we need to be more like the young man in "Star Wars"
who after learning what "secrets" there were to be imparted, gained
confidence, went out to use what he had learned for the bettennent of
mankind.

Rights sought to ensure these rights. Along with the social aspect came
political stability for their favored position.

As I thought of the ways that Masonic ideas could be imparted
to these two stories and the dichotomy of the static and changing parts of
our world and our fraternity, one question kept coming into my thinking:
"Who do men join Freemasonry?" Is the answer to this question a static,
unchanging one or has the answer changed from th_at of our earliest
fonnal beginnings?
I may have raised another question in your minds. "Does it
matter as long as I know why I asked for admission?" I think it does and
by the way, could we all answer that question?
Our fraternity is concerned about membership. Well, we cannot
and should not change our standards and our goals. Maybe we can make
the fraternity more viable if we stop to consider what induces men to join
us. Maybe we can get a message out to those about us - those in our
communities, our work places, in our churches and our synagogues, on
the golf course or in the supennarket, or our neighbors next door to us at
our homes. Anciently, when the Craft was operative, men joined for
protection and freedom - protection from local taxation and servitude by
feudal barons and for freedom to move unrestricted from place to place
to practice their skills - the erection of cathedrals and palaces and other
types of edifices. With these privileges they became a somewhat elite
socjety and as such found it necessary to limit their numbers to ensure
their place in society.
Sometime in the 14111 century- 500 years ago - a profound
change occurred. The word "accepted" appears in the writing about
Freemasonry. Speculative Masonry was born and with it different
reasons to join the Craft. Buy why would the operative craft accept
unskilled members? For three reasons: financial, social and political.
The Accepted Masons were usually the patrons of their lodges and they
contributed to financial stability of the craft. These men were also of the
so called "upper class" and their membership satisfied the working man's
desire to achieve equal status - long before Constitutions and Bills of

But why would non-operative men desire to join the Craft? One
of the prime factors apparently was knowledge or education. It was
believed that Masons possessed esoteric knowledge of the ancient
mysteries and in an age when education was closely related to the church,
it gave men the opportunity to gain knowledge and freely exchange it
among the brothers.
Another factor undoubtedly was the social aspect of Masonry.
Before the advent of mass media, much social diversion was obtained by
the pomp and ceremony of the Masonic activities. In fact, Masonic ritual
well perfonned developed an entertainment value.
A final reason perhaps, was that of personal gain. Some felt that
this gain would be derived from personal contact and material
improvement. Many felt the gain would be moral and spiritual selfimprovement.
In summary, some used the Craft for material or worldly gain but
most sought membership for reasons in concert with truly Masonic goals,
intellectual or moral enlightenment.
Let's superimpose those ancient reasons upon contemporary man
and detennine if they are still valid, if we can go out among our
communities· and prove to those out there that we are worthy of
membership, if we can imbue them with the sense of camaraderie that
millions before us have enjoyed, that millions today still do enjoy
throughout the world. Four million of them. Two million of whom are
in our own United States.
First, there is no body of esoteric know ledge that can be obtained
from Masonry. In fact, you have all kinds of publications found in many
libraries, even on television and the Internet, which yield up most, if not
all, of Masonry's secrets and rituals. The know ledge of today's Masonry
deals with moral and spiritual matters, not esoteric knowledge and this
knowledge can be found in places other than a lodge if one chooses.
The factor of socialization has been changed by the change in
social climate. Men can have a social or intellectual interchange in a
variety of settings, free of societal or political pressure. In fact, several
quasi fraternal organizations provide social meetings in a setting not in
keeping with Masonic rules. However, although slipping in numerical
strength, our organization, the organization we call the Family of

47

48

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Freemasonry, still provides the finest in moral and altruistic values and
leadership.
The advent of mass media, specifically television, has caused
many inroads upon the time allotted to fraternal organizations and ours is
no exception. We constantly seem to be in competition for the time of
men. Oh, there still exists men who join Freemasonry for personal gain
but this is totally contrary to Masonic regulation and his absence from our
ceremonies and gatherings usually renders him ineffectual in helping or
harming the fraternity.
So, why then, today, do men join our organization? What is it
we have that they would like, if only they knew about us? Certainly we
do continue to "make good men better". Certainly we do offer beautiful
rituals encompassing the loftiest ideals man knows, that of a belief in one
Supreme Being by whatever name He may be known, in whatever way
we may worship Him. And we are His children, all of us. The fraternity
ofFreemasonsrecogn izesthat regardless of race, color or creed, all men
are brothers. All men are created under the great blue sky and live in
Freemasonry as one great fraternal organization. Oh, we have
differences, indeed we have. We may differ as to social ideas, we may
differ as to personal or religious concepts but we don't discuss these
things within our lodges. Discussion of politics and religion has no place
within the confines of a Masonic hall. We put aside our differences so
that we may join together in Freemasonry.
When I visited our nation's capital some years ago I was told by
a very prominent Mason that after his term as President of the United
States, Most Worshipful Harry Truman, Past Grand Master of Masons in
Missouri, frequently went to Masonic lodge and Masonic activities with
his counterpart, Chief Justice Earl Warren, Past Grand Master of Masons
in California, together with the late Senator and Brother Barry Goldwater
33 °, Grand Cross. These men had little in common politically and yet
they enjoyed each other's company and participated in the Masonic
fraternal and charitable events which are a part of their and our daily
existence. They knew, as we know, that Masonry is good, that it breeds
the social relationship and friendship, honor and integrity upon which this
nation was founded. We have only to recognize that in the early days it
was Washington, Franklin, Lafayette, John Hancock, so many signers of
the Declaration oflndependence and of our Constitution, together with 14
subsequent presidents of the United States and other distinguished
governmental, industrial and commercial leaders who were and are
members of our Craft, who recognized the worthwhile nature of

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

49

Freemasonry. They saw in it, as we see in it, the camaraderie of men,
where men of all walks of life can meet together as brothers, where men
can share the activities of the lodge and bring their families into the lodge
knowing that there will be integrity and honesty and dignity and lots of
fun as members and associates of our great organization, of what we call
the Family of Freemasonry, for our ladies and our kids are a part of us, a
part of our great family. We do wonderful things, we think, for others,
contributing $2 million each and every day, almost 3/4 of a billion dollars
each year for our Masonic sponsored charities in which we, as the family
of Masons ourselves, receive but a little part. We enjoy ourselves
together, but recognize that as long as one man is in want, we are all in
want; as long as one man is not free, we cannot be free.
I know I can talk forever, I suppose, and those of you who know
me know well I can do so because this is something I feel very strongly
about, the need to let others, you who are not Masons, you who have not
been in lodge very often, to let you know that we are doing something.
We are doing something good for you, for us, in bringing to the world
what we have and offering to share it with you because it is good as the
Great Father of us all has indicated, that which we have we should share
with our fellow men, and we have an awful lot to share.
So as we continue to this day into the future, we think ahead and
we plan aheap with our five-year plan, our Town Halls and our great
Professional Public Relations Program. We plan ahead knowing full well
that the future is uncertain, and indeed it is.
We can think of the past. We can plan for the future, but my
dear friends, "The Best of Times is Now- What a Wonderful World"
it is in which we live, today. Look about you, indeed we do. And as we
think about the future, may we use and live this day, this great and
wonderful time that God has given us. May we use the experience of the
past to plan and build for the future and as we do - may the Force be
with us.

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
Anthony P. Wordlow, Grand Master

Thirty nine years and twenty-seven days ago, a young man of two score
and three, was raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason in Tehama Lodge No.
3 in Sacramento.
The members of Tehama Lodge No. 3, true Masons all, took that young
man, me, nurtured me and provided me with Masonic mentors and heroes.
They gave me unlimited opportunities to serve, to learn about Masonry;
they allowed me to grow and expand my horizons even beyond my dreams.
They gave me a sense of purpose and direction, yet they encouraged me
to try my wings, to experiment, to be innovative. They gave me a sense of family.
They accepted me as I was. They have supported me without question, every step
of the way.
The Masons of Tehama Lodge No. 3, do what Masons do best ... they
care.
The Masons of Tehama No. 3, each of whom has signed his name in our
historic Miner's bible, those who have gone before me ... those who now serve
Masonry with me ... even those yet unborn, have made my Masonic odyssey
possible and shared it's promise with me.
To the Masons of Tehama Lodge No. 3, I am eternally grateful for
making Masonry come alive for me and to become my passion and joy in life.
Somehow it seems fitting that this grand old lodge, Tehama No. 3, one of
the five lodges to found the Grand Lodge of California, the lodge who gave the
second Grand Master, Most Worshipful John Tutt, now gives the second to last
Grand Master in this century.
It is written, to everything there is a season and a time to every purpose
under the Heaven.

The season of this Grand Lodge year is about to close. It is time for me
to account to you.
With humility, honor, pleasure, and deep fraternal love, I wish to convey
to you, my thoughts, reflections and impressions of the state of our kind and gentle
Craft and my concerns, hopes and prayers for the future of Masonry as we are
about to cross the threshold of time and space to the next century and the new
millennium.

Membership:
Friend-to-Friend has come to California.
This program has proven very successful in some of our sister
jurisdictions. It provides us with a graceful way to bring up the subject of
Masonry. The video and brochures are excellent.
Each lodge received the Friend-to-Friend materials early this year.
Preliminary reports indicate eighty-six candidates are directly attributed to the
Friend to Friend program.
Society once again seems to be seeking morality, integrity, responsibility,
concern for others, honesty, ethics, fairness, justice, respect for individual
freedoms. We hear about returning to family values.
Well, guess what? Masonry offers all that and more!
Men ... men of diversity, young men, educated men, family men, decent
men are studying about Masonry and seeking us out.
The Northern California Jurisdiction of DeMolay posted a membership
gain last year for the first time in thirty years. The Southern California Jurisdiction
has also seen a growth in members.
With Friend-to-Friend, more senior DeMolays, and the natural renewed
interest in Masonry coming at the same time our lodges must be ready to receive
new members.
But, are the lodges of California ready?
Ready to accept the new candidates who are knocking at our door? Are
we ready and willing to extend our hand in true Masonic fellowship?
Will we, our lodges, do the right thing?
Will we do what Masons do best ... care?
Care enough to properly investigate these men who will petition to
become a Mason? Care enough to provide comprehensive, continuing Masonic
education for their members?
Care enough to make Masons, not just members?
Care enough to provide Masonic heroes and mentors?
Care enough to encourage the new Mason and his family to become
involved, to allow him to grow in Masonry, to allow him to serve?
Care enough to provide excellent, relevant programs to include the
family?
Care enough to send our officers to the Officers' Management Seminars
and the Wardens' Retreats given by Grand Lodge?

Care enough to participate in service projects in our communities?
Care enough to respect, tolerate and celebrate diversity among our
members?
Care enough to appreciate traditions and the past, yet embrace new ideas
and the future?
Care enough to break the cycle of stagnation?
Care enough to march shoulder to shoulder, Freemasons united to cross
the intersection of time and space into the next century and the new millennium?
Care enough to do the right things?
The resounding answer must be affirmative.
Yes, not just in our Blue Lodges, but every organization within the
Masonic Family for we are a mirror to each other, we are all interdependent.
My Brothers, the alarm has sounded at our lodge room door and we are
finally answering it.
Our luxury of time has expired. Complacency, apathy, and benign neglect
must end. We must prepare our lodges to accept and welcome new Masons, but
the greater challenge is to recapture the excitement and renew the spirit of interest
of our current members.
In the year ending June 301\ 3842 California Masons died.
During the same twelve month period, 1381 Masons requested a dimit or
a withdrawal; I 027 were suspended for non-payment of dues.
We cannot change the fact of death. I pray those Masons who took a
dimit will affiliate in another jurisdiction or return.
But, my Brother, we must do something to stop suspensions.
We, our lodges, have failed those members who simply stopped paying
their dues.
Have we allowed Masonry to be so boring and dull that they no longer
care to be associated with us? Have we ignored them? Is their non-payment of
dues a cry for attention; a plea to make our lodges a haven for them?
Have we only sent them the required dues notices and letters?
Did we bother to send a caring member to ask why they have taken this
drastic step?
I am sorry to admit I think we have failed too many members.
We can, we should, we must and we will do better.

school in Sacramento County. She had transferred from another school that had
a good relationship with a Masonic Lodge. She wanted to work with a Masonic
Lodge at her new school. She contacted a local Mason who referred her to the
lodge nearest the school. Someone from that lodge told her they did not intend to
do anything for Public Schools Month. The Mason she spoke with didn't even
give her the courtesy of suggesting another lodge that might work with her.
By the time she called me, she was dismayed. I called the Master of
another lodge; even though his lodge had an ongoing relationship with a school.
Without hesitation, he told me they would be glad to work with two schools. They
put together an essay contest complete with monetary prizes. Masons attended the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

assembly when the students read their essays, and the winners proudly collected
their prizes.
Thanks to the Master who helped, the kids in that school know that
Masons care about them and their future. The principal once again has faith in us.
A binder of the survey sheets is available at a counter on "G" Floor,
please look through it. You will be inspired and amazed at the variety of ideas.
Two lodges even sent a collection of thank you letters from students .. . grrreat
reading!
Lodge Programs:
There have been many inventive, intriguing, innovative, exciting and
imaginative programs presented by lodges this year. From outstanding speakers
at meetings to celebrating a certain country each month with ethnic foods and a
report of Masonry in that country. Entertaining and informative.
Several lodges report visits with a sister lodge, exchanging ideas. Some
lodges have offered group trips, cruises, mystery trips; some have had community
projects involving many members and their families. One had a murder mystery
dinner with the officers putting on the show.
One lodge held an unveiling of a long-lost portrait of Past Grand Master
Earl Warren at their Constitution Observance night. It was an evening of living
history.
A lodge here in this city held a dinner dance in the cat house at the zoo.
The tigers, lions, panthers and leopards enjoyed the event too! I understand one
tiger moved his tail to the macarena. I'm sorry I missed that evening!
At various receptions and events honoring this Grand Master, the
decorations and entertainment have been special. Magic moments in Santa
Barbara, celebrity treatment at Hollywood, tartans and tigers, my own fan club and
a great tiger in San Diego, my own lodge homecoming, and so many others are
now cherished memories.
I wish I could report to you on each visit, they were all just grrreat.
My single regret this year is that I could not visit each lodge or Masonic
District.
We have been treated so well ... with many courtesies extended to us.
We are overwhelmed and very grateful.
Again, I requested a sample survey. The results are impressive. This
binder is available to review on "G" Floor. I suggest the junior officers check it
out and get some ideas for their lodges.

63

The Futµre of our Craft:
I am optimistic.
I feel we are turning the corner and entering upon a new Masonic
Renaissance, but I know that each Mason must give his unconditional love,
dedication, devotion, concern and passion to our kind and gentle Craft.
Yes, I am optimistic, but not naive. Masonry has had attackers since her
beginning.
Just a few years ago, Freemasons United finally answered those detractors
from the some factions within the religious community. Outside attacks will
continue. I pray we answer them.
Sadly, we have attackers from inside our lodges; these are the most
distressing.
We have had fifteen consolidations this year. Some of the consolidated
lodges will emerge stronger, more vibrant and will succeed. Some are doomed to
fail.
A few of our lodges are in dire circumstances.
Some lodges have a group of Past Masters, with an occasiona~ Secretary
in the mix, whose favorite mantra is, NO ... we have never done it that way
before.
They interfere ... even block the Master and officers at every turn. They
have a stranglehold and will not let go. They make it difficult for the officers to
even function, let alone make progress and do the right thing.
I was told by a Warden at one of the Wardens' Retreats that his Secretary
paid for the Retreat upon the vote of the lodge, but threatened him, "DO NOT
BRING BACK anything you learn to this lodge."
That is outrageous, yet it happens.
A few Secretaries grudgingly finally give the members a dues receipt
stating they are too busy, or the lodge doesn't pay enough. These lodges d~ not
attract new members, in most cases they do not participate in any community or
public school activities. Most do not send their officers to the Grand Lodge
Officers' Seminars or the Wardens Retreats.
Their lodge programs are boring, at best, or even non-existent. These
lodges complain they cannot get anyone to serve as an officer.
I wonder why?
Some of these lodges will fail, probably not ~ realizing they caused
their own demise.

64

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN1A

Some lodges are not good stewards of their finances, sometimes even
risking their buildings by not providing reserve funds for maintenance or repair.

Masonry in the future will evolve in ways we can't even imagine, but her
principal tenets will never ever change. May it be said in the future, just as now,
there goes a good man, for he is a Mason.

Unfortunately, there are brothers among us who have forgotten our basic
tenets of brotherly love, relief, and truth. Most of our problems are caused by
individual Masons or a small group stirring up trouble.
When a lodge is tom apart by its own members, it can take years to heal
the wounds and sometimes never. It can destroy a lodge. If it involves loss of
money, whether by outright theft or carelessness, it is most distressing.
We all know of instances where we have lost good Masons because they
will no longer put up with difficult people in their lodge. They simply walk away.
I would like to quote Prince Hall Past Grand Master, Most Worshipful Joe
Nicholas. He said at their recent Annual Communication, "All personal feelings
and problems should be left outside the lodge room. If a Brother cannot do this,
he should not be in Masonry."
The only solution to these problems is diligence on the part of each of us.

If we recognize a problem starting, we owe it to our lodge and the
brothers involved, to whisper counsel in the erring brother's ear and pray that he
listens. Grand Lodge does not want to become involved in any local lodge
problem, but when it is not solved, that is the inevitable. Some lodge officers and
some Inspectors have not paid attention causing larger problems.
It seems crystal clear. Some of our members should once again kneel at
the altar of Masonry and renew their obligation. Have they forgotten brotherly
love, relief, and truth? At times, it seems that way.

I would encourage each of us to step back, take a look at our own
behavior and take action to improve ourselves. After all, we sought to join
Masonry to become better than ourselves.

65

I would further caution our great fraternity, to not think so cheaply.
People seem to value more something they have to sacrifice to achieve.
In 1912, Frank Land's grandmother gave him fifty dollars to petition a
Masonic lodge. The other day at a seventy-five year pin presentation, the recipient
stated the fee was fifty dollars in 1923 when he applied. In both cases, the fee
amounted to about a month's salary.
At Christmas in 1958, my father-in-law gave me a check made out to
Tehama Lodge No. 3, suggesting I might wish to use the check to petition the
lodge.
That check was for one hundred and twenty five dollars, which was about
two weeks wages at that time.
Today, the application fee in my lodge is one hundred and thirty-nine
dollars. Hardly a financial sacrifice for most men.
Something is wrong with this picture. Even our dues structure in some
lodges is not in keeping with expenses. Of course, some lodges are blessed with
substantial funds, but others are not.

If we don' t address this issue in our lodges in the near future, we will
suffer the consequences.

The preceding is addressed to those who may have forgotten, to those who
think they are above Masonry's ideals and rules, to those arrogant trouble makers
that create our problems. I hope they heed my remarks.

May history write in her pages that together we have served Masonry we! I
and left an indelible impression. Most of these masters have provided their lodge
with good programs, have worked well with their officers, have communicated
with their members, have done the right thing and have included the family. They
care.

Masons.

Those lodges whose members care enough to do the right thing will grow
and prosper.
They will boldly march shoulder to shoulder, one by one, Freemasons
United into the future ... stronger, more dedicated, and more committed than ever
before.

I am privileged to serve with them; the class of 1998. We have shared our
lives with our common bond of Masonry; shared the joy of living and serving.

I 998 Grand Lodge Officers:
Every Grand Master who has preceded me considers his Grand Family as
the best ever. The difference with me is the fact that I KNOW it is the best ever.
To each of you, thank you for your service.
The Grand Lodge office staff has been a joy, we thank them for their
assistance and dedication.
A couple of weeks following my Third Degree in 1959, our Church group
went to Columbia State Park in the gold country to help repair a church that had
suffered a fire. We stayed with local church members.
Our host was an active Mason who had served as Master of his lodge and
was very involved in York Rite. We discussed Masonry as we worked, and in
front of his cozy fireplace in the evenings.
Everyone got together on the last day of our project for breakfast at the
church.
My host had told the minister, a Mason, that I had just been raised. They
managed to seat me between them at breakfast.
The minister casually remarked ..... "I hear you have traveled East".
Innocently, I replied, "Oh no, we went north to British Columbia on our
vacation."
They laughed so hard they almost fell off their chairs. I've never made
that mistake again.
But to those Masons I would reply now, "Yes, my brothers, I've traveled
Lodge is Tehama No. 3." But I would add that as the 1998 Grand Master,
my
East;
"I have literally traveled some ... east ... west ... north ... south, and loved
every step of the way."
There have been times our schedule was hectic, rushing from place to
place. But that's part of the job description of Grand Master, and it's the part we
love, being with the members as often as possible.
There are as many descriptions of Masonry as there are members. For
me, the top of the list is being with good people; for Masonry is people to me.
You, my Brothers, and members of your family.
I have tried to accommodate every lodge, every Master, every district,
every concordant and appendant body that has issued an invitation to me this year.
Regrettably, there are not enough days in the year.
Every function has been memorable, full of vitality and excitement.

67

In addition I have participated in many Third Degrees this year, including
several very special outdoor degrees. It's always a pleasure to welcome a new
candidate.
The Third Degree of my son, Chris, in Western Star Lodge No. 2 in Apri 1
of this year, shall ever be close to my heart. A father's dream come true.
Rose Parade Float:
I hope you saw our float at the Rose Parade this year. Thanks to t~e
continued hard work of that committee, it was once again a beauty; the old lady m
the shoe, or in our case a roller blade. We received a lot of media coverage.
Our lady in the shoe was Dollie Burke, a resident at Covina. Well, today
is her one hundredth birthday!
My heart is full as I address you this morning. It does not seem possible
it was a year ago that I knelt at that altar to take my vows as Grand Master; resting
my hands once again on Tehama's historic Miner's Bible.
But the time has come when I will tum the mantle of leadership to Mel
Nahin, I am confident that he will serve you well.
Is Masonry ready for the challenges of the future, have the leaders of this
year been good stewards of our Craft?
The answer is Yes!
In conclu~ion, I would like to thank my son and Masonic Brother, Chris,
and his lady Teri, for their support and taking over for us at our shop.
He made it possible for me and Marilyn to travel throughout the state
representing you.
My wife, Marilyn, made this year special with her untiring support_, ~er
enthusiasm, and love for our fraternity. She was always ready to go, always giving
more than any husband could ask. I thank her from the bottom of my heart.
As this year comes to an end, as all terms of office do, we are sad because
it was much too short; yet happy in the knowledge that we have done the best we
could.
I feel very good about this year.
I thank you, the Masons of California, and the members of Grand Lodge,
for the honor, privilege, pleasure, and thrill of serving you.
Thank you.

MASONIC YOUTH ORDERS MONTH
~qn:eas:

Brother Frank Sherman Land, a Master Mason with Louis G. Lower and eight other
young men in their teens founded the Order of DeMolay on March 15, 1919; and

~qn:eas:

Ethel T. Wead Mick organized the International Order of Job's Daughters on May 27,
1921 to band together girls for spiritual and moral upbuilding; to inspire a desire for
knowledge, to teach love of country and flag, love of home, respect for parents and
elders and reverence for the Holy Scriptures; and
Reverend Brother W. Mark Sexon formed the International Order of Rainbow for Girls
on April 6, 1922 to prepare girls for a brighter, better and more beautiful womanhood;
and
for the past three quarters of a century these outstanding Youth Orders sponsored by
dedicat~ Master Masons have inculcated great Moral and Masonic lessons which are

sadly lacking in today's society. These values taught at the Altar of every Masonic Youth
Order include among others: Filial Love, Reverence, Courtesy, Comradeship, Fidelity,
Oeanness, Patriotism, Faith, Hope, and Charity together with lessons which are found
in the Volume of the Sacred Law insure that young men and women who take them to
heart will not fail as they assume leadership positions in our society;
Now therefore, do I, ANTHONY P. WORDLOW, Grand Master of Masons in California

hereby

Jrodaim:

the Month of March as MASONIC YOUTH ORDERS MONTH; and I direct every constituent lodge in this jurisdiction to arrange appropriate programs to recognize the International Orders of DeMolay, Rainbow for Girls and Job's Daughters; further I direct
that this Proclamation be read at the February and March stated meetings of each lodge
and where practicable published in each lodge trestleboard or newsletter.
In Testimony whereof I have heretofor set my hand and caused the seal of the Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Maaons of California to be affixed this fifth
day of January, 1998.
Attest:

(/~~

CJ John L Cooper Ill

Anthony P. Wordlow
Grand Master

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

These funds provide the base for a much larger coordinated public
relations program involving, as appropriate, the other Masonic entities and many
of the concordant bodies. As now structured, the aggregate expenditures will be
approximately $850,000 over three years, of which only $97, 199 comes from
Grand Lodge. From all organizations participating, a Public Relations Oversight
Committee has been formed to select and monitor a public relations firm to
spearhead this effort.
My Brethren, we are the original promise keepers. We have agreed and
we have the last several years, reduced the amount of the budget. We have had a
surplus. As we have asked you to commit yourself to the 4.00% increase that our
Senior Grand Warden will discuss with you. We feel that we are honoring our
promise to you and you are honoring your promise to each other. And, indeed, you
are.
As your Deputy Grand Master, I pledge to you the continuation of
responsible and prudent management of the resources of Grand Lodge in 19981999. Working together we can use our limited resources to strengthen
Freemasonry in California, while supporting programs importantto our Lodges and
to our members.

Melville H. Nahin, Dq>uty Grand Master
Alvin J. Weis, Senior Grand Warden

SUBJECT:

1998-1999 GRAND LODGE BUDGET
1999-2000 GRAND LODGE PER CAPITA

Section 7040 of the California Masonic Cock requires the Deputy Grand Master to prepare the Grand Lodge
Budget for submission to Grand Lodge at the next Annual Communication. That budget is prepared with
the assistance of the f Jrand Lodge Committee on Finance and the Grand Treasurer. It is based on the~,.
capita adopted by Grand Lodge at the previous Annual Communication, and collected from each Lodge in
accordanl:e with the number of Master Masons canied on the rolls of the Lodge as of June 30 next preceding
the forthcoming Ann:iu Communication. At the 148"' Annual Communication in October, 1997, the pu
capita was established at SI 7.44 (including SI .30 for the California Fnema.ton magazine). As of June 30,
1998, our Lodges reported 99,798 Master Masons, less 2,599 whose dues had been remitted. The net
assessable membership is therefore 97, I 99 Master Masons (a 4,778 decline from a year ago).
1998-1999 Grand Lodge Budget:

The 1998 ~,.capita ofSl7.44 assessed on the basis of97,199 Master Masons is expected to produce a
revenue ofSl,695,151. This year's per capita revenue is S25,003 less than last year due to the decline in
assessable members. Miscellaneousim:ome, including interest income and the increased dividend from Nob
Hill Masonic Management, Inc., will result in a total estimated income ofSl,891,029.
The estimated expenses for 1998-1999 are Sl,561,019, plus Sl26,359 for publishing the Califomla
Frt1emason magazine. The difference between income and total expenses is S203,65 I, and is allocated to
Depreciation Reserve (S50,000}, and the Grand Lodge Endowment Fund (Sl53,651). The Grand Lodge
Endowment Fund was established to help offset future declines in membership, thus helping to soften the
impact of the rapid decline in membership expected to continue over the next few years. The Endowment
Fund was established by vote of Grand Lodge to smooth out future increased in per capita by reserving
some present income for future need.

109

REPORT OF THE SENIOR GRAND WARDEN

Per Capita Recommen dations for 1999-2000
Alvin J. Weis, Senior Grand Warden
In accordance with the principles outlined by our Deputy Grand Master,
the 1998-1999 Proposed Budget recommends that the per capita for 1999 be
established at $18.14, which is a 4% increase. With income expected to drop by
another 5.4% in 1999 from the continuing decrease in membership, this increase
will allow us to support programs important to our Lodges and to your Grand
Lodge, while funding a lesser budget in 1999-2000 than the current year. This
continued reduction in expenses reflects the reality we face, while also recognizing
the reality of the need to support important programs and activities. The proposed
1999 per capita includes an amount for the California Freemason magazine, our
prime means for communicating with all our members.
Grand Lodge will not continue the Special Grand Lodge Per Capita of
$1.00 for Professional Public Relation Use adopted at the 1997 Annual
Communication. Once again, the $1.00 special assessment was for 1998 only.
Please remember that the 1999-2000 Proposed Budget and the per capita
needed to fund it represents many hours of hard work to bring to you responsible
budget based on the best information possible. It represents a commitment to
prudently manage the resources of the Grand Lodge now, and for the future. And
it represents my commitment to you to continue to strengthen our beloved
Fraternity by ensuring a sound financial base of operations for your Grand Lodge.

REPORT OF THE GRAND TREASURER

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
The Grand Treasurer is charged with the responsibilityofreporting on the
financial condition of Grand Lodge and its related investments, businesses and
charities at the Annual Communication. This includes the financial statements,
operations and planning for Grand Lodge, as well as for those of the Masonic
Homes of California, the Masonic Homes Pooled Income Fund, the California
Masonic Retirement Plan, the California Masonic Foundation, the California
Masonic Memorial Temple, and the Nob Hill Masonic Management, Inc. (please
refer to the opinion letters attached in the annual Proceedings by your auditors).
The reports and comments of the Grand Treasurer are based on the official
examinations and statements of our Certified Pub lie Accountants whose reports are
an integral part of the Grand Treasurer's Report. Their audits cover the years most
recently ended and contain both a complete statement of assets under management
as well as a record of the income and expenses for the period.
As delegates to the Annual Communication, you are, in effect, the
shareholders of Grand Lodge and its entities. You are encouraged, and it is
recommended therefore, that you read and review this report. Your observations
are appreciated. •
Both the Grand Lodge and each of its related entities are in sound
financial condition. The extent and size of our investments, businesses, and most
importantly our charitable activities were financially possible in large measure due
to the generosity of prior generations. To ensure the future of these fine programs,
we must continue our Masonic tradition of financial support.
Respectfully submitted,
Thomas C. Holm, Grand Treasurer

7. PENSION PLAN:
The Grand Lodge, Masonic Homes, the Temple and Nob Hill sponsor a defined benefit pension
plan (the Plan) that covers all employees. Benefits are to be paid to eligible employees at
retirement based primarily upon years of service and compensation levels near retirement.
Contributions to the Plan reflect benefits attributed to employees' services to date, as well as
services expected to be provided in the future. Plan assets consist primarily of common and
preferred stock, investment-grade corporate bonds and US. government obligations.
Pension expense of the Plan for the year ended October 31, 1998, includes the following
components:
Service cost of the current period
Interest cost on the projected benefit obligation

To the Board of Trustees of
Masonic Homes of California:
We have audited the accompanyin g statements of financial position of Masonic Homes of
California (a California nonprofit corporation) as of June 30, 1998 and 1997, and the related
statements of activities and changes in net assets and of cash flows for the years then ended. These
financial statements are the responsibility of Masonic Homes of California management Our
responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements based on our audits.
We conducted our audits in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards. Those
standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about
whether the financial statements are free of material misstatement. An audit includes examining.
on a test basis, evidence supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. An
audit also includes assessing the accounting principles used and significant estimates made by
management . as well as evaluating the overall financial statement presentation. We believe that
our audits provide a reasonable basis for our opinion.

In our opinion. the financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material respects, the
financial position of Masonic Homes of California as of June 30, 1998 and 1997, and the results of its
activities and changes in net assets and its cash flows for the years then ended in conformity with
generally accepted accounting principles.
Our audits were made for the purpose of forming an opinion on the basic financial statements
taken as a whole. Supplementa ry fund information included in the accompanyin g statements of
financial position and statements of activities and changes in net assets is presented for purposes of
additional analysis and is not a required part of the basic financial statements. This information
has been subjected to the auditing procedures applied in our audits of the basic financial
statements and, in our opinion, is fairly stated in all material respects in relation to the basic
financial statements taken as a whole.

San Francisco, California,
September 4, 1998

in perpetuity

Masonic Homes of California (Masonic Homes), a California nonprofit corporation, administers a
home for adults at Union City, California, and a home for adults and children at Covina, California.
The homes are supported by The Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the state of
California (the Grand Lodge) and members of the Masonic Fraternity in California.
The adult residents who enter Masonic Homes are required by a life-care agreement to assign all of
their assets to Masonic Homes in exchange for continuing care for the remainder of the their lives.
In the event that a continuing care contract is canceled by the resident through withdrawal within
the first 90 days of residency, the resident is entitled to a pro rata refund of all his or her assigned
assets. No assigned assets were subject to refund at June 30, 1998 and 1997.
Masonic Homes is subject to statutory reserve requirements. At June 30, 1998 and 1997, Masonic
Homes' reserves as calculated in accordance with Continuing Care Contract Statutes of the
California Health and Safety Code were in excess of such requirements.
Masonic Homes annually calculates the present value of the net cost of future services and the use
of facilities to be provided to current residents and compares that amount with the present value of
related anticipated cash inflows. II the present value of the net cost of future services and the use
of facilities exceeds the present value of related anticipated cash inflows, a liability is recorded with
a corresponding charge to income. Masonic Homes has determined, using a discount rate of
6 percent, that no accrual for the obligation to provide future services and use of facilities to current
residents was required at June 30, 1998 and 1997.
TilX-Exempt Status
Masonic Homes is a nonprofit corporation as described in Section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue
Code and has been granted tax-exempt status by the Internal Revenue Service and the California
Franchise Tax Board.

General and Uirthquake Funds- Resources are available to support the operations of the

Pmnanent Endowmmt fund-Ordinances of the Grand Lodge provide that no portion of
the principal of the Permanent Endowment Fund shall be expended for any purpose, and
income from the principal shall be used only for the maintenance and general operation of
Masonic Homes. Therefore, the historical dollar value of contributions made to the
Permanent Endowment Fund are permanently restricted, while the accumulated
investment earnings and net market appreciation are temporarily restricted until the
associated donor restriction on use has been satisfied.

Union City fund-The Union City Fund provides for the operation, rehabilitation.

preservation and betterment of the home at Union City, as deemed necessary. The Union
City Fund was established with bequests from the estates of Hugo M. Lorber and
Florence V. Grider, which provided that the amounts be used for the home for adults at
Union City, California. Because the purpose restrictions related to the principal of the
bequests have been met and no donor restrictions were placed on the investment earnings
and net market appreciation from the principal. the net assets of the Union City Fund are
unrestricted. The net assets of this fund have been designated by the Board for construction

Restricted Trust Funds- Restricted Trust Funds include bequests made for various
restricted purposes and various irrevocable trusts of which Masonic Homes is the trustee.
The historic dollar value of bequests is permanently restricted for investment in perpetuity,
while the earnings &om the bequests are either restricted for scholarship purposes or
available for unrestricted use. Masonic Homes' interest in the irrevocable trusts is restricted
as to time. Once received, the contribution is temporarily restricted or unrestricted
according to the donor stipulations.

Cash and Equivalents
Cash equivalents consist of highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or
less. Cash and equivalents, for purpose of the statement of cash flows, include unrestricted and
restricted cash.
Restricted cash includes residents' accounts at Union City and Covina, which comprise
unexpended portions of monthly allowances made to residents and a construction retainer account
related to the construction at the home for adults at Union City, California. For the residents'
accounts, a corresponding liability for such agency funds is included in accounts payable and
accrued liabilities.

3. INVESTMENTS IN MARKET ABLE SECURITIES:

1. ORGANIZATION:

Fixed income mutual funds

The Masonic Homes Pooled Income Ftind (the Fund) was organized in 1974 as a trust Donors
contribute irrevocable remainder interests in property while retaining an income interest for life for
one or more beneficiaries. The donors are entitled to a tax deduction equivalent to the present
value of the remainder interest in the property contributed to the Fund.
The property transferred by a donor is held in trust by the Board of Trustees of the Fund and is
commingled with and invested and reinvested with other properties transferred to the Fund. All
dividend and interest income of the Fund is distributed quarterly to the income beneficiaries, based
on their proportionate share of the Fund. Upon the death of each donor's last income beneficiary,
the remainder interest is distributed to Masonic Homes of California, a charitable corporation.

2. SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES:
Basis of Presentation
The Fund acts in the capacity of an agent on behalf of the life and remainder beneficiaries of the
Fund. The accompanying financial statements include the activities and trust principal for the
period presented.
Investments
Investments in marketable securities are stated at estimated fair market value based on quoted
market prices. Property received through gifts is recorded at estimated fair value at the date of
donation. Gains or losses resulting from sales or market fluctuations are recognized in the period
such sales or market fluctuations occur.
Income Taxes
The Fund is administered in conformity with all provisions of the Internal Revenue Code, Internal
Revenue Regulations and Rulings, procedures and guidelines covering pooled income funds . The
Fund pays no income tax on income distributed to the income beneficiaries nor on long-term
capital gains. Applicable federal and state income taxes are paid by the beneficiaries on their share
of distributed income.
Use of Estimates
The preparation of financial statements in conformity with generally accepted accounting
principles requires management to make estimates and assumptions. These estimates and
assumptions affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities and disclosure of contingent assets

We conducted our audit in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards. Those
standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable ~~urance about . .
whether the financial statements are free of material misstatement. An audit mcludes exanurung,
on a test basis, evidence supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. An
audit also includes assessing the accounting principles used and significant estimates made by
management, as well as evaluating the overall financial statement presentation. We believe that
our audit provides a reasonable basis for our opinion.
In our opinion. the financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material r~~· the
financial position of California Masonic Foundation as of June 30, 1998, and the changes m 1ts net
assets and its cash flows for the year then ended in conformity with generally accepted accounting
principles.
