CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION
NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
JUNE 30, 1998

1. ORGANIZATION AND SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES:

161

• Temporarily restricted net assets represent contributions whose use by the Foundation is
limited by donor-imposed restrictions. The restrictions can be fulfilled by incurring expenses
satisfying the restricted purposes.
• Permanently restricted net assets are restricted by the donor for investment in perpetuity.
These permanently restricted net assets consist of original corpus.
The Foundation categorizes its financial position by fund based upon donor restrictions as follows:

Organization
The California Masonic Foundation (the Foundation) was established in 1968 by the Grand Lodge
of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California (the Grand Lodge). The Foundation is
formed as a nonprofit charitable corporation to further all phases of education, charity and science.
Use of Estimates
The preparation of financial statements in conformity with generally accepted accounting
principles requires management to make estimates and assumptions. The estimates and
assumptions affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities and disclosure of contingent assets
and liabilities at the date of the financial statements and the reported amount of revenues and
expenses during the reporting period. Actual results could differ from those estimates.
Ca.sh and Ca.sh Equivalents
The Foundation considers all highly liquid investments with an initial maturity of three months or
less when purchased to be cash equivalents.
Investments
Investments in marketable securities are stated at fair value and, to the extent that management
intends to hold such investments for more than one year, are classified as noncurrent assets. Gains
or losses that result from market fluctuations are recognized in the period in which such
fluctuations occur.
Equipment
Equipment, which consists of data processing equipment and furniture and fixtures, is carried at
cost and is depreciated on the straight-line method over three and five years, respectively.
Net Asset Categories
The Foundation reports information regarding its net assets and activities according to three classes
of net assets: unrestricted, temporarily restricted and permanently restricted.
• Unrestricted net assets are available for support of the Foundation's programs and
supporting services.

General Fund-Resources are available for support of Foundation programs and
supporting services.
Masonic Model Student Assistance Fund-This fund was established by the Grand Lodge
to provide financial support to ongoing programs aimed at assisting studentll in
furthering their academic careers. All amounts in the fund are donor-restricted
specifically for use in these programs.
Scholarship Funds
Amaranth Fund- Resources are restricted by a trust agreement with the Amaranth
Homes of California. The agreement specifies that principal is to be invested and the
income is to be used to provide educational grants to women under age 21. Net assets
of $366,433 are restricted.
Wade-Amaranth Fund-This fund was established by a bequest from W.0. Wade.
Income from the fund is to be expended for scholarships and other like purposes for
female students seeking degrees from educational institutions in California. Net
assets of $1,-096,258 are restricted.
F.M. Robinson Memorial Fund-This fund was established by contributions from
Mrs. F.M. Robinson. The principal of the fund cannot be expended. Income from the
fund is to be expended for scholarships. Net assets of $74,790 are restricted.
Harry Walker Lister Scholarship Fund-This fund was established from a
contribution of a variable appreciable life insurance policy. The policy was redeemed
during 1988. The principal of the fund cannot be expended. The income of the fund
can only be used to fund scholarships. Net assets of $340,373 are restricted.
Starr King Lodge No. 344 Scholarship Fund-This fund was established by the Starr
King Lodge from the Robert Swartz Charitable Trust. The principal of the fund
cannot be expended, and the income of the fund is to be expended for scholarships for
the benefit of Starr King members, their children, grandchildren, nieces and nephews.
Net assets of $64,684 are restricted.
MacKechnie Fund-This fund was established by a bequest from Jack I. MacKechnie.
The principal of the fund cannot be expended and is held by the Grand Lodge. The
income of the fund is transferred to the Foundation to be expended for scholarships
for needy high school graduates of proven outstanding athletic achievement. Net
assets of $22,251 are restricted.

middle-class young men and women. Net assets of $158,156 are restricted.
Brotherhood Lodge Fund-This fund was established by the Brotherhood Lodge

3. FEDERAL EXCISE TAX:

Chowchilla Masonic Scholanhip Fund-This fund was established by the Chowchilla
Lodge through a cash donation. The principal cannot be expended, and income of the
fund is to be expended for scholarships for deserving graduating seniors at
Chowchilla Union High School and/ or Le Grand High School Net assets of $45,518
are restricted.

The Foundation is a not-for-profit organization that is exempt from income tax under
Section ~1(c)(3)_ of th~ Internal Re~enue Code (the Code). The Foundation is classified as a private
fo~dation and IS subject to ~ exrue tax on net investment income, including realized gains, as
defined by the Code. Accordingly, federal excise tax has been recognized in the amount of $12,300
for the year ended Jwie 30, 1998.

Soquel-Pajaro Masonic Lodge for T. Fenton Ham Scholarship Fund-This fund was
established by the Soquel-Pajaro Lodge through a cash donation. The principal of the
fund cannot be expended, and the income of the fund is to be expended for
scholarships for engineering students who are accepted into an Engineering Council
for Professional Development (ECPD} accredited engineering program. Net assets of
$255,153 are restricted.

4. COMMITMENTS:

Warren J. Blomseth Scholarship Fund-This fund was established by contributions
from Warren J. Blomseth. The principal of the fund cannot be expended. Income
from the fund is to be expended for scholarships. Net assets of $160,261 are restricted.
Earold H. Barton and Merna L Barton Memorial Scholarship Fund-This fund was
established by a bequest from Earold H. Barton and Merna I. Barton. The principal of
the fund cannot be expended, and the income is to be expended for scholarships for
worthy candidates selected by the Foundation. with preference to children or
grandchildren of Master Masons preparing for a career in education who participate
in extracurricular activities and attend summer school Net assets of $333,574 are
restricted.

Scholarships are renewable annually through the completion of four years of education if the
applicant meets renewal criteria and is approved for renewal by the committee. Total potential
renewals for previously awarded scholarships for the 1998/1999 school year are $266,000. Total
potential renewals for school years beyond 1998/1999 are $730,000.

We have audited the accompanying statements of financial position of California Masonic
Memorial Temple (a California not-for-profit corporation) as of June 30, 1998 and 1997, and the
related statements of activity and changes in net assets and cash flows for the years then ended.
These financial statements are the responsibility of the organization's management. Our
responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements based on our audits.
We conducted our audits in accordance with generally accepted auditing standards. Those
standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about
whether the financial statements are free of material misstatement An audit includes examining,
on a test basis, evidence supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. An
audit also includes assessing the accounting principles used and significant estimates made by
management, as well as evaluating the overall financial statement presentation. We believe that
our audits provide a reasonable basis for our opinion.

In our opinion, the financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material respects, the
financial position of California Masonic Memorial Temple as of June 30, 1998 and 1997, and the
changes in its net assets and its cash flows for the years then ended in conformity with generally
accepted accounting principles.

1. ORGANI ZATION AND SUMMAR Y OF SIGNIFIC ANT ACCOUN TING

POLICIES:

Organiza tion
California Masonic Memorial Temple {the Temple) is a nonprofit organizati
on. According to the
Articles of Incorpora tion, income from the Temple, less operating expenses
and reserves, is to be
transferre d to the Endowme nt Fund of Masonic Homes of California {Masonic
Homes) and/ or the
California Masonic Foundatio n (the Foundatio n). The amount and proportion
s of such
distributio ns are at the sole discretion of the Board of Trustees.
Use of Estimates
The preparatio n of financial statements in conformit y with generally accepted
accountin g
principles requires managem ent to make estimates and assumptio ns. These
estimates and
assumptio ns affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities and disclosure
of contingen t assets
and liabilities at the date of the financial statement s and the reported amount
of revenues and
expenses during the reporting period. Actual results could differ from those
estimates.
Cash and Cash Equivalen ts
The Temple considers all highly liquid investmen ts with original maturities
of three months or less
when purchased to be cash equivalent s.

Temporar ily restricted net assets represent contributi ons whose use by the
Temple is limited by
either donor-imp osed stipulation s or from circumstan ces surroundi ng the
receipt of the
contributi on that make clear the donor's implicit restriction on use. These
restriction s may either
expire by the passage of time or be fulfilled by actions of the Temple pursuant
to those stipulatio ns.
Collection of Books and Nonvalua ble Contribut ions
The Temple library contains a book collection of approxima tely 10,000 volumes.
The collection
includes approxima tely 8,500 works on Masonic and related philosoph ic topics
and nearly 1,500
non-Maso nic volumes, including historical, religious, scientific, political and
biographi cal works.
Fewer than 50 works in the collection could be considere d rare. The Temple
museum contains
donated items such as works of art and historical treasures contribute d by
members of the Free and
Accepted Masons of California . The Temple museum collection contains donated
items from the
membersh ip of The Masonic Fraternity in California and elsewhere. Artifacts
in the collection
include works of art, Masonic regalia and numerous historical pieces. The
Temple does not
recognize books and nonvaluab le contributi ons in its financial statements .
The Temple does not
recognize these assets as contributi ons, as they are protected and preserved
, held for public
exhibition and subject to an organizati onal policy that requires proceeds from
the sale of collection
items to be used to acquire other items for collections. Accessions and deaccessio
ns of books and
nonvaluab le contributi ons during 19'17 and 1998 were not significant.
Revenue Recogniti on
Contribut ions are recognize d when received or unconditio nally pledged.

Investme nts
Investmen ts in marketabl e securities are stated at estimated fair value based
on quoted market
prices. Investmen ts received through gifts are recorded at estimated fair market
value at the date
of donation.
Property and Equipmen t
Property and equipmen t are carried at cost and are depreciate d on the straight-li
ne method over
the following estimated lives:
Buildings and improvem ents
Equipmen t
Furnishing s

5-50 years
5-10 years
3-20 years

Functiona l Expenses Allocation s
Expenses, such as depreciati on, supplies, travel, personnel and occupancy
costs, are allocated
among program services and general and administra tive services classificat
ions on the basis of
estimates made by the Temple's manageme nt.
Tax-Exem pt Status
The Temple is a nonprofit corporatio n as described in Section 501(c){3) of the
Internal Revenue
Code and has been granted tax-exemp t status by the Internal Revenue Service
and the California
Franchise Tax Board. As discussed in Note 5, the Temple is subject to certain
federal excise taxes.

4. OPERATING LEASES:
Nob Hill has an operating lease with the Temple, expiring June 30, 2003, under which Nob Hill
manages the Temple auditorium. exhibit hall, parking garage and various rental properties. Under
the terms of the lease, Nob Hill is required to pay rent equal to 90 percent of the gross rental
revenues in excess of $860,000 per year, adjusted annually for inflation. until Nob Hill has paid
$240,000, after which payment shall be one-third of the remaining gross rental revenues.
Beginning in 1998, the aggregate rent calculated under this formula is subject to a limit that
increases with inflation. The aggregate rent for the year ended June 30, 1998, is limited to $400,000.

Organization

Lodge). It operates the California Masonic Memorial Temple (the Temple) auditorium. parking
garage, exhibit hall and various rental properties under the terms of an operating lease with the

Standards (SF AS) No. 109, "Accounting for Income Taxes."

5. OPERA TING LEASES:
The Compa ny has an operat ing lease with the Temple
, expirin g June 30, 2003, under which the
Compa ny manag es the Templ e auditor ium. exhibit
halL parkin g garage and variou s rental
proper ties. Under the terms of the lease, the Compa
ny is required to pay rent equal to 90 percen t
of the gross rental revenu es in excess of $860,000
per year, adjuste d annual ly for inflatio n, until the
Compa ny has paid $240,000, after which payme nt
shall be one-th ird of the remain ing gross rental
revenu es. Beginn ing in 1998, the aggreg ate rent calcula
ted under this formul a is subjec t to a limit
that increas es with inflation. The aggreg ate rent for
the year ended June 30, 1998, is limited to
$400,000.
For the year ended June 30, 1998, adjuste d gross rental
revenu es, as define d in the lease agreem ent,
were $2,153.878, which genera ted $400,000 in lease
payme nts. For the year ended June 30, 1997,
adjuste d gross rental revenu es, as defined in the lease
agreem ent, were $1,708.519, which genera ted
$418,384 in lease payme nts.

.

The Compa ny has a manag ement agreem ent with
AMPCO Auto Parks, Inc. (AMPCO) for the
operat ion of the parkin g garage. Under the terms
of agreem ent, the Compa ny receives all receipt s
collect ed by AMPC O. The Compa ny pays AMPC
O a manag ement fee of $1,500 per month plus
1.5 percen t of the net revenu e, as defined , of the garage
. Net receipt s under the agreem ent were
$801,056 and $703.342 for 1998 and 1997, respectively.
The agreem ent can be termin ated by either
party with 30 days notice.

L DESCRI PTION OF THE PLAN:
General
The Californi a Masonic Retireme nt Plan (the Plan) is a defined benefit
plan that provides
retireme nt benefits for substanti ally all employe es of Masonic Homes
of Californi a, Masonic Grand
Lodge and Compon ent Organiza tions (collectively, the Grand Lodge)
who have reached the age
of 21 and complete d one year of service. It is subject to the provision
s of the Employe e Retireme nt
Income Security Act of 19'74 (ERISA). Participa nts should refer to
the Plan's documen ts for a more
complete descripti on of the Plan.
Employe es with five or more years of service are entitled to annual
pension benefits beginnin g at
normal retireme nt age (65). For service prior to January 1, 1993, the
annual retiremen t benefit at
normal retireme nt is equal to 2 percent of the average annual compens
ation earned during the five
calendar years prior to January l, 1993, times years of service through
1992. For service after
Decembe r 31, 1992,. the annual retireme nt benefit at normal retireme
nt is equal to 2 percent of the
compens ation earned in each full and partial year of service.
The Plan permits early retiremen t at ages 55 to 64 for participa nts
with a minimum of 10 years of
service. Married employee s may elect to receive their pension benefits
in the form of a joint and
suzvivor annuity. U employee s terminate before renderin g five years
of service, they forfeit the
right to receive the portion of their accumul ated plan benefits attributa
ble to the Grand Lodge' s
contribut ions.

U an active employe e dies at age 55 or older, a death benefit equal to the
value of the employe e's
accumul ated required contribut ions is paid to the employe e's beneficia
ry. A death benefit will also
be payable to an employe e who dies after accumula ting five years
of service. Active employee s
who become disabled and totally incapacit ated may receive an annual
disability benefit that is
equal to the normal retiremen t benefits they have accumula ted as of the time
they become disabled,
reduced for early withdraw al Disabilit y benefits are paid until normal
retiremen t age, at which
time disabled participa nts begin receiving normal retiremen t benefits.
The assets of the Plan are maintain ed in a trust establish ed pursuant
to a trust agreemen t between
the Grand Lodge and Wells Fargo Bank, N.A
Funding Policy
Prior to January l, 1982. contribut ions to the Plan had been made
by participa ting employe rs and
employe es based upon a percentag e of covered payroll. Effective
January l, 1982. the requirem ent
for employe e contribut ions was terminate d. The Grand Lodge contribut
es actuarial ly determin ed
amounts sufficien t to amortize the unfunde d present value of accumul
ated plan benefits over the

-4-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFO RNIA

193

working lifetime of the active participa nts. The Plan complies with
the minimum funding
requirem ents of ERISA.
Plan Termina tion
Although the Grand Lodge has no intention to terminate the Plan,
it has .the ability to. do so.
Should the Plan terminate at some future time, its net assets generally
will not be available on a pro
rata basis to provide participa nts' benefits. Whether a particula r
participa nt's accumula~ plan
benefits will be paid depends on both the priority of those benefits
and th~ level of benefits.
guarante ed by the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporat ion (PBGC)
at that time. Some ~efits may
be fully or partially provided for by the then-exis ting assets and the
PBGC guaranty , while other
benefits may not be provided for at all.
Informat ion about the plan agreemen t, the vesting and benefit provisiom
, and the PBGC s benefit
guaranty is available from the Grand Lodge.
Investm ent Managem ent and Adminis trative Expenses
Investme nt managem ent and administ rative expenses are principal

ly paid by the Plan.

2. SUMMA RY OF SIGNIFI CANT ACCOU NTING POLICIE S:
Basis of Accounti ng
The financial statemen ts of the Plan are prepared based upon generally
accepted accountin g
principle s.
Use of Estimate s

principle s requires managem ent to make estimates and assumpt iom
that. aff~ the reported
amounts of assets and liabilities and disclosur e of continge nt assets
and liabilities at the date of the
financial statemen ts and the reported amounts of additiom and deductio
ns during the reporting
period. Actual results could differ from those estimates .

Investme nts
Investme nts in marketab le securities are stated at fair value based
on quoted market prices or net
asset values as reported by the asset custodian .
Income Recognit ion
Securitie s transacti om are recorded as of the trade date. Interest income
is recorded on an accrual
basis. Dividend s are recorded when received.

REPO RT OF THE GRAN D SECR ETAR Y

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M o/Cali fornia

:

Most Worshipful, and Brethren,
This is my seventh report to you as Grand Secretary. Mindf
ul of our very
full schedule, I will only cover a few items briefly. My
complete report will be
printed in the 1998 Proceedings.
First, our membership dipped below the 100,000 mark for
the first time
since 1922. In 1922, at the 73rc1 Annual Communication,
Grand Secretary John
Whicher reported that we had 93, 179 members. The next
year, in 1923, at the 74lh
Annual Communication, he reported that we had 100,283
members. The numbers
increased steadily after that, until we began our declin
e in 1966, after having
reached a peak of244 ,586 in 1965. In 1998 we have 101,17
3 members as of June
30, 1998, and when those whose dues were remitted by their
lodges are subtracted,
we had 98,376 who paid dues to our lodges, and for whom
the lodges paid a per
capita. The figures speak for themselves.
Secondly, on a more positive note, the combined
Secretaries'
Administrative Workshops and the Officers' Management
Workshops were well
attended, and feedback from those attending was very positiv
e. Six workshops
were offered in different parts of the jurisdiction, and
the teamwork between
secretaries on the one hand, and other lodge officers on the
other, was evident. Six
more workshops have already been announced for ~e next
Grand Lodge Year,
with the first beginning in November, and the last next
July. Secretaries'
Associations also continued to be an important communicat
ion link between the
Grand Lodge Office and our lodge secretaries. Ten are now
active, and an eleventh
one is on the way to being revived in the Fresno area. I
met with each of these
associations at least once, and on more than one occasion
with several.
Nineteen ninety-eight saw the installation of the new
Grand Lodge
Membership Database and a new computer system. The Grand
Lodge 0 ffice now
reports quarterly to each lodge on the status of its memb
ership, giving vital
feedback to lodges to ensure that information sent to us in
the monthly reports is
being accurately recorded. My thanks go to all the lodges
who worked so hard
with our staff to ensure the accuracy of the Grand Lodge
records.
Finally, I am pleased to report that the Grand Master extend
ed interim
recognition to three new Grand Lodges this year. The
first was formed in the
Canadian Province of Newfoundland and Labrador, the
second in the former
African country once known as Upper Volta, and now known
as Burkina Faso.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The last was fonned in the Republic of Bulgaria. I therefore move full recognition
be given to the following Grand Lodges.

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURE R
Most Worshipful, Brethren:

..

At the outset, the Ritual Committee takes this opportunity to say thank
you for the privilege of serving this past year.
The annual Inspector's Reports have disclosed much information
regarding the condition of our Lodges.

1

Since our last Communication, the attrition rate has shrunk our
membership roster by another 5,000 to below the l 00,000 mark plus the loss of 14
Lodges.
Lack of officers continues to plague our Lodges and rely more and more
on Past Masters and the spontaneous request of sideliners for assistance. Of
course, their help is appreciated, realizing that this is only an ephemeral solution.
The attendnace at our seventeen seminars throughout the jurisdiction is
most gratifying and we thank you.

ln closing, we say thanks to our Grand Lodge Officers who have acquitted
themselves so well at our ceremonies throughout the year.
To our Grand Secretary and his entire staff, much thanks for all your
assistance whenever we needed it.
To our Inspectoral corps, all l 08 of you, for all the time and service you
give to our Fraternity - thank you, thank you, thank you.
To all our coaches for all your efforts, a grateful fraternity says thank you.
To my colleagues on the Ritual Committee, my sincerest thank you for all
your help.
And to you, my Brethren, for making it all possible - thank you.
Respectfully submitted,
Ulysses G. Patropulos, Grand Lecturer

GRAND CHAPLA IN'S MESSAG E

Devotiona l Service
Sunday, October 11, 1998
V. Kent Annstrong, Grand Chaplain
Invocation
Great Architect of the Universe, we ask that you look with favor
on this gathering of our Masonic Family and our endeavors here in San
Francisco this week. Grant to our members peace and hannony as they
make the legislation that will lead us into the next century. Give them
Wisdom to make decisions that are good for our Fraternity, Strength to
keep their convictions and values and the Beauty that comes from
knowing that they have helped make Masonry stronger and better in
California and have done their best to make this indelible impression clear
and beautiful. Watch over our Grand Master and his corps of officers and
grant to them that watchful care that you give to those who follow your
path. We ask that you watch over our Masonic Family, especially the
youth that are the cornerstone of the future and in whom we must trust to
carry on our traditions and values. All this we ask that we may honor
your Holy Name. Amen.
I wish to welcome all of your. Thank you for helping us begin our Grand
Lodge week as all great and important undertaking should begin, by including in
our schedules time to make a joyful noise unto the Lord. Our Grand Master has
for his theme this year, "Freemasons United an Indelible Impression," and in our
time together here today we would like to share with you some indelible
impressions that scriptures have made on our lives.
As a young child in Oakdale, I was exposed to many different Christian
churches. When I was about seven, my Grandmother Annstrong, who was
babysitting me, enrolled me in Vacation Bible School at the local Naz.arene
Church, and it was there that I received one of the most indelible impressions of
my religious life. During that week were required to learn a "Bible" verse and to
tell why we had chosen that verse. The verse that I choose was the JOQlh Psalm.

236

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Make a joyful noise unto the Lord, all ye lands
Serve the Lord with gladness; come before his presence with
singing
Know ye that the Lord he is God; it is he that hath made us, and
not we ourselves; we are his people; and the sheep of his
pasture.
Enter into his gates with thanksgiving and into his courts with
praise; be thankful unto him, and bless his name.
For the Lord is good; his mercy is everlasting; and his truth
endureth to all generations.
This verse seemed to my young mind to be the way I wanted to worship
my Creator, with joyful praise and singing, not with fire and brimstone ~nd
damnation. When you are uyoung those are not the things that lead you to enjoy
worship. Having fun, singing and laughing was how I wanted to worship my
Creator; it was how I wanted to live my life. I loved singing the songs that we
learned in Sunday school and in Vacation Bible School. Even though I couldn't
carry a tune I belted out with all the volume of my voice my praise to the Lord. I
wanted the world to know that I loved my Creator and I enjoyed making a joyful
noise unto him.
What a wonderful way to approach our Creator. Singing and making a
joyful noise, laughing and enjoying His presence and the wonde~l w~rld he m~e
for us. Imagine if we lived our lives with this verse as our gmdmg hght. Gomg
through life making a joyful noise, not grumbling; singing, not muttering under our
breath about how rotten we are being treated; praising the Lord and our fellowmen,
not trying to chop them down or spread vicious rumors about them; d~c~g and
singing, not stomping angrily about telling the whole world how rotten 1t 1s. We
would spend our lives making a joyful noise and the world be so much more
pleasant.
In this world we should be happy to serve the Lord with gladness and to
come into presence singing. How wonderful it is to serve the Lord and come into
his presence singing and rejoicing. Truly this is the way to approach the Lord.
Goodness and Thanksgiving are surely the results of following this verse
and of making it your personal philosophy.
Poets and philosophers have written about a world that is filled with joyful
noise, one that sings the praise of our Creator, songs of Thanksgiving, not songs
of war and hate. This world does not yet exist; sadly the latter world seems to be
the one that is prevalent. I hope that each of us can use our lives to make a joyful

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

237

noise, singing and praising, loving and laughing, not hating and shouting in anger.
Knowing the Lord as our Creator and the shepherd of our flock. Imagine how
much nicer this world of ours would be.
Another verse of Scripture that has truly made an indelible impression on
me comes from my time in De Mo lay. At the opening of each meeting the candles
are lighted and the Master Councilor gives a short bit of ritual about each candle.
As the seventh candle is lit, the ritual quotes Matthew 5-15: "Let your light so
shine before men that they may see your good works and glorify your Father which
is in Heaven."
This verse is one that each of us should make our personal philosophy.
Each day we should let our light so shine so that we truly do glorify our Father
who is in heaven. How do you let your light shine? You can follow the principles
laid down by our Masonic Virtues, doing things that are kind and helpful without
making glaring bids for publicity.
Masons do lots of these acts and they do not "Let their light shine." Our
Fraternity spends lots of money and time to help children who have disabilities
lead normal and productive lives. Our Shrine Hospitals, Scottish Rite Clinics and
Knights Templar Eye clinics are only a a few that come to mind. Our scholarships
help children gain higher education; our Lodges spend time working in the schools
helping the children learn to read and supporting the public schools programs in
cities throughout this state. All of these acts are ways of letting our Light shine,
but we seldom let Cilthers see those good works. Every part of our Ma sonic Family
does things that can only be considered shining lights, yet we seldom publicize
those good works; in fact we seem to try extra hard to hide those things. Our
modesty has been one of our biggest detractions and this is the time that we should
begin to truly make the Light shine and to call attention to it.
Now is the time to make a joyful noise. In your programs there is a song
printed that I will ask all of you to join with me in singing the praise of the Lord.
Brother Grand Organist, if you will, please start.

These Are The Times That Try Men's Souls
One of the great patriots of our Revolutionary War, Thomas Paine, began
his pamphlet Common Sense with these words: "These are the times that try men's
souls. The summer soldier and the sunshine patriot will, in this crisis, shrink from
the service of their country; but he that stands it now, deserves the love and thanks
of man and woman." This was written December 1776, at a time when our country
was deeply involved in a war that would eventually give our country it's birth. It
was a tumultuous time, one full of anger, resentment, injustice and revolution. It
was a time when moral outrage at the inequities and injustices imposed upon the
American Colonies by the British King were so strong that only acts of violence
and aggression would relieve the situation. Common sense and reason could not
justify those acts of the British government and so the people of the Colonies were
engaged in a war to bring relief to the people of that future United States from
those injustices.
Masons were very instrumental and influential in those times. Men like
George Washington, Benjamin Franklin, Paul Revere and many other Masons led
the way and guided this country through those times and into greatness. We can
find many examples of Masons leading the people. Masons were members of the
Continental Congress, they were the signers of the Declaration oflndependence,
and later the Constitution of the United States. Masons were generals and soldiers
in the anny. They were Governors of the States and leaders in the houses of
government. They were the merchants, the manufacturers and even the fanners
who fed the country. In every aspect of this time that tried men's souls, Masons
were deeply committed and involved with their country and their society.
I believe that the days we are now living in are also the times that try
men's souls. This is not a period of political crisis, we are not rebelling at
injustices and tyranny of government, but we are in the midst of a crisis. Our
country is currently experiencing a moral and ethical turmoil that truly tests our
moral fabric. Today, we, as Masons, must determine if we are summer soldiers
and sunshine patriots or if we are those souls who are the fabric and foundation of
our society. We must determine if we will follow our Masonic virtues and remain
as the foundation of our Society or if we will fly away as leaves from the trees
break away and scatter in the storms of the fall. We must hold fast and see our
beliefs through this winter of crisis and into the spring where our values will burst
forth like new leaves to again regain their rightful position as the true foundations
of this country's beliefs. We must not relax our position and let our values be
decimated or trampled by the masses who are currently in fashion in this country.

242

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Our political and religious leaders are at the apex of this crisis. We see
our political leaders publicly admit to adultery and sexual crimes. They have been
accused and often found guilty of illegal fund raising, of teaching college classes
to improperly raise money for their political causes, and of making telephone calls
to raise money from inside government buildings. They are censured for sexual
harassment, found to have had homosexual relationships with pages, sexual
encounters with interns and admit to having affairs. This is true not only of the
. President but members of the House, the Senate and state and local offices as well.
Even members of the judiciary and candidates for the Supreme Court are guilty of
these offenses. This is not limited to one political party, but is found in both the
major parties. Drug and alcohol problems frequently are exposed and these
legislators and their wives or husbands go off to "dry out" at clinics with little or
no censure. The mayor of the Capital of the United States was an admitted and
convicted drug abuser and was re-elected.
Religious leaders also have been in the news lately. Famous leaders of
denominations have publicly admitted or been convicted of crimes and moral
offenses. They have affairs with their assistants, with prostitutes and sometimes,
even persons of the same sex. We frequently read in the news that some Priest,
Minister or Rabbi is convicted or accused of molesting children. Sometimes this
abuse is of children of the same sex, sometimes of the opposite sex. These are not
infrequent items in our newspapers, they happen much too often. These acts have
been going on for years and frequently the church and those who are in power
within that church have covered them up. We also see in the news stories of
embezzlement of church funds by the members of the clergy, secretaries or
members of the leadership of that church. These types of articles appear much too
often today in our news. Those stories underline the moral and ethical depravity
that seems to permeate our society and is rotting the structures of family values and
the morals of our society today.
We cannot go to the movies or watch television without being exposed to
violence, sex and crime. Our children's cartoon heroes are Ninjas, Power Rangers
and other figures that go about fighting, maiming and killing. Saturday morning
acts of violence are all too prevalent on television and the cartoons and shows are
children are exposed to seem to extol the virtues of violence. Computer games that
our children love glorify violence and arcades dedicate aisle after aisle to games
that teach our children that they must blow away someone or something to be a
winner. Children of every age are exposed to these games. Children of both sexes
are exposed to these games and programs. Violence permeates our entertainment
and our children are learning from an environment that extols maiming,
bloodletting and killing. Even public television presents programs that depict
animals hunting, killing and even killing members of their own species.

GRAND ORATION

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Most Worshipful Past Grand Masters,
honored officers of Grand Lodge, and my distinguished Brothers of Grand Lodge
- this has to be the most exciting and most humbling moment of my Masonic life.
Most Worshipful Tony, Virginia and I owe this wonderful Masonic Year
to you - and Marilyn, and we shall always remember this period in our lives as
long as we live.
It has been thrilling from the moment you asked if I would accept the
appointment as Grand Orator, to these final hours. My only wish is that every
Mason in California could have equally shared this year with us. From the socials,
the traveling, the cornerstones, the dedications and rededications, the awarding of
50 and 75 year pins, the business meetings, and, of course your grrreat trip through
the Scandinavian countries.
But most importantly, we wish all Masons in this jurisdiction, and their
families, could see the new excitement in our fraternity, the acceptance of new
challenges by so many, and the renewed pledges from the hearts of our members
throughoutthejurisdiction. I've never felt such an exhilaration, nor ever been so
optimistic about something good, getting better.
I'm truly proud to have had the opportunity to serve you and the
Freemasons ofou&Grand Lodge during the years 1997-98. To you Grand Master,
Marilyn, and all the members of the California Grand Lodge, my everlasting
gratitude. I'm sure, with the warm and friendly leadership you have given, an
indelible impression in the footsteps of time has been left for those who follow.
I know you all are waiting to hear a "Grand Oration", which is traditional
from the Grand Orator; however, what I'm aboutto say, will not necessarily be an
oration. My duty, as the Grand Orator, is to deliver an address to you, the Grand
Lodge, on matters appertaining to the craft. I'm not really sure what I'm about to
say is even an address or even on matters appertaining to the craft. What I am
going to say today- are the feelings about Freemasonry that are in my heart; and
I pray some of you may have these same feelings.
But first, I would briefly like to share with you a story about a 93-year old
mother who believes that Freemasonry is next to Godliness. A woman, who upon
the birth of her only son, prayed to God that one day he would become a DeMolay
and subsequently one day would become a Mason. She lived in a small coal
mining town, there poverty was as common as the noon day sun.
But, one very important thing about this small village was obvious- and
that was the fact that the leaders in this town were the most respected people. They

248

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

were the business owners, the church goers, and in her sight, were the elite of the
community. They were all Masons to the man. She dreamed and prayed that her
son would not become just another coal miner, but that he would fit into this
special earthly heaven of her mind, that he would become one of the Masons in
town.

hours, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. These volunteers are also from the Masonic
community.

The beginning of her dream was fulfilled fifteen years after her son's
birth, when he was initiated into the Order of DeMolay; and climaxed six years
later when he was Raised a Master Mason. The dreams of her little world were
then fulfilled.
Fifty years after her son's acceptance into DeMolay, she still had the
canceled check for his initiation, showing evidence of her pride in the Fraternity,
and she even saved the Lodge's photograph of her son's first Stated Meeting as a
Master Mason, which now is nearly a half century later. As a Past Worthy Matron
of Eastern Star, she has, throughout all these years, shared each thrilling moment
of her son's activities in Masonry. Time is running out for her and she may not
have many years left, but her daily prayers includes her thanks to God for her son,
and appreciation to the Masonic Fraternity and what it has meantto her, and to her
son.
I wonder how many of you can repeat a similar story? I'm sure this
scenario is not unique, for this great and wonderful Fraternity has grown
throughout time on the foundation of love and dreams.
And why not? We give to mankind more love and charity than any other
body or organiz.ation in all of history. So, why don't we flaunt it, brag about it,
advertise it - in other words why aren't we telling the world just how good we
really are? I know that inside the breast of each Freemason is a heart filled with
a special pride, unmatched by any pride that has ever been earned or received,
throughout all time.
Each year, hundreds of millions of dollars are spent on children
numbering in the hundreds of thousands across this vast continent. We boldly face
every conceivable mental and medical problem known to man. I am well
acquainted with several Masonic children's hospitals, that together, treat over
300,000 children each year, with every conceivable childhood disorder.
Everything from pediatric orthopaedics, to cystic fibrosis, brain tumors,
critical bums, cancer, epilepsy, you name it, and we treat it. One of the hospitals
not only treats about 150,000 children each year, but has a startling statistic, that
of over 49,000 visits to their emergency ward, in just a single year. They enjoy
over 500 volunteer workers from the Masonic community. One of the other
hospitals is proud of it's 850 volunteer workers that assist the staff on assigned

249

And of course, we cannot forget the 160 Childhood Language Disorder
and Learning Centers around the country, and the ever present care for the eyes,
the contributions to the muscular dystrophy research, and many more human needs
- far too numerous to share today. And don't let us forget the medical research
for those children who will need help in the future; and the loving care given to
those in their golden years.
Forgive me, I know I'm addressing the choir, but I just can't help
reminding you of "who" we are. There is no question or doubt, that you who are
here today are the workers, the leaders and a vital and integral part of the backbone
and stability of our house - not built with hands.
You all have heard about our forefathers, and their accomplishments. Just
to name a few: Mozart, Beethoven, Bach, Washington, Franklin, Edison; and in
this century alone- Presidents Teddy Roosevelt, Taft, Franklin Roosevelt, Harry
Truman - Generals Pershing, MacArthur, Doolittle, Bradley, Marshal - Admiral
Byrd, King George of England, Winston Churchill, Lindbergh, Dr. Mayo, Sousa,
Will Rogers, Rudyard Kipling- I could go on and on all day, and not name them
all. Yes, and I am sure that I could name most everyone in this Grand Lodge as
being great for something. You get the picture, don't you?
But there is one name I haven't mentioned. It's a name quite obscure to
most of our members, but if I had to list the top twenty influential Mason's in this
century, I would certainly include this man among the most worthy. The more I
read about him, the more I am impressed with his contributions to our society and
his presence in our lives today.
He lived at a time in Masonic history when our fraternity grew from 1.3
million members to 2.57 million. The time period was 1910 to 1920. This was a
period when increased membership meant expanded administration for the various
Grand Lodges and the concordant and affiliated bodies. All the officers had
enlarged responsibilities. It meant more staff, more equipment, increased welfare
work, and the establishmentofnew educational programs, and a new emphasis on
Americanism. This was a period just right for a person like this man, or put
another way, this person was just right for this period in Masonic history. Hie
enthusiasm for Masonry was the same energetic, continuing eagerness as that of
his Masonic father.
At the age of 35, he joined the Army to fight in the Spanish-American
War. It wasn't long before he was promoted to Captain, a title he enjoyed for the
balance of his life. Ten years after leaving the Army, he was Raised a Master
Mason in Louisville Lodge No. 400, and it wasn't long after, that he became

250

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Master of his Lodge. Shortly after his term as Master, he joined the York and
Scottish Rite Bodies, and again, it wasn't long before he became Venerable Master
of his Scottish Rite Valley. He was a special person, a knowing person, and
everyone that knew him, agreed he as destined for greatness. A short time later he
was coronated a 33 ° Scottish Rite Mason, and was crowned Sovereign Grand
Inspector General for the Orient of Kentucky. His special aptitudes were so
evident, that it only took a short while before he was voted the Secretary General
for the Southern Jurisdiction of the Scottish Rite Supreme Council. He served in
this capacity for ten years, and then was voted into Scottish Rite's highest position,
that of Grand Commander. His name is John H. Cowles.
Illustrious Cowles was not a well-educatedman, not wealthy, and thought
by many to be very controversial, but everything he did in life was for the good of
the Masonic Order. He single handedly, persistently pursued an exhaustive
campaign against the bureaucrats of Washington for a Department of Education
and compulsory education for the children of America. Even though his efforts
were not passed immediately by Congress, our neighboring State of Oregon
decided to go ahead and adopt a referendum requiring compulsory attendance for
all children in the public schools.
He was one of the first to establish a permanent foundation for the care
of sick children in America - this was long before government welfare agencies
were heard of. His penetrating focus on childhood disease, which was killing
thousands of children throughout the nation, was long before vaccination programs
and the development of antibiotics. As we all know, polio was a cruel adversary
of children' s health in those days. And it was during this period that the now
world famous Scottish Rite Children'sHospital was built in Atlanta, Georgia. This
hospital, I'm sure, was the inspiration and guiding light for the first Shriner's
Hospital to be built in Shreveport, Louisiana in l 922.
Cowles once said, "A nation cannot last as a money-making mob; it
cannot with impurity and simply plain existence, go on despising literature,
despising science, despising art, despising nature, despising compassion and
conceding its soul to every penny. The values inculcated by Freemasonry were
needed for the common good of the nation, in danger of being spoiled by the
excesses of the rich patterns of life."
Cowles was concerned about the disuse of public Masonic ceremonies,
the little attendance at Masonic Burial Services, the reduction of laying
cornerstones for public buildings. His belief was that Freemasonry offers a
"spiritual oasis, a retreat from this world; that it reinforces traditional morality, so
that the idea of the asylum promised harmony in a world, so sorely lacking it."
Does this remind you of today?

Just think, nearly l 00 years ago, it was said that the fraternity was
concerned chiefly with membership and the individual Mason, and thereby had
concentrated its attention on religion and the personal morality of its members. We
were developing a consciousness of the external world, and desired some visible
part in it, as Masons. They were saying then, that the problem of low attendance
at Lodges revealed that a large number of members had come to regard Masonry
"more as symbolic than a participatory organization".
John Cowles was a tireless promoter of job placement for our members
throughout the nation who were unemployed, and as such, set up an unofficial
national employment service. He was also exceedingly generous with his own
personal resources, rarely refusing the appeal of any family in need. It wasn't
uncommon for him to respond to a letter requesting help - with a sizeable check
from his own personal account.
Of course, Masons do this today, and they always have, and I pray they
always will. And like many men we know today, those sitting to my right, and
many of you around this Lodge room, John Cowles as a Mason's Mason.
The straight lines of history appear rarely, perhaps as often as baseball' s
seventy home runs or as infrequently as Halley's Comet. Instead, the crooked
grains of the past bend toward the present, usually bulging into the future by
rounded curves like those encircling a dark knot in a pine board. As I have learned
in my philosophy class at school, some philosophers of history insist on the grand
theme of returning cycles. They believe starting points and destinations share a
similarity approaching sameness. Consequently, we find that history does repeat
itself.

251

Surprisingly, history is not simply a turning wheel with compass points
fixed and known in advance. History indeed has its circles, but it also has its
crooked roads.
This is apparent in the ever-ancient and ever-new question - where are
we going? It is, however, a far more problematic question than - where have we
been?
From the past, a historian can extrapolate a few tendencies, underline
noticeable trends, examine causes and outcomes. But these variables do not help
predict next year's weather. Rathertha n a sense of inevitability about the cyclical
lessons of history and their bearing on what happens next. A trustworthy and
memorable coincidence occasionally offers the interlude that lets us have history
both ways - as nothing new under the sun - and surprisin gly- as a direct beam
of light to direct our future.

253

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

No time or place on earth, in all of history, has the work and deeds of the
Freemasons been more evident than today. Our history and our future certainly has
the direct reflection of a perfect light.
I've often been puzzled, as you have been, why doesn 'tthe general public
- yes, and even some of our own members- see us for what and who we really
are?
Do you think, maybe, we might need a uniform of some kind, like the
Salvation Army, or wear an arm band with a cross on it, or hang a stethoscope
around our neck or a uniform like the paramedics? No, I don'tthink so! For when
you think about it, we do have a uniform, but its one that can only be seen by those
who see our good works. The uniform we wear is a perfect fit, for it fits around
our heart. It's given to us when we kneel at the altar, and take our obligations.
You may not have noticed it at the time, but you were fitted with a coat of human
relief, trousers with pockets full of caring love, shoes that will take you to every
needy person you can find. You wear a shirt of purity, and a tie of brotherly love
with the design of charity written all over it. Your gloves are of pure lambskin in
which you carry.the Holy Writings of your individual faith, and under your arms
are the square, compass and level, all three so symbolic of our way of life.

Remember the standards that Grand Commander Cowles exemplified.
We must keep those same standards in our vision to make possible that which is
impossible, make honest that which is dishonest and reinstitute goodness as a
standard in our everyday life.
We know that when Freemasons stand united, they truly will leave an
"Indelible Impression".
So in conclusion and with remembrance of the past, and a heart filled with
love and gratitude from the little lady of93, who always believed in her son and
in Freemasonry - and also with my heart hull of teary eyed sentiment and
wonderful memories and dreams - my mother of 93, my children and
grandchildren, Virginia and I - thank you for the privilege of serving the greatest
and most honorable fraternity in the history of mankind. Thank you.

252

Yes, you have a beautiful uniform, and many in this world have seen it,
but many more have not - and this is our challenge. You see, I have a vision and
a challenge. Maybe it's the same as yours. I can see men of all ages searching for
a better life, better surroundings, a better universal world to live in. This vision and
challenge includes a society of people without needs of the flesh, a happy people
with purity in their souls. A society void of selfish wants. I see men of all ages
wanting to share their lives with others, to maintain an environment of traditional
values worthy of our Lord's plan for all mankind.
At the front of this vision and challenge, I see the square and compass
being handed out to every man who understands the purpose for our creation as a
brotherhood, with a charge to lead the way to that perfect life, as it was intended
in the beginning. We have all been given the tools of learning, and with these
tools, we can teach and influence those who follow us in the ways of righteousness
and of goodness.
There still are, as there always have been and always will be, frontiers to
conquer, discoveries undreamed still remain. The greatest literature has not yet
been written; the finest painting has not yet been painted; the finest symphony has
not yet been composed, our wonderful fraternity has not yet seen its finest day. In
this vision and challenge, I see new and exciting horizons.
If we can but maintain the initiative and develop the imagination to
penetrate them, we will see that society which is reserved for only the good.

Respectfully submitted,
Thomas M. Boles, Grand Orator

GRAND MASTE R'S DECISIO N AND RECOMM ENDATI ONS

Grand Master Wordlow 's Decision No. 1
Last year Grand Lodge approved Grand Master Gresham's Decision No.
1, which was to suspend the Master of Pasadena Lodge No. 272, pending further
investigation into alleged financial irregularities in the Lodge. My Decision No.
l was to continue that suspension pending the conclusion of the investigation.
The investigation led to the filing of Masonic charges, and ultimately to
the expulsion of the Master. Although my Decision No. l is of historical interest
only now, you must still vote on it. I therefore request your approval of my
Decision No. 1.
Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes :
The Grand Master continued the suspension of the Master of Pasadena
Lodge No. 272 until the conclusion of the present investigation of the
circumstances outlined in the letter of October 6, 1997 from Grand Master
Gresham.
Section l 050c of the California Masonic Code authorizes the Grand
Master to suspend the Master of any chartered Lodge until the next Annual
Communication. This situation involves serious financial irregularities and
therefore the Grano Master's Decision is in accord with our policy and general
purposes.

Decision AFFIRMED.
Grand Master Wordlow 's Decision No. 2
After due deliberation, I have decided that the reduction of the
Candidate's Proficiencies for the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Degrees,
as approved by Grand Lodge at the last Annual Communication, is optional rather
than mandatorv.
It is therefore my decision that each candidate in this jurisdiction may
decide on his own whether or not he proves his proficiency by learning the
traditional "long form" of the proficiency, or by learning the Obligation, and the
signs, words, and modes of recognition .QD!y. In each case, the demonstration of
the proficiency of the candidate shall be in a tiled Lodge in the manner approved
by the Grand Lecturer.

however, I received a copy of a letter sent to our Grand Master castigating me and
saying that I was a "Jew hater". My Brethren, I do not deserve either that abuse
or that label.

Resolution No. 97-05
Substitutes 'Holy Writings' for 'Holy Bible' in the Ritual
The proponents of this Resolution seek to substitute the words 'Holy Writings' for
the words 'Holy Bible' everywhere they appear in the Ritual.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
WHEREAS, numerous members of our beloved ancient and honorable
fraternity are voicing concern over the use of the term 'Holy Bible' in the
California Masonic ritual;
WHEREAS, a strong implication exists which indicates the JudeoChristian persuasion is to be held in reverence above all other religious bodies;
WHEREAS, our Craft teaches that we recognize and accept men of all
faiths, as long as they believe in a Supreme Being and life hereafter;
WHEREAS, while most members acquiesced in the past and did not
question the use of the words 'Holy Bible' in ritual work, individuals openly
voiced concern about having to refer to their Holy Writings as a 'Holy Bible' once
our California Grand Lodge adopted the use of alternate Holy Writings;
WHEREAS, no member, thus far, has objected to use of the term 'Holy
Writings' in lieu of the term 'Holy Bible';
WHEREAS, our Third Degree lecture begins, "[w]e read in the Holy
Writings that it was decreed in the wisdom and counsels of Deity aforetime, that
a house should be built, erected to God and dedicated to His Holy Name"; and
WHEREAS, the words 'Holy Writings' may be substituted for the words
'Holy Bible' everywhere they appear in the Ritual without great difficulty, as the
syllables are the same and changes can be readily made in the Monitor and Cipher
by lining through the word 'Bible' and writing in the word 'Writings' in the space
immediately above.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVEDthatthe Ritual be amended to
substitute the words 'Holy Writings' for the words 'Holy Bible' everywhere they
appear.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that any Brother who so desires may be
re-obligated in the Degree of Master Mason on the Holy Writings of his choice
selected from those authorized by Section 26295 of the California Masonic Code.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

271

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to substitute the words "Holy
Writings" for the words "Holy Bible" everywhere they appear in the Ritual. They
also have added a second part, that would make it possible for a Brother to be reobligated on the Holy Writings of his choice. The word "Bible" is defined in every
dictionary as including the sacred writings or books of any religion. Therefore, the
words "Holy Bible" and "Holy Writings" are synonymous.
Further, if one were to address every slight difference between the
monitor, cipher ritual, etc., there would be no end to the changes that make no
difference in the intent of the Ritual. To make available the re-obligation of many
men on a different"Holy Writings" would not be consistent with the intent of our
obligation.
This Resolution is not consistent with Grand Lodge policy or general
purposes.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

Resolution No. 97-12

To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F.& A.M of California:
WHEREAS, Section 23080 of the California Masonic Code states that
members are entitled to be present and participate in Lodge proceedings;
WHEREAS, Section 160 IO of the California Masonic Code states the
Tiler is present while at his post in the Tiler's room;
WHEREAS, these two sections conflict, because a Tiler cannot
knowledgeably participate while in his room;

274

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

WHEREAS, many Lodges are experiencing decreased membership and
many Masters are having difficulty appointing a Tiler who is content to sit in his
room and unable to participate in all Lodge proceedings;
WHEREAS, many Lodges are built with one or more outer doors that can
be locked, and may be equipped with bells, video, intercoms and/or other means
of alarm; and
WHEREAS, Lodges that lock these doors past the room immediately
adjacent to the Lodge room can use the locked doors as a barrier to the profane.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that, in Lodge meeting
facilities with one or more outer doors which can be locked and are equipped with
bells, video, intercom or other means of alarm, the Master shall have the option of
allowing the Tiler to sit within the Lodge anteroom doorway (half in and half out)
during such periods when the doors immediately adjacent to the Lodge room are
locked. Should any alarm be detected, the Tiler shall retire, close the Lodge room
door, ascertain the cause of the alarm and initiate appropriate action. When the
premises are again secure, he may reopen the Lodge room door and return to his
chair in the Lodge anteroom doorway.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
WHEREAS, while Masonic Lodges and the Grand Lodge recognize the
Hiram Award and have awarded such with a certificate, medallion and lapel pin
available through Grand Lodge, there is no actual criteria established for the award;
WHEREAS, there has been no clear guidance on the award, its purpose
and its title since the original concept of the award was proposed in Resolution No.
4 at the Grand Lodge 1979 Annual Communication, such resolution having failed
to pass because it was too restrictive on who was entitled to the award, its limit of
one award a year not taking into account a Lodge which may on occasion wish to
award more than one in a year; and
WHEREAS, the present understandingthat the award is the highest honor
that can be bestowed upon a brother by his Masonic Lodge is not proper as the
highest honor that can be bestowed on a Mason is the lambskin apron which he
received in his First Degree.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that a new Section 23155 of
the California Masonic Code be added to read as follows:
§23155. HIRAM AWARDS.

The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit the Tiler to sit in the
doorway of the Lodge Room when the premises are adequately secured.
This Resolution opens the Lodge door and is not consistent with our
current Grand Lodge policy. However, in a secure environment, it does allow the
Tiler to observe Lodge proceedings and is consistent with the purposes of Grand
Lodge.

Resolution No. 97-14

Establishes Rules/or the Hiram Award
The proponents of this Resolution seek to establish qualifications and procedures
for bestowing the Hiram A ward.

275

The Grand Lodge, upon request of a Masonic Lodge under its
jurisdiction, shall furnish a certificate honoring the Master
Mason designated by the Lodge as a recipient of the Hiram
Award. The certificate shall be delivered to the Masonic Lodge
for presentation to the recipient. The Grand Lodge shall make
available for purchase a medallion and lapel pin for recipients of
the Hiram Award.
The Lodge may only designate for the Hiram Award a Master
Mason who has served the Lodge and the Masonic Fraternity
with devotion over and above the ordinary. Service as an officer
or as Master of a Lodge shall not be in itself sufficient
qualification for the award nor shall it be a disqualification. The
award should be based on what the recipient has done, not what
positions he has held.
The Hiram A ward shall be considered the highest honor for
service that can be bestowed upon a member by a Masonic
Lodge. The presentation should be made with appropriate
ceremony. When a selection has been made, it should be
announced so the recipient may invite family and friends to the
award presentation. To maintain the prestige and importance of

276

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the Hiram Award, a Lodge may present only one Hiram Award
in any one calendar year. Such limitation should not suggest
that this award should be presented every year.

§26060. JURISDICTION TO RECEIVE APPLICATIONS.

procedures for bestowing the Hiram Award.

Hiram Award to a Brother who, through the years, has served the Lodge with
devotion over and above the ordinary.
This Resolution establishes guidelines for the reception and presentation
of this prestigious award. This Resolution is consistent with Grand Lodge policy
and purposes.

notify any other Lodge or Lodges within IO miles of its place of meeting of any
applications it may receive ... ";
WHEREAS, the California Masonic Code also provides that the
notification of the Masonic Service Bureau in the area shall be deemed notification
to other Lodges;
WHEREAS, in some areas of California the Masonic Secretaries
Association has for many years received these notifications and in tum made
notification to the Lodge in the area; and
WHEREAS, in these areas such notification is not in compliance with the
California Masonic Code.

This Resolution is consistent with current Grand Lodge policy and
purposes.
Resolution ADOPTED.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
WHEREAS, it is presently required that the Junior Warden-elect of a
Lodge be qualified to give the work and lectures of the Entered Apprentice Degree,
that the Senior Warden-elect be qualified to give the work and lectures of the
Entered Apprentice Degree and the Fellow Craft Degree and that the Master-elect
be qualified to give the work and lectures of all three degrees;
WHEREAS, in order to qualify each of these officers must learn the
obligation, signs and modes of recognition of each of the respective degrees as a
part of this qualification;
WHEREAS, Masons are now required to memorize only those portions
of the Candidate's Lectures of the Entered Apprentice Degree and of the Fellow
Craft Degree consisting of the obligation, signs and modes of recognition of each
of these degrees;
WHEREAS, the need to learn the Candidate's Lecture of the Master
Mason Degree is an added burden on the Master-elect (as long as the "long form"
is still required); and
WHEREAS, it is unnecessaryto have a separate requirement for the First
and Second Degrees, and may be unnecessary ifthe requirement for memorizing
the Candidate's Lecture of the Master Mason Degree is shortened to consist of the
obligation, signs and modes ofrecognition of that degree.

California Masonic Code be amended as marked:

Resolution No. 98-06

Defines Which Past Masters May Participate
in the Past Master's Collective Vote
The proponents of this Resolution seek to define who can cast the collective Past
Masters' vote, and under what conditions it cannot be cast.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

§620.

289

VOTES.

The following shall each be entitled to one vote:
A.

Elective and appointive Grand Lodge Officers except
the Grand Tiler and the Assistant Grand Tiler;

B.

Past Grand Officers;

C.

Masters, Senior Wardens and Junior Wardens of
chartered Lodges; and

D.

Past Masters collectively of each chartered Lodge.
Only those Past Masters registered and present at an
Annual Communication shall be entitled to participate
in the collective vote. If there are an equal number of
such Past Masters on opposite sides of a question, the
collective vote shall not be cast on that question. If a
majority of such Past Masters favors a particular vote
on a question, the vote shall be so cast. In the event of
a contested election for a Grand Lodge office, the
collective vote shall be cast in accordance with the
wishes of a plurality of such Past Masters. If there is
no such plurality, the vote shall not be cast on that
ballot.

.

WHEREAS, there is confusion among the craft as to which Past Masters
are eligible to participate in the single vote accorded the Past Masters collectively
ofa Lodge;

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

WHEREAS, in the past some Past Masters not in attendance at an Annual
Communication have participated in voting on questions;

The proponents of this Resolution seek to define who can cast the
"collective" Past Masters' vote and under what conditions it may not be cast.

WHEREAS, in the past some Past Masters have participated in voting on
questions before those questions have been debated on Grand Lodge floor; and

Passage of this Resolution will establish guidelines to assure that all Past
Masters of a chartered Lodge in attendance at the Annual Communication will
have an equal opportunity to participate in casting the collective vote.

WHEREAS, in the past some Past Masters, registered and in attendance
at an Annual Communication, have not been allowed to participate in the Past
Master's collective vote.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 620 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:

This Resolution is consistent with Grand Lodge policy and general
purposes.

Resolution No. 98-08
Permits Stated Meetings in the Entered Apprentice Degree

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

The proponents of this Resolution seek to give each Lodge the option to hold its
Stated Meetings i? the Entered Apprentice Degree.

This Resolution proposes to establish a Legislation Information
Committee charged to identify current Masonic interests as well as legislative bills
which relate to those interests. The committee will also track the votes of
legislators on those bills. The proponents state that the interests of the Fraternity
"may be in jeopardy", apparently because current politicians are reinventing
government. They justify the creation of a committee which clearly has political
overtones by observing that Masons of the 18th Century were involved in political
activities, namely the creation of the United States of America.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:

WHEREAS, as an historic perspective, it is acknowledged that,
throughoutthe formative years of Freemasonry, Entered Apprentices made up the
bulk of the membership in our Fraternity, and Fellow Crafts and Master Masons
were rare;

Masonry has a fundamental tradition of non-involvement in politics.
Section 380 of the California Masonic Code states: "Grand Lodge and the
constituent Lodges shall not interfere or voice an opinion with regard to political
or religious matters." Even in the case of the public school system, an institution
Masonry is dedicated to preserving, Section 15060 of the California Masonic Code
expressly forbids us from taking any action to endorse, approve, or disapprove any
candidate or ballot issue.

WHEREAS, in the 1840's many Grand Lodges in the United States
revised their rules to require Lodges to hold Stated Meetings only in Lodges of
Master Masons, originally done to encourage all Masons to become Master
Masons;
WHEREAS, this change eventually resulted in the exclusion of Entered
Apprentices and Fellow Crafts from the core life of their Lodges, and
contemporary Masonic experience teaches us the importance of including Entered
Apprentices and Fellow Crafts whenever possible in the life and activities of the
Lodge; and

The proponents are historically correct in noting that Masons were
instrumental in the creation of the Declaration of Independence and the
Constitution. However, these men were not acting as official agents of Masonry
in this effort. Rather, they were individuals who were supporting principles of

§16015. OPTIONAL CONDUCT OF BUSINESS IN A

All business, except the examination of candidates in the

conferring of the Fellow Craft and Master Mason degrees, shall

Lodge has exercised the following option:
A.

At a Stated Meeting of the Lodge, a resolution shall be

Lodge be conducted in a Lodge of Entered Apprentice

B.

Following this meeting, written notice shall be given to
•each Lodge member setting forth the text of the
resolution and the date of the Stated Meeting at which
the vote is to be taken.

C.

At the Stated Meeting designated for the vote, the
resolution shall be adopted by a two-thirds vote of the
members present.

D.

The resolution shall have no effect until approved by
Grand Lodge or the Grand Master, and until approval
has been transmitted to the Grand Secretary. The
Grand Secretary shall then notify the Lodge that it shall
thereafter conduct all Stated Meetings in a Lodge of
Entered Apprentice Masons.

E.

The Secretary of the Lodge shall note in the minutes of
the Lodge the notice of the proposed resolution when
made. When transmitting a resolution for approval, the
Lodge Secretary shall forward a certificate, under seal,
showing that the law has been complied with and that
the resolution has received the required vote.

The proponents of this Resolution seek an option for a Lodge to hold a
Stated Meeting in the Entered Apprentice degree in order that a new member may
be involved as soon as he joins our fraternity.
This proposal has been before Grand Lodge many times and rejected each
time. Our current policy continues to be to encourage members to achieve Master
Mason status and take their rightful place among the brethren. Recent changes in
our proficiencies have shortened this process considerably.

While a Lodge is holding its Stated Meetings in a Lodge of
Entered Apprentice Masons, Entered Apprentices and Fellow
Crafts may speak and vote on all matters to come before the
Lodge with the following exceptions: only Master Masons may
ballot on candidates for the degrees of Masonry in that Lodge
and for the election of officers.

This Resolution is not consistent with current Grand Lodge policy or
general purposes.

When an Entered Apprentice is obligated in a Lodge that is
authorized to hold Stated Meetings in the Entered Apprentice
Degree, he shall commence paying dues starting with the month
following his Entered Apprentice Degree as if he were a Master
Mason.

Resolution CARRIED-OVER.

Permits Quarterly Stated Meetings

The proponents of this Resolution seek to give each Lodge the option to hold

To the Most Wor:Jhipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:

FELLOW

WHEREAS, some Lodges do not have sufficient business to warrant a
business meeting every month;

Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts have only the right to sit
in the Lodge in which they received the degree or degrees when
open in a degree taken by them, and the right to advancement
therein after satisfactorily passing a strict examination in open
Lodge. They may, with the consent of the Master, visit another
Lodge working in a degree taken by them, if accompanied by a
Master Mason who has sat with them in open Lodge and
vouches for them.
They are not required to pay dues and are not entitled to vote or
speak in Lodge, except as provided for elsewhere in this Code.
They may be buried with Masonic honors upon the request of
their family. Neither they nor their widows or orphans are
entitled to relief from the Lodge. They shall not exercise any
control over Lodge funds for charity, or for other purposes,
except as provided for elsewhere in this Code.

WHEREAS, such Lodges could devote the time otherwise employed in
holding a Stated Meeting to some other useful Masonic endeavor, if our law
allowed them the option to meet less frequently than monthly;
WHEREAS, Lodges should meet in the monthsofFebruary,May, August
and November to receive semi-annual reports from the Lodge Treasurer and
Secretary and to hold the annual election of officers; and

298

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

§ 16030. STA TED MEETINGS.
A Lodge shall hold a Stated Meeting for the transaction of its
regular business once in each calendarmonth of February, May,
August, November and such other calendar months as the Lodge
by its By-Laws may provide, except that Lodges whose Bylaws provide for meetings fixed by the phase of the moon shall
hold a Stated Meeting each lunar month in each lunar month
which includes February 15th, May 15th, August 15th and
November I 5th and in such other lunar months as the Lodge by
its By-Laws may provide.
A Lodge may be opened for a Stated Meeting prior to the time
fixed in its By-Laws. No business shall be transacted prior to
such time.
The Inspector may grant a dispensation to change the date of a
Stated Meeting, as provided for elsewhere in this Code.
In the event that the Master of a Lodge determines that
inclement weather, including ice, snow, and flood conditions,
existing on the day established in the By-Laws of the Lodge for
its Stated Meeting, makes it hazardous for members of the
Lodge to attend the meeting, he may, with the consent of the
Inspector of the District to which the Lodge is assigned,
postpone the Stated Meeting to the same day of the week next
following the week scheduled for the Stated Meeting. Upon
such postponing, the Master shall notify, to the extent possible,
all members of the Lodge residing within 50 miles of the
meeting place of the Lodge.
Should a Stated Meeting be postponed, the business transacted
at the postponed Stated Meeting shall be limited to the reading
of the minutes of the last Stated and subsequent Special
Meetings, action thereon, payment of the invoices of the Lodge,
and such other business of an emergent nature as determined by
the Master to require immediate consideration. No other new
business shall be considered.
