Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow solicitationofp_ro~pec~i~e
members, by deleting all references to solicitation in our ritual and cod1fymg 1t ~n
a new Section 23035. The Ritual for the Third Degree has a reference to free will
and accord. There are other references to asking the candidate if he has been
solicited in our ritual.
Our California Masonic Code Section 220, paragraph D, recognizes and
supports the Ancient Landmarks as an established policy of th~s G.rand Lodge. I_n
1927, Alfred Mackey distinctly enumerated those Landmarks m his Encycl~ped1a
of Freemasonry. To be noted is the fact that the 25 Landmarks do not contam any
reference to "Free Will and Accord" or "Solicitation". The current Grand Lodge
booklet on Constitution and By-Laws, given to Master Masons, contains the 25
Landmarks which similarly do not include the word "Solicitation" or the phrase
"Free Will ,and Accord". However, Brother Mackey did state, under the section
"Free Will and Accord" that: "it is wholly uncongenial with the spirit of our Order
to persuade anyone to become a Mason." "This is a settled Landmark of the

Resolution No. 98-13

Order."
The Grand Lodge pamphlet on Masonic Law and Custom, 1992, page 13,
does refer to "Free Will and Accord". The Grand Lodge pamphlet "12 Questions
on Freemasonry" indicates in number IV, that a candidate is not to be solicited. In
1993, Grand Master Stephen Doan, in his Decision No. 2, differentiated ~~~en
solicitation and providing information. The decision states, in part, that sohc1tat1on
is unacceptable to the Masonic Fraternity.
Upon reading the available sources, notwi~standing the absen~e of any
reference to solicitation in the Landmarks, the existence of the term m Grand
Lodge publications would indicate that it is the policy of this Gran~ Lodge not to
allow solicitation. Therefore, this Resolution is not consistent with our Grand
Lodge policies and general purposes.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

305

Requires Appointment ofa Committee to Study the
Allocation of Resources Between Teaching of
Ritual and Other Aspects of Masonic Education
The proponents of this Resolution seek to have the Grand Master appoint a
committee to study the allocation of volunteer time and other resources of the
fraternity between the teaching of the Ritual and other aspects of Masonic
education.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
WHEREAS, Grand Orator Eugene N. Dueprey's 1895 oration challenged
the Brethren to proudly discourse on Freemasonry's mission as an instrument of
friendship, benevolence and compassion toward others; as a model for man's plans,
purposes, hopes and strivings to be better; and as a platform to strengthen and
express a belief and devotion to God;
WHEREAS, Delmar D. Darrah in an article published by The Masonic
Book Club of the Grand Lodge of Illinois in 1915 stated: "Every effort is made to
post a candidate in the several lectures appertaining to the degrees but the moment
he signs the by-laws, the Lodge seems to forget its obligation and leaves him to
secure necessary Masonic Information the best way he can. It is no wonder that
many Masons lose their interest in the fraternity which might have been retained
had proper instruction been given them. The greatest need of the present Masonic
period is definite information upon Masonic subjects and the relationship which
Masons bear to the fraternity."
WHEREAS, in an Article titled "Worthy and Well Qualified", published
in the Alberta Grand Lodge Bulletin of 1936, explained the problem in this
manner: "Freemasonry may be, as is all too often the case, at fault in failing to
properly instruct its neophytes, but if the material with which the teachers must
work is missing, the chances of making Masons rather than Lodge members is
small."
WHEREAS, in the Proceedings of the Fourth Joint Meeting of the
California Research Lodges under the auspices of the Grand Lodge Masonic
Education Committee held June 26, 1965 appears an article by V. W. Donald G.
Campbell, Past Grand Lecturer, Titled "Masonic Education for the Candidate",
stating: "The subject of Candidate Education has been a major concern to
California Masonry for many years. In fact the early proceedings of Grand Lodge

306

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

show that one of the problems of the jurisdiction was not only ritual, but also the
imparting of Masonic Knowledge.
WHEREAS, in the 1989 Spring Issue of the California Freemason, Ralph
H. Head, Editor, published an article titled "Applied Masonry", states: "In the new
era Masonry should inspire all Masons to live a Masonic life. How a Mason lives
outside the Lodge is much more important than what he does in it. Taking another
Degree, another path, learning a new sign do not necessarily evidence forward
steps in Masonic living. We need not change our rituals. What we need is a
change in the understanding of them. We need not change precepts or doctrines
or duties. What we need is to recognize their significance and how to apply them
in practical and useful ways in our daily lives."
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Grand Master appoint
a Special Committee to study problems arising from the existing inequities in the
allotment of personnel, time and finances to the teaching of Masonic Ritual,
Masonic Communication, Masonic Education, Masonic Information and Masonic
Application to the officers and members of this Grand Lodge in order that they
may obtain the knowledge required that they can practice out of the Lodge that
which they have been taught in it.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that this Special Committee report its
findings to the Grand Master in sufficient time for him to review and study the
report and to submit his recommendations and/or decisions on the subject matter
of the report at the next Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

307

This deficiency in ongoing Masonic education has been recognized at the
Grand Lodge level for several years. It has been discussed in the Executive
Committee and the Masonic Renewal Committee, and, since three of the five
proponents are members of the Masonic Education Committee, it is likely that that
topic has arisen there as well.
Section 6160 of our California Masonic Code charges this latter
committee to promote Masonic education. Hence, the mechanism to launch such
a study is already in place, as it would fall within the purview of that committee.
It is contrary to Grand Lodge policy and general purposes to promote duplication
of effort.

Resolution No. 98-14
Establishes a Ladies Service Pin Designed by the
Grand Lodge Committee on Awards and Recognition
The proponents of this Resolution seek to establish a ladies service pin for women
who have performed admirable service to the craft or its charities.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M ofCalifornia:

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution note that a numberofMasonic scholars
believe that the craft spends more time emphasizing rote memorization than in
teaching the meaning of our Fraternity. It is true that an institutional emphasis on
memorization has been present, as is typified by our candidates' and officers'
coaching programs. On the other hand, education relating to the history, the
meaning and, perhaps most importantly, the relevance of Masonry has received
much less formal support. In fact, while each Lodge has designated coaches and
Inspectors, the only constituted individuals for Masonic Education are the members
of a single Grand Lodge committee.
The proponents wish to establish a special committee to study the
problems which this potential inequity has created, and to report back to the Grand
Master in time for recommendations to be drafted for the next Annual
Communication. The Finance Committee estimated that this will cost Grand
Lodge about $5,000.

WHEREAS, it would be appropriate to establish an award to honor ladies
for their service to the fraternity as the Hiram Award honors men who have served
the fraternity; and
WHEREAS, such award could be presented to the wife ofa Hiram Award
recipient.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Grand Lodge adopt
and make available for purchase by the constituent Lodges of this jurisdiction a
Ladies Service Pin and Certificate which shall hereafter be designed by the Grand
Lodge Committee on Awards and Recognition.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the pin and certificate may be
presented to any lady selected by the Lodge.

§27020. LIFE MEMBERSHIP.
A Lodge may adopt a standing resolution providing for a system
of life membership, which shall forever exempt a member from
the payment of dues therein. The resolution or any amendment
shall not be acted on at the Stated Meeting at which it is
introduced, or until notice in writing has been forwarded by mail
to every member of the Lodge. It must provide that life
membership shall be granted upon payment of a sum of money
named therein, which sum shall in case the annual dues are $12
be not less than $250 and the minimum amount be
proportionately greater as the dues are greater; or, in the
alternative, it may provide for the granting of such a life
membership upon payment of a sum of money equal to the
annual dues of the Lodge multiplied by the factor indicated
opposite the member's age in the following schedule:

It is the policy for Grand Lodge to make work as easy as possible for the
constituent Lodges. This objective will be accomplished in one respect, in that
Lodges will no longer have to change their dues simply to account for the changes
in the per capita assessment.

Under age 49, 21 times annual dues;
50 to 54 inclusive, 19 times annual dues;
55 to 59 inclusive, 17 times annual dues;
60 to 64 inclusive, 14 times annual dues;
65 and over, 11 times annual dues;
shall then become an executed contract requiring the consent of
the Lodge and the life member to rescind it. The resolution shall
take effect only upon its approval by the Grand Master.
When the annual dues of the Lodge are increased, the Lodge's
standing life membership resolution shall be deemed to have
been amended without further action of the Lodge to increase
the dollar amounts required for a life membership by the same
percentage that the Lodge dues have been increased.
For purposes of this Section 27020, the Lodge's "annual dues"
shall mean the rate of dues in effect on the date that the life
membership is purchased.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

This Resolution proposes to change a Lodge's dues notice to reflect the
component due to the Grand Lodge per capita assessment.

1
I~

313

This Resolution will more clearly identify the amount of the per capita to
each Mason, in particular those who are not present when this figure is announced
to his Lodge at a Stated Meeting. This is consistent with the Grand Lodge policy
of having an open financial policy for the membership.
The Resolution will create some other technical, albeit usually short term,
problems for the Lodges. It is unclear to this committee whether or not Lodges
will have to amend their By-Laws on a one-time basis to establish a new annual
dues figure. Lodges will not be able to mail the next years' dues statements until
after the close of Grand Lodge every year. This Resolution may also impact the
life membership plan. Lodges which are financially able to charge only $12/year
because they can supplement the difference will be compelled to charge their
members $12 plus the Grand Lodge per capita. As it is not the policy of Grand
Lodge to create confusion and/or extra work, the creation of such short-term
problems is inconsistent with Grand Lodge policy.
Report of the Committee on Finance:

The Finance Committee was concerned about the impact on existing life
memberships should this Resolution pass. We were assured by both the
Jurisprudence Committee and the proponents of this Resolution that the existing
life membership contract, which exempts the life member from all dues, including
per capita tax, will not be changed.
This report is for clarification purposes only as the Resolution has no
financial effect on the Grand Lodge. Therefore, the Finance Committee has no
recommendation.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

Admissions Committee
by Victor HrJward, Ph.D., and Ernest A. Poo/eon, Co-Chairmen
The Admissions Review Program of the Board is a carefully developed
analysis and evaluation process that continues to be improved and refined to meet
the evolving needs of our Applicants, as well as the Homes Staff, and the Board
itself.
Over the past several years, experience has confirmed the value of the
required overnight visit to one of the facilities by all applicants in order that
Administrators and Medical Staff can evaluate them and assist in determining the
most appropriate placement. (The facility visited is not an indication of where the
most appropriate placement might be.) A report on this overnight visit is then
added to the information sent to committee members.
Prior to the regular Board Meeting on the first Wednesday of each month,
the six Trustees who form the Admissions Committee (three from the North and
three from the South) have each received and carefully studied the applications for
Masonic assistance. Each Trustee reviews and evaluates the applications and
accompanying data, and then submits his comments and votes to the two cochairmen, who discuss the results of the vote by phone, and then present the results
at meetings of the entire committee, at which time Homes Staff Representatives
and Administrators attend and assist in the discussion. The committee's
recommendations are then presented to the full Board for final confirmation.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

319

The number of applications handled by the committee for couples,
individuals and children varies from month to month. This past year the high was
nine applications handled in one month for seniors, and three applications in one
month for children.
The ongoing reconstruction at the Union City facility continued to require
close control of admissions. However, as room became available in the Assisted
Living-Ambulatorysection, some admissions were accepted for this level of care.
And as space permitted, a number of couples were admitted where one of the
members of the couple required Assisted Living Non-ambulatory or Skilled
Nursing level of care while the other member was capable of living at the
Independent Living level of care.
During this past year the adult facility at Covina continued its expansion
of Assisted Living services. The number of Assisted Living beds was doubled, and
as a result, the need to transfer residents to facilities that offer higher levels of care
was largely diminished.
Building upon its success in providing Assisted Living care, the Covina
facility sought, and was granted, a waiver by the State of California to provide
hospice care to its terminally ill residents. This allowed Covina's residents a
palliative care option that previously was only available through placement in a
skilled nursing setting. Several residents availed themselves of this new care
option during the past year and the families of these residents were deeply
appreciative oftl\e services provided.
The Child Care Program at Covina continued to develop, and the
introduction of a limited number of non-Masonic children has proven to be of
benefit to all concerned. Careful screening by the Home's Child Care staff and
consulting psychologists has resulted in the admission of children who have
benefitted from our program of care, while developing mutually positive
relationships with our Masonic children.
The co-chairmen gratefully acknowledge the hard work and dedication of
the Trustees who are on the Admissions Committee. These members are David C.
Decker, Charles H. Alexander, Robert D. Peters, and Thomas F. Joy. We also
acknowledge the assistance and support of our two Administrators, Kelly Wiest
and Dale Ankney, and their staff.

Centennial Celebration Committee
by Jeff H. Eichner, Jr., Chairman
The Centennial Celebration Committee is charged with planning events
and activities during 1998 to celebrate the l 00-year history of the Masonic Homes.
The committee consists of Stanley M. Cazneaux, Alvin J. Weis, Kelly Wiest, Dale
Ankney, and Jeff H. Eichner, Jr.
After being formed in late 1995, the committee quickly set the theme for
the centennial, "Buildinga Future Upon a Century of Caring". Numerous activities
and events were carried out during the first half of the year that not only celebrated
the first l 00 years of the Masonic Homes of California, but strengthened rapport
and increased awareness of the Homes' facilities, services, and programs with
California Freemasons, their families and the general public.
One of the largest events of the year was the 68th Annual Conference of
the Masonic Homes Executives' Association of North America (MHEANA), that
was hosted in June 1998 by the Masonic Homes of California. Nearly 200
representatives from Masonic and Eastern Star Homes from all over the United
States attended the 4-day conference and toured the Union City Home.
A highlight of the year was the issuance of a special publication

com~e~ora~g ~e.centennial of your Masonic Homes of California. The 32-page
pubhcat1on, Butldmg A Future Upon A Century Of Caring/Masonic Homes of
California: 1898-1998",also the theme ofour centennial year, reflected in photos
and _text the loving environment provided to our residents at Union City and
Co~ma a~ the ~asonic Homes of California looks to another century of caring.
This special ed1t1on was sent to every California Mason and to other Grand Lodge
jurisdictions.
Titroughout the year the Homes at Union City and Covina hosted many
events to commemorate the Homes' centennial. The year started out with the
Family ofFreemasonry"Fun on Wheels" float in the Tournament of Roses Parade
that featu~ed children from Covina and "The Old Woman in the Shoe", a 99 years~
young Mildred Burke, also a resident of the Covina Home. Another centennial
event was a "Run for Life" to raise funds for charity and the Masonic Home at
Covina. Brother Tom Jones, a resident of the Covina Home from 1976 to 1980
ran the length of California from the Oregon border to the Mexican border (se;
California Freemason, Spring 1998 Edition).
Planning is proceeding to rededicate the Home at Union City on Saturday,
October l 0, 1998.
The Centennial Celebration Committee acknowledges with sincere
appreciation the support provided by Gloria Cazneaux and Kim Hegg in making
the MHEANA Conference a success.

Medical Advisory Committee
by Victor Howard, Ph.D., Chairman
The Medical Advisory Committee, initially established July 1, 1992, has
had as its purposes, the following:
A.

Assure the Board of Trustees that on-going medical services are
consistent with the best medical practice.

B.

Provide advisory assistance and guidance to the Board of
• Trustees as required.

C.

Provide assistance and counsel to both Medical Director and
Board when "second opinions" are appropriate or when citations
are received.

D.

Provide "Advisory Assistance and Guidance" to Medical
Director and Administratorson on-going issues or problems, as
requested by Medical Director or Administrators.

E.

Provide counsel and guidance to both Medical Director and the
Board in areas of Long Range Planning for issues, needs, and
concerns likely to arise in the future.

During the past year, the committee has worked closely with both
Administrators in reviewing the special needs of their facility. Dr. Weinreb visited
Covina on several occasions and consulted with Dale Ankney on the planned
expansion of the Assisted Living area, as well as the provision of Hospice
Services.

Under the direction of our Covina Administrator, Dale Ankney, the child
care program continues to strengthen as more House Parents received their
professional certification in the Family Home Model of Care (also known as the

house parents who had not received their professional certification. The result of

Again this year, while the rebuilding of the Union City complex is ongoing, the Administrator, Kelly Wiest, has continued to carefully monitor and
manage the staffing of the Home to ensure a continuinghigh level of flexibility and
adaptability. In addition, with the support of our Director of Human Resources,

Planned Giving Program
by Jeff H. Eichner, Jr., Director ofCharitable Giving
The Planned Giving Program is charged with the responsibility of
providing information and assistance to people on how to make gifts to the
Masonic Homes of California. During the year assistance and information was
provided to individuals, financial advisors, attorneys and accountants on various
ways to make charitable gifts.
Some of the Planned Giving Program options provide attractive and viable
ways for donors to receive a lifetime income, receive an income tax deduction, and
avoid capital gains tax, if applicable, while supporting the Masonic Homes. These
options include the Pooled Income Fund and Charitable Remainder Trusts.
The Pooled Income Fund offers an easy way to make a charitable gift to
the Masonic Homes of California and receive a lifetime income, avoid capital gains
tax, if applicable, and receive a charitable tax deduction that can be spread over six
years if necessary. During the year $82,000 was added to existing accounts, one
new account was established for $25,000, and $334,062 was transferred to the
Masonic Homes. As of June 30, 1998, the Pooled Income Fund had 69
participants with a year-end principal of$4,534,168.
During the year information and assistance was provided to many
individuals on how to establish Charitable Remainder Trusts that benefit the donor
as well as the Masonic Homes of California. In these cases, the donors receive a
lifetime income based on the full value of their gifts, avoid capital gains tax, if
applicable, and take a charitable tax deduction for up to six years.
Making a request in a will is one of the most common methods of making
gifts to the Masonic Homes and information and assistance on wills and bequests
was disseminated throughout the year. The Totten Trust is used, also, to designate
the Masonic Homes of California as the beneficiary of an individual's savings
account(s) in banks and other savings institutions. The money in the savings
account(s)belong to the donor, who can withdraw it at any time with the balance
of the account(s) going to the Masonic Homes of California at the time of the
donor's death.
Charitable giving through a living or family trust is another popular
method of making gifts to the Masonic Homes of California and information and

Policy Committee
by Charles H. Alexander, Chairman
The Policy Committee is charged with preparing changes in the Policy of
the Masonic Homes of California. These may include the preparation of a policy
statement reflecting changes made by the Board of Trustees, or the proposing of
policy changes that have been suggested by administrators ·or staff. Proposed
changes are submitted to the Board in advance, usually at the month preceding the
regular meeting when the change is scheduled for adoption. When adopted, new
pages are furnished to the staff and members of the Board for replacement of the
changed pages in the Policy Manual.

to August 1998.)

Real Estate Committee
by Robert D. Peters, Chairman
The Real Estate Committee of the Masonic Homes of California is
charged with the responsibilityof disposing of all real estate and automobiles made
available to the Masonic Homes through asset assignment, wills and bequests, gifts
and grants.

We reduced notes receivable by $518,061 during the year, and were left
with 23 notes and $737,948 in receivables at fiscal year end.
We almost always have an inventory of unsold properties, due to the Life
Care Contract signed by each new resident of the Homes. This affords them a
ninety (90) day period to adjust and satisfy their own minds that they have no
intention of withdrawing from the Masonic Home. The resident then signs a
release authorizing the sale of their property.
The Real Estate Committee and the entire Board of Trustees of the
Masonic Homes of California wish to thank the office staff in San Francisco, the
co-ordinators in the respective Home, and particularly Brother Tom McKinney,
Mrs. Betty Blidy, and Brother Doug Scott, CFO, for their continuing assistance and
support in all of these various transactions.
Scholarship Committee
by Charles H. Alexander, Chairman
1998 Grants
We madt: two continuing grants this year. Adam Perry was granted
$10,340 to continue his work in Communications and Computer Science. He
needs to "get caught up on math." (His words) He plans to eventually transfer to
a four-year college. He was encouraged to limit his work hours and concentrate on
improving his academic performance.
Joey Burns' ultimate plans are to become a Landscape Architect. He was
given his requested grant of$7,200. Again we stressed the necessity of performing
academically, and minimizing work hours if need be. He reported that he had
raised his GPA to 2.00, which is encouraging.
We made an initial grant of $4,000 to Daysha Shunn, a graduating senior.
However, this was conditional on her graduating from high school. At the time of
the interview, there was some question. Having heard nothing to the contrary, it
may be assumed that she did graduate. I tried to verify this, but Barbara TenBroek
was not available at the time of the writing of this report.
We rejected two applications for very valid reasons. In one case, the
Administrators at the Covina Home recommended that a grant be dependent upon
the applicant remaining at the home for the first year of higher education. This the

330

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

applicant declined to consider, even though we indicated that her grant might
depend upon it.

our Administrators, Staff and Residents. The theme chosen for this Centennial
Year's events is, "Building A Future Upon A Century Of Caring".

The second rejection was based upon an incomplete application. No
record was submitted of her current classes at the community college where the
applicant was currently enrolled, although it has been repeatedly requested by the
administrators.

The first major project of this special year was the publishing of our
Centennial Magazine, a copy of which was sent to every Mason in our Grand
Jurisdiction. This highly successful publication entitled, "Building A Future .upon
A Century Of Caring", was developed under the direction of Worshipful Ronald
E. Cooper, a Past Master of Burbank Lodge No. 406. The magazine portrayed
through pictures and articles an historical biography of the growth, development
and accomplishmentsof the Homes over the last one hundred years. The Board of
Trustees wants to extend our thanks to Brother Cooper for an outstanding job.

Cultural Enrichment Program
The Scholarship Committee Recommended, and the Board of Trustees
approved the initiation of a program for cultural enrichment. The funds to support
such a program would be limited to 2% of the funds available for scholarship. The
rationale for this recommendation was that many of our child residents come from
disfunctional families with related cultural deprivation.
Future Concerns
As noted in the June 1998 report of the Scholarship Committee, the funds
currently available for scholarships is larger than any foreseeable need. Without
touching the corpus of the initial bequests, there is approximately 1.2 million
dollars in accrued interest and appreciation. This amount may vary due a change
in the value of the equities, but the Board of Trustees, together with the Board's
Attorney and ChiefFinancial Officer, needs to explore ways in which these funds
can be used without violating the terms of the wills and bequests of the donors.
IRS regulations could be involved if we simply let the funds continue to accrue
without limit.
President's Report
by Stanley M Cazneaux, PGM
Nineteen ninety-eight is an historical year in the history of the Masonic
Homes of California, as it ushers in the Centennial Anniversary of our beloved
Homes. Over these one hundred years our Homes have grown, flourished and
progressed, producing facilities and care of the highest quality and caliber. The
Masonic Homes of California, should be justly proud of their accomplishments,
and for the care and concern they show for their fellow man.
On Saturday, October 10, 1998, in celebration of the Centennial
Anniversary, the Most Worshipful Anthony P. Wordlow, Grand Master of Masons
in California, conducted the Centennial Rededication Ceremonies on the steps of
the SiminoffCenter, at our Masonic Home at Union City. This was the final event
of a year long celebration. It has been an exciting year for your Board of Trustees,

331

Included in the Centennial Celebration this year, was another major event,
the hosting of the Masonic Homes Executives' Association of North America on
June 20-24, 1998, at the San Ramon Marriott Hotel at Bishop Ranch. Two hundred
(200) participants attended this annual event. Three (3) days of high quality
educational training was provided for Administrators, Staff and members of the
Boards of Trustees. In addition, there were several social events and tours provided
for the families of the delegates. The event concluded with a wonderful Banquet
Dinner and Installation of the new officers of the Association. At the dinner a gift
of three ceramic quail, made by the residents of our Homes at Union City and
Covina, was presented to all those in attendance. The Board of Trustees wants to
thank Jeff Eichner, Director of Charitable Gifts, for participating as the Chairman
of this event and to the Administrators Kelly Wiest and Dale Ankney for their
assistance in making this one of the highlights of this Masonic Homes year.
To commemorate this Centennial Year your Board of Trustees
commissioned Nancy Pratt, a well known local artist, to paint a montage painting
that would give the viewer an insight into the warmth and love in our Masonic
Homes. Nancy far exceeded our expectations with her finished work. We have
now made copies of this beautiful painting available, in limited editions, to our
lodges or for private collections. I would encourage each lodge in our Grand
Jurisdiction to purchase one of these paintings and proudly place it in a prominent
location in the lodge.
In July the Board of Trustees met in Sacramento for its Annual Weekend
Retreat. The main focus of this retreat, in addition to its regular business, is to
update the Long Range Plan for our homes. We revisited and revised our Mission
Statement as well as making some major changes in the operation of our Homes.
One change, which I am sure will meet with the approval of all lodges in our
jurisdiction, is the abolishing of the requirement for the lodges to conduct the
investigation of applicants for the home. The Homes staff will now relieve the
lodges of this time consuming task. Another major change, will be a change in the
requirement of asset assignment. Applicants will still be required to tum-over

332

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

assets but will be able to keep or gift a certain percentage. Final details are being
worked on and a policy statement will be forwarded to the lodges in the near future.
I want to extend my personal thanks to Fred Sorsabal, Chairman of the Long Range
Planning Committee, for a job well done.

Report of the Administrator

I want to take this opportunity to express the Boards appreciation for the
work done by Kira Reginato, Director of Masonic Assistance and her staff.
Without her guidance and direction many of the changes described above would
not have happened. She has carried a very heavy workload while still finding time
to train her new staff. I know that those lodges who have required her assistance
appreciate her as much as the Board Members. She is truly a great asset to our
Masonic Homes.

Centennial Year

There are many hard working Committees on our Board of Trustees, but
none harder working than the Physical Facilities Committee, under the
Chairmanship of Warren T. Buschmann. He along with Thomas F. Joy and Alvin
J. Weis, put in many hours each month to assure the very finest facilities for our
residents and staff. They are currently in the middle of a fifty (50) million dollar
earthquake retrofit program, requiring many hours of dedicated work. On behalf
of the Board, I extend our deep appreciation for their tireless work.
This report would not be complete without words of appreciation for Kelly
Wiest, Administratorofthe Union City Home and Dale Ankney, Administrator of
our Covina Home and their staffs. They are professionals of the highest quality
and their efforts on behalf of our residents is appreciated by the Board of Trustees
and every Mason in our Grand Jurisdiction.

Masonic Home, Union City

1997-1998

This year marked a major milestone for your Masonic Homes. Back in
December 1891, Grand Master William Johnston gave his official approval to the
plan for organization and maintenance of the "Masonic Widows and Orphans
Home", and a Board of Directors was appointed to oversee the project. This was
followed by the purchase of 268 acres of land near the town of Decoto on March
I 0, 1893. Construction of the Home began in 1896, and the completed Home was
dedicated by Grand Master Thomas Flint on October 12, 1898. During the first
year of operation 16 men, 5 women, I 0 boys and 6 girls were admitted to the new
Home. More information about the original dedication of this great Home can be
found in Chapter XIV "Masonic Widows' and Orphans' Home" in the book, Eifiy
Years of Masom:y in California.
On October I 0, 1998, rededication ceremonies celebrating the first 100
years of the Masonic Homes of California were held at the Union City Home with
the same excitement and commitment as the original dedication in 1898!
One highlight of this event was the display of the 1896 cornerstone casket

During the Home's Centennial year, I feel it is important to acknowledge
the previous men who played leadership roles in this distinguished 100 year
history:

"Building a Future Upon a Century of Caring" has been our year long
theme to celebrate this historical occasion. In May, all California Master Masons
received the Masonic Homes of California Centennial magazine by this same
name. This publication has an excellent historical time line, and life at both
Masonic Homes is depicted by many wonderful pictures.
However, due to major renovations underway at the facility, in another
short year the magazine could be updated to include the newly remodeled North
Wing residence containing 36 modem spacious apartments, as well as
Environmental Services, Transportationand Maintenance offices in the basement.
This renovation will also include major earthquake renovation work and a brand
new enlarged elevator.
By the tilne my next Annual Report is printed, I will be advising you of
the Main Administration or South Wing renovation. Our historic red brick exterior
will remain for these last three major building renovations.
The residents of the Home were quite active this Centennial year in
participating in several public and vendor open houses, and in making two
Centennial quilts. One of these quilts is on display in the Siminoff Center and the
other one is displayed in the Adams Residence Recreation Area. The following
residents were involved in these quilt projects:

Another notable accomplishment in this special year was the hosting of
the 68th Annual Meeting of the Masonic Home's Executive Association of North
America. On June 22, 1998, 200 participants of this conference visited our Home
for tours and a barbecue. These 200 delegates were Administrators, Chief
Executive Officers, Trustees, Grand Lodge Officers, and staff and family members
of other Masonic and Eastern Star Homes from across the country. They were
truly impressed with our Home and the care provided to our residents. Below is
a quotation from one of our visitors:
"The reception and tour that we were treated to was of
exceptional quality and of commendable pride and thoroughness. Our
entire group was continually amazed by the high degree of professional
care and first class accommodations that residents receive at the Home.
It was indeed a refreshing exhibit of how well older adults can live out the
golden years of their lives in comfort, serenity and complete peace of
mind that they will be cared for physically, emotionally, medically and
spiritually.
As we toured the different areas of the Home, the staff was
cordial, polite and very interested in showing us the areas of their
responsibility and appeared to be genuinely involved with the residents.
And, we could see the reciprocal feeling by the residents toward the
employees as if they were an extended family."

337

The Board of Trustees had the foresight to capture our Centennial History
on canvas. Nancy Pratt, a well known Bay Area water color artist, was
commissioned to do a Limited Edition Centennial watercolor.
Both Masonic Homes of California, that of Union City and Covina, are
showcased in this beautiful watercolor montage using an early Italian architectural
style. The five arches and columns of the old and new entrance to the Union City
Home provide the perfect design for the painting which provides the viewer
glimpses of indoor and outdoor scenes of the Victorian treasure. The flowered
borders show off the flora and fauna around the Home, including gladiolus from
surrounding hillsides, roses, deer, the California State flower, the Golden Poppy
and the California State bird, the Valley Quail. If you haven't seen this magnificent
painting, you are in for a real treat! Paintings may be ordered through my office
and proceeds will support the Masonic Homes.
When not involved in Centennial events, the residents of the Home
continued to use the Grider Health Center which was built in 1996 to keep our
residents healthy and active. This year the center recognized 22 residents who
earned the President's Sports Award. The President's Council, in conjunction with
national sports organizations and associations, offers the Presidential Sports _Award
Program to recognize and promote "the commitment to fitness through a~t1~e and
regular participation in sports and fitness activities." The program, adm1mstered
by AAU (American Athletic Union), has been adopted by the Grider Health Center
to encourage and reinforce consistency in participation. And it works!
Our annual population report indicates that as of June 30, 1998 we had
226 residents, 58 Masons and 168 spouses/widows. There were 20 couples and the
average age is 87.
Once again we are grateful to the many Masonic affiliated groups who
have assisted the Home in various ways. During the past year there were 60
Masonic Lodge visits, 14 Eastern Star Chapter visits, 33 Assemblies of Rainbow
Girls visits, and 6 Bethels of Jobs Daughters visits.

As the dawn of a new century approaches, the Masonic Home at Covina
is well-positioned to continue serving children and adults alike. Thanks to the
generosity of our membership and the dedicated service of a professional staff,
there is little doubt that the Covina Home will continue to set the standard of care
for those in need in the new millennium.
Last year I described the many innovations we have implemented in order
to better serve the residents of the Home. That tradition has continued during this
past year, but it has taken on somewhat of a new form. Our goal during this past
year was to refine our existing programs, and through that refinement process,
identify enhancements to our programs that will allow our residents to receive the
maximum benefit from our staff's efforts.
Perhaps the greatest effort put forth at Covina during the past year was on
the children's side of our campus. As I have previously reported, the Covina
Home elected two years ago to revise its child care program in order to better meet
the needs of a more challenging clientele. By challenging, I mean that the children
who were in residence at the Home when we revised our program were children
who had little understanding of what the meaning of family really was. Typically,
a child resident at.the Home had come to us from an environment that included
neglect, abuse and sometimes abandonment. Family support was foreign to their
way of thinking, and because of the child's unfortunate family experience, the term
family took on a negative connotation. Our ultimate goal was to change that way
of thinking.
The means we chose to help our children was to implement the Family
Home Model of Care, a care model developed by Dr. Montrose Wolf of the
University of Kansas, and practiced with great success at Boys Town group homes
nationwide. The primarycomponentofthis program is the employment of married
couples to serve as Family Specialists (formerly known as house parents) in each
individual cottage. These married couples, often accompanied by their own
children, live with our child residents and serve as family role models. Now in our
third year with this model, we have made great strides in improving our staff's
professional skills and establishing a nurturing environment for the children we are
here to serve.
During the past year, three of our Family Specialist couples have been
certified as professional practitioners of the Family Home Model of Care. The
process of becoming certified is extremely difficult, requiring many hours of

350

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

classroom training; in-home observations by our psychologists, consultants and
Director of Children's Services; and evaluations by consumers, including the
children for whom the Family Specialists are held accountable, the children's
school teachers, and their families. More importantly, it is a continuous process
of review. Re-certification is required every year, and only after a Family
Specialist couple receives their re-certification are they entitled to consideration for
a merit pay increase. Failure to become re-certified after a number of attempts is
grounds for severe disciplinary action.
To date, the increased professionalism of our staff has led to marked
improvements in the lives of the children we serve. Most of our children are
gaininga betterunde rstandingo fwhat"fam ily"really means, and because ofthis,
our children are learning to respect one another. That respect has translated into
improved behaviors, not only at home, but in the classroom as well. This in tum
has led to improved academic performance and heightened self esteem. As a
further sign of the success we are enjoying with our new model of care, at the
conclusion of the annual survey conducted by the California Department of Social
Services, our licensing analyst rewarded us with a deficiency-free report.
An additional refinement of our child care program during the past year
was the implementation of improved assessment methods for children applying for
admission. As a direct consequence of the Fratemity'soverwhelmingendorsement
of the Board's recommendation to open the Home to all deserving children within
the jurisdiction, we made it a priority to establish assessment tools that would
ensure only appropriate children were admitted to the Home. By appropriate, we
mean children who can benefit from the model of care we employ, and who are
judged by our professionals and staff to possess the capability of positively
influencing our overall community. To date, our new assessmenttools have served
us well.
At the close of the past year there were 25 children in residence at Covina.
In addition to those in residence, our Director of Children's Services was in the
process of conducting assessments on five young people. As our reputation for
serving non-Masonic as well as Masonic children grows, we expect our census to
increase dramatically. Our new fiscal year budget provides funding for 35
children, or a 40% increase over last year. If in fact we have 35 children in
residence by year end, we can all share a sense of pride in knowing that our great
fraternity has provided much to the many, who are all too familiar with the least
in life.
Similar to the children's side of our campus, our adult home experienced
a year ofrefineme nt and limited expansion. The overall census for the adult home
remained on par with last year, but the character of that census continued to

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

351

change. With the average age of our residents climbing to 86 years, the nature of
our care continued to move in the direction of assisted living.
Assisted living care can best be described as personal care required by
elders who are unable to independently provide for their own activities of daily
living. Assistance in dressing, bathing and ambulating, as well as assistance in the
administration of a resident's centrally stored medications are common
characteristics of this level of care. Despite the quasi-medical nature of assisted
living care, state regulations do not require licensed medical personnel to
administer to assisted living residents. As an example of our commitment to
quality care however, we employ licensed vocational nurses around the clock,
seven days per week. These highly qualified professionals are assisted by certified
nurse assistants, and the entire program at Covina is regularly reviewed by a
Medical Director and our licensed Director of Adult/Health Services.
By the end of this past year, over one-half of the adults residing at Covina
were receiving some type of assisted living service. This tremendous escalation
in demand caused us to expand our Assisted Living accommodations to include the
Beachwood building in addition to the existing Ashwood building. We have also
taken the step of re-licensing our entire campus as a non-ambulatory facility,
thereby allowing us to provide Assisted Living care throughout the entire facility,
should the need arise.
Because of the success we have enjoyed with our Assisted Living
program, manage111entrecommended,and the Board approved, the construction of
a new building designed to provide an improvement in our care delivery service.
Known as our Assisted Living complex, the new building will be centrally located
within the adult community and will be connected to each of our adult residential
buildings. Housed within the building will be our nursing staff; medical facilities
such as examination rooms, therapy rooms, and a dental office; and dining and
activity rooms. At the maximum, the distance from any one of our resident's
rooms to this new complex will be half what it is to our main adult complex today.
It is our sincere belief that this central location coupled with the overall expansion
of building space will enhance our ability to serve our residents, and will improve
the overall quality of care at Covina.
In addition to expanded Assisted Living care, the Covina Home applied
for, and received, the necessary licensing to provide hospice care to its residents.
For those terminally ill residents who choose the hospice care option, it will no
longer be necessary for them to receive their hospice care outside their home. Our
new licensing, togetherwith our newly establishedrelationship with Citrus Valley
Health Partners, will allow our residents to remain in their homes, near their
families, while they receive the palliative care offered by the hospice service. To
date, six residents have chosen the hospice service offered by the Covina Home,

352

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

and the residents and their families have been extremely pleased with the care
provided.
As I hope you can see from this report. it was indeed a busy year at the
Covina Home, but one that was different than those of the recent past. We
deliberately slowed the pace of change a bit in order to allow ourselves the
opportunity to refine the innovative programs we introduced just several years
earlier. That pause has served us well, and we now look forward with renewed
optimism to the challenges that confront us in the new millennium.
It would be misleading if I did not mention that in addition to the
important programs we refined during the past year, we also had quite a bit of fun
around here. We hosted many events to celebrate our Centennial year of service,
including an Easter egg hunt, which attracted in excess of 200 children; a
Children'sday celebration, which included every game imaginable, as well as the
antics of those world famous Shrine clowns; and our children had the special treat
of vacationing on the east coast where they visited such noteworthy sites as
Colonial Williamsburg, Fort Sumter, South Carolina, Cape Canaveral Space
Center, and Walt Disney World in Orlando, Florida.
Our adults even got into the swing of things this past year. Thanks to the
generosity and flexibility of Mount San Antonio College, the College conducted
water color painting classes on our campus. Many of our residents participated in
the classes and were enthusiastic about the success of the program. In fact, the
program was such a success that in September, 1998, our campus will become a
satellite school for the college. In addition to our own seniors, seniors throughout
the nearby community will be attending classes at our Home. This will be a
wonderful way for our senior residents to make new friends, and in the process, it
will allow the outside community to better understand why we think Freemasonry
is something very special.
I would be remiss ifl did not thank you, the members of the Fraternity,
who make all of these good works possible. Not only are we at the Home thankful
for your financial support, we are equally grateful for your personal interest in our
Home.

Children Residents
July 1, 1997 - June 30, 1998

I receive calls throughoutthe year asking if it would be an inconvenience
if the caller were to stop by to learn more about the Home. Let me assure you that
your visit will never be inconvenient for us. A key part of our mission is to make
sure that you understand how we are serving the needs of our residents. By
acquiring this knowledge, we know you will feel pride in your continuing support,
and you will be better prepared to explain to those outside the Craft what
Freemasonry stands for. Working together, we will most assuredly succeed in
making our Homes and Freemasonry even better in the future.

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers and Members of the Grand
Lodge. Brethren: I am happy to report to you a very successful year for your
Masonic Homes Endowment Fund for the fiscal year that ended June 30, 1998. If
you paid close attention to the latest issue of the Ca/ifornai Freemason you will
have seen a three page listing of your Brethren who contributed at least $100 to the
Fund during last year. In the next issue you will see an even larger list of those
who contributed between $50 and $100. It is gratifying to recognize that over three
thousand of our Brethren are numbered in this distinguished group. The reported
numbers of those major contributors this year was over twice the number for last
year. This is a significant accomplishment.
Because of our declining membership, we have seen, during the past few
years, a steady decrease in the total dollars received annually into the Endowment
Fund. This year, however, there was the possible indication that the trend may be
reversing. Whereas previous years have dropped as much as ten percent below the
year before, this year's decrease was only one half of one percent! I certainly hope
that this represents a renewed interest in the support for our Homes, and a
regeneration of the dedication that caused the Homes to be created l 00 years ago.
It is time that the contributions begin to increase instead of decrease, at least to
keep up with the growth of inflation.
Total gifts to the Endowment Fund last year were as follows:
Wills & Bequests

$2,267' 772.58

Contributions through Lodges

1,008,780.42

Through United Way

7,877.39

Undesignated Gifts

7,118.00

Memorial Contributions

3,815.32

Total Gifts

$3.295 363 71

There are a few significant things about the giving pattern to this major
Masonic activity that are worthy of note. First, the average contribution for the
Grand Lodge overall (that is total giving divided by total membership) was $10.15
- a five percent increase over last year. The average among actual contributors
was $28.13. That latter number has increased by over 50 percent in the last ten

359

The negative part of the picture, however, continues to be that the
percentage of California Masons making any contribution to the Homes decreases
every year. This year only 36 percent of us participated in this important charity.
That is a pretty small representation. I often wonder why that is. Perhaps the
reason is that the brothers who recognize the significance of the Endowment Fund
are either passing on or not able to participate any more. Perhaps we are not
educating our newly-raised brethren to the importance of their support to the
Homes. If that is true, then I must challenge each one of you to return to your
Lodges and make a significant effort to pass the word along. The Masonic Homes
of California, that fantastic facility that is taking care of our needy brethren and
their wives, and helping us as Masons to fulfill our charitable obligation, absolutely
depends on ~ to give it the resources needed to continue its outstanding efforts.
I now want to give you some interesting news that will make it easier, and
hopefully more attractive, to support the Homes Endowment Fund. We have set
up a system whereby donations can be made by credit card. You can make a taxfree gift to the fund, and earn frequent flyer miles at the same time! Your Lodge
Secretary will have the necessary information. There are new envelopes available
to use for direct, credit card gifts. I encourage you to take advantage of this new,
modem, twenty-~rrst century method to fulfill your Masonic duty.
We have had a pretty good year, and I trust that next year will be even
better. I challenge each of you to renew your dedication to this weighty
responsibility. For what you have done, and what you will do, I thank you, the
Endowment Board thanks you, the Grand Master thanks you, and every resident
of the Masonic Homes thanks you with all of their hearts.
Respectfully submitted,
W. Bruce Pruitt, Chairman

to our fraternity .

Most Worshipful Grand Master, Grand Lodge Officers, Past Grand
Masters, Distinguished Visitors, and my brethren all.
It is with a great sense of pride and appreciation that I stand before you
today, as this will be my last annual report as President of your California Masonic
Memorial Temple Board of Trustees. I have been on the Board seven years with
the last five of those years as your President. By California Masonic Code law I
must step down. Not only as President but also off the Board completely. But fear
not my brethren our Deputy Grand Master has already see to it that I shall be heard
from again from a different direction.

As you will hear about shortly from Nob Hill Masonic Management, we
have jointly entered into an agreement where Nob Hill is taking over the normal
wear and tear items of the building. ADA upgrades that were funded by CMMT
are almost completed. The new meeting room where the old library and museum
used to be that was funded by CMMT is almost completed.
The primary purpose of CMMT, as I see it, is now to look to long term
capital expenditures. Things such as $300,000 boilers that are 40+ years old.
Things like $85,000 compressors that are also 40+ years old, or the $750,000
elevator. The list goes on and on. So there was a definite need for this mutual
agreement between the two entities. Without it we would still be spending our
time fighting fires instead of preventing them.
Part of the joint agreement was a new lease arrangement with a cap on the
lease payments that NHMM pays to CMMT. There are several reasons we agreed
to this. Many of which wil be explained by NHMM's report on the fair wear and
tear part of the agreement. The other, of course, is to allow more funds to flow into
Grand Lodge each year. The cap on the lease also allows for a modest 4% or so
increase each year. With the cap less our usual expenses plus already planned
projects we will still be able to put a little aside each year for capital expenditures.
I might mention that one project that is still ongoing is the feasibility study
of cleaning and or restoring the beautiful mosaic in the lobby. We have had several
professional people involved in looking it over. Brother Doug Scott, our Chief
Financial Officer, is heading up the project.
I would be remiss ifl didn't mention Brother Kevin Tuck and the job he
has done with our newest gem on top of Nob Hill, The Henry Wilson Coil Library
and Museum. It truly is a magnificent edifice. It is a showcase for Freemasonry
just as it was planned to be.

My brethren, yes I may be the President and be in the spotlight, but let me
tell you this, it is these hard working brethren that make things happen. One
person cannot make things happen. It takes a team approach. If I may borrow the
definition of TEAM from our Prince Hall Brethren, Together Each Accomplishes
More. Brethren, this team has worked together for over 5 years. Look around you
my brethren and see if Together Each "HAS" Accomplished More.
I would like to extend my heartfelt thanks to the office staff on the third
floor. Teena, Pam, Kimberly, Gloria, Judy, Brother Mark Johnson, as well as all
the rest of the staff, have done an exemplary job of meeting our every requirement.
Very Worshipful John Cooper has picked his staff well!
To all the Past Grand Masters that I have served under, it has been both
a privilege and a pleasure to work with all of you. Thank you all for your support.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
As a preface to Nob Hill's formal report it is important for you, our
stockholders, to know that the Temple Board (owner's of this center) and Nob Hill
( the operators of this Center) enjoy the power of a shared vision mutually
developed That shared vision briefly stated is" .... to do everything necessary
and required to prepare The Masonic Center for another forty or more years of
service to Freemasonry." Because of this shared vision it is nearly impossible to
report the activities of one without including the activities of the other. As an
example, later when I report to you concerning the ADA work you should be
aware that the Temple funded the work and Nob Hill either performed or
administered the entire project. When, two organizations (The Temple and Nob
Hill) have a shared vision mutually developed the accomplishments of each
contributes to the success of the other. In this instance the real beneficiary is
neither organization, but rather, as it should be, California Freemasonry and you
my brethren its members.
As President and on behalf of the Board of Directors, I am pleased to
present the sixth annual operating and financial report for Nob Hill Masonic
Management, Inc. (Nob Hill). This report is different in content and scope from
all other reports presented during the Annual Communication because Nob Hill is
the one and only for-profit entity owned and operated by this Grand Lodge. Nob
Hill was established to operate the California Masonic Memorial Center's
auditorium, parking garage, exhibit hall and various rental properties under terms
of a lease with the California Masonic Memorial Temple. This report deals with
the operationsofNob Hill forthe fiscal year just completed, July 1, 1997 through
June 30, 1998, and will cover operations with limited financials. As you are
aware, full, complete and audited financial statements for Nob Hill are provided
together with all other Grand Lodge financial reports by the Grand Treasurer and
published in the Annual Proceedings.
Having spent most of my working life in a publicly traded corporation I
am well aware that truly outstanding, across-the-board record performance is as
rare as it is exciting. And I am both excited and gratified to be able to report both
record revenue and record profit. How successful was fiscal 1997/1998?

Record financials reflect only a part of this past year's overall success.
About halfway through the past fiscal year Nob Hill assumed responsibility for all
Fair-Wear, and Tear expenses connected with the Masonic Center. In doing so
Nob Hill established a Five (5) Year Fair-Wear and Tear Project Schedule.
The budget and commitment was for a minimum average annual
expenditures of $100,000. As can be expected with all such programs the first
year or two call for the largest expenditures. By the end of fiscal year 1998-1999
these special projects are expected to cost in excess of $300,000. Obviously to
generate the required funds we expect to spend-down a large portion of the
$195,000 in retained earnings reported to you, a moment ago.
Before I address this special category of expenses, I would first note that
the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) settlement we reported to you last year
caused us to delay nearly all of the Fair-Wear and Tear Project work until the ADA
work was substantially completed. I would also note that the ADA work itself
cost us an estimated three months of bookings in order to allow time for design and
engineering, permits, construction and clean-up all as needed to meet or exceed the
ADA requirements. How fortunate it was that last year's extradorinaryand record
performance prov1ded the funds needed to carry us over what would have been a
difficult period in our history. Because of the extensive scope and considerable
impact of the ADA work (which cost the Temple over $350,000), I would like to
highlight a few specific ADA work items. As I do so, those lodges who own
Masonic Centers and similar facilities rented to the general public may want to
consider what work, if any, they may need to undertake to comply with ADA
requirements. As you are aware from previous Nob Hill reports our ADA work
was fully defined as a result of a legal settlement. Without such guidance most of
us find the ADA requirements difficult to identify, define and understand. Our
advice based on extensive experience is to retain, at the earliest possible date, one
or more qualified experts: Architects, Consultants and Contractors, familiar with
ADA compliance.
Now to the specific ADA work we have undertaken here in the Masonic
Center:
I.

Accessible seating in the front of the Auditorium (required us to
level this area, create seating for 10 wheelchairs, with permanent

REPORT OF THE
COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE

Respectfully submitted,
R. Stephen Doan, PGM, Chairman

To the Most Worshipfal Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
The Committee on Jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the Grand
Master and the legal adviser to Grand Lodge when in session. The Committee
reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations to be considered at the next
Annual Communication and prepares any necessary legislation to carry out the
intent of the proponents. At the Annual Communication, it comments on the
legality of the Grand Master's decisions and dispensations and on the legal effect
of the proposed recommendations and resolutions.
After the Annual
Communication, it prepares the changes to the California Masonic Code to reflect
the legislation which was adopted.
In the Committee's view, those of Grand Master Wordlow' s decisions and
dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within his discretion. In the
Committee's view, the legislation mailed by the Grand Secretary on July 15th of
this year is sufficient to carry out the intent of the proponents, and the legislation
contained in GrandMasterWordlo w'srecommendations which he will present in
his message is sufficientto carry out his intent. We believe that each piece of this
legislation has the legal effect set forth in it.
The legislation mailed by the Grand Secretary on July 15th of this year and
the legislation contained in Grand Master Wordlow'srecommendations require no
separate motion because they are automatically before this Annual
Communication. The presiding officer will announce the vote required for passage
of each item before discussion begins. The presiding officer will announce the
vote required for passage of each item before discussion begins. Any legislation
which does not amend the California Masonic Code or the Ritual requires a simple
majority only for adoption. Any amendment to the California Masonic Code or
the Ritual must be adopted by a five-sixths affirmative vote. If the amendment
receives a simple majority but less than a five-sixths affirmative vote, it carries
over to the next Annual Communication when only a two-thirds affirmative vote
is required for adoption.
We thank the Grand Master for the opportunity which he has given us to
serve this year.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
MASONIC HISTORY
The work of the Grand Lodge Masonic History Committee during 1998
has been largely concerned with carrying out the 1984 Recommendation No. 4 of
Grand Master E. Arthur Haglund that the Masonic History Committee ... "plan the
writing and printing of an appropriate history to commemorate the 150th
Anniversary of this Most Worshipful Grand Lodge and to recommend other
possible activities." The Recommendation was approved.
At the 1990 Annual Communication, it was voted to set aside the money
to finance the publication. Because of the magnitude of planning and writing of
the proposed publication, this year, the "other activities" were assigned to another
committee.
When the History Committee was reorganized following the 1997 Annual
Communication, it was decided, following consultation with the Executive
Committee, that a collection of individual Lodge histories was not the desired
format for the publication. As a result, the Committee determined that an "issue"
oriented publication was desired. A publication is now being planned for release
early in the year 2000. It will consist of one-year write-ups of each of the years
1950 to 1999. These write-ups will be very condensed, with only one page for
each year. Living Past Grand Masters have been asked to review the year of their
presiding, and have made many helpful suggestions for additions, deletions, or
clarifications.
In addition, a series of articles on various issues that have been central to
the last fifty years are planned. Examples of these are: "Modification of
Proficiencies," "Physical Qualifications," "Formation of the Grand Lodge of
Hawaii," "Adoption of the Cipher Ritual," "Rose Parade Floats" and "Recognition
of Prince Hall Masonry." There are several other timely topics as well. In addition,
short histories of our Masonic youth groups, and Masonically related bodies, the
York Rite, Scottish Rite and the Shrine are included. Where appropriate, and
available, we will make extensive use of pictures.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON MASONIC SERVICE BUREAUS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
The Committee on Masonic Service Bureaus, serving the Grand Lodge
of California for 71 years, submits the following data as its Annual Report for the
fiscal year ending June 30, 1998.
The Committee takes its directive to supervise the operations of the
several Masonic Service Bureaus within the borders of the great state of California
most seriously. These Bureaus which now number 10, extend from Sacramento
in the North to San Diego in the South. Their charge is to render assistance to
distressed worthy Brothers, their widows and orphans residing in the jurisdiction
of the Grand Lodge F.& A.M. of California. Sojourners as well as California
Masons are entitled to receive assistance when the situation requires it. The
Committee also assists the Masonic Service Association in the continuing
development of its "Hospital Visitation Program" at several of the Veterans
Administration Facilities in California. Members of the Committee in conjunction

Committee Members
The 1997-98 Committee consists of Wor. Paul Brown of San Diego, Wor.
Robert W. Meier of Los Angeles, Wor. William H. Murphy of Fresno, Wor.
George C. Hesse of San Jose and Wor. Howard J. Dumont of Elverta, who serves
as Chairman.
In Memoriam
It is with heavy hearts this committee reports the loss of Committeeman
Paul Brown. He was called to that house not made with hands on May 16, 1998.
There are few who will pass by this way as good and noble as he.
Executive Secretaries
The Executive Secretaries of the 10 Service Bureaus who serve our
fraternity deserve special recognition for the long hours that are required to
perform the duties required of the office. The full spectrum of their duties cover
such items as: answering questions from the general public (about Masonry);
tracking down those Brethren that have lost touch with their home Lodge;
communicating with the member Lodges regarding Masonic funerals,
investigationsand dissemination of information regarding charlatans who wish to
defraud a Masonic Lodge and tracking the financial condition of the respective
Bureau. To these Brethren, this Committee expresses its' deepest gratitude.
Bush Masonic Relief Inc.
Bush Masonic Relief Inc. is the primary source of funding for the three
Service Bureaus (Los Angeles, Long Beach & San Gabriel Valley) in the greater
Los Angeles area. This fund which provides a majority of the funds for these
Bureaus, is the result of very careful investment by the trustees of the fund. This
Committee wish to acknowledge the hard work of the Trustees, Wor. Bro. A.
Bruce Ivie, Very Worshipful Herbert P. Wilkins, Past Grand Treasurer of this
Grand Lodge and the Right Wor. Bro. Mel Nahin who is currently serving as our
Deputy Grand Master.

Pasadena Scottish Rite Center on Saturday, April 18, 1998. The purpose of the
meeting, as in years passed, was distribution and explanation of the several report
forms required to put together the annual statistical analysis. This year's analysis
is detailed at the end of this narrative. A meeting of the Executive Secretaries for
the northern part of California was not held as a cost cutting measure. The
distribution of the annual report forms required by this Committee was via U.S.
Mail.
The Committee encountered two items that were not resolved during this
fiscal year. The first was a hold over from the preceding two years, that of
consolidation of the Bureaus in the San Francisco Bay Area. Many of the member
Lodges were of the opinion that loss oflocal control and having this consolidation
pushed upon them was unfair. The Most Worshipful Allen B. Gresham asked for
a meeting to be held on July 12, 1997 in which the member Lodges could
participate in an open discussion. Most Worshipful Gresham moderated the
meeting and ended it with a promise to seek an amenable solution to their
concerns.
In March of 1998 the Grand Secretary, John L. Cooper III, Assistant
Grand Lecturer of Division I, Edward P. Margherio and the Chairman of this
Committee, met at the offices of our Grand Lodge in San Francisco. The Very
Worshipful Cooper and Worshipful Margherio proposed that the business of the
San Francisco Service Bureau be handled by two "sub" offices. One would be
located in Oakland(to handle the affairs of the old East Bay and Southern Alameda
Bureaus) and the other in San Francisco. The offices would be located at a
Masonic Lodge with a qualified Brother from each area to perform the duties of
Executive Secretary. The funds for the operating expenses would be from two
sources: Per Capita taxes from the member Lodges and the income generated by
the funds held by the San Francisco Bureau. This proposal has been approved by
the Most Worshipful Anthony P. Wordlow.
The second problem emanated from the Central Valley Bureau. Hanford
Lodge No. 279 joined the Central Valley Bureau in January 1997. In September
1997, the Lodge voted to withdraw from the Bureau citing their reason( s) for such
action as "... no services or visits were afforded Hanford Lodge." This Committee
rejected their request as the reasons given were not of a substantial nature to
warrant "good cause" as required by the California Masonic Code Section 28020.
This matter has been put in the hands of the Grand Master and this Committee
awaits his decision.

Four of the Service Bureaus provide and maintain a Blood Bank. The
Bureaus which provide this service to our Fraternity are: Sacramento, San
Francisco, Bakersfield, and Central Valley (Fresno).

380

Uniform Compacts
Uniform Compacts, which serve as a written agreement between the
Masonic Lodge and the local Service Bureau, were finalized for the following
Lodges:
Orange County, Yorba Linda No. 469
San Diego, Black Mountain No. 845
Conclusion
This Committee sincerely appreciates the support it has received from the
Most Worshipful Anthony P. Wordlow, the elected and appointed corps ofofficers,
and the staff of the Grand Lodge office in San Francisco. Recognition is also given
to those special Masons who give of their time to act as Officers of the Masonic
Service Bureaus. Last, and of course not least, this Committee extends its greatest
admiration and appreciation to those ten Master Masons who serve this Fraternity
as Executive Secretaries of their respective Service Bureaus.

TOURNAMENT OF ROSES PARADE FLOAT

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
Your Committee is charged with the responsibility of arranging all of the
necessary details associated with entering a Masonic Float in the Pasadena Rose
Parade on New Year's Day each year. The purpose of entering a float in this
Parade is summarized briefly as follows:
l.

Freemasonry is presented to the public in a positive manner by
displaying some of our principles and accomplishments,
especially our concern for children and our charitable support in
the community. We hope that this exposure will offset the
negative perceptions of Freemasonry promulgated by our critics
and adversaries.

2.

The anniversaries of the various Masonic organizations provide
opportunities to demonstrate to the public that these groups have
long been a part of the Family ofFreemasonry, working together
for the benefit of the community.

3.

The float provides an exciting opportunity for our young people
to be involved in an outstanding project.

4.

The float videos which record the entire process of putting a
float in the Parade also provide some information about the
fraternity which is helpful in explaining Freemasonry to nonMasons.

The committee has participated in meetings for Inspectors, Lodge officers
and Temple Association officers by making presentations and answering questions
from the floor in each meeting.
During the year, the committee has received numerous requests for
approval of purchase, sale or renovation of Temple sites throughout the state, in
excess of $50,000 each, which were analyzed and reviewed by the Chairman for
decision by the Executive Committee of the Grand Lodge. In accordance with the
regulations established by the Grand Lodge, when requests were received for
approval of renovation of Temple sites which were less than $50,000 in total
expenditure, these requests were dealt with by the committee members individually
or by the Chairman of the committeewithoutreferenceto the Executive Committee
based upon the amount to be considered.
Respectfully submitted,
Harry G. Golden, Chairman
