The scope of the Committee's tasks includes the selection of the float
theme, design of the float, contract negotiations with the float builder, fund raising
from members of the Masonic fraternity on a voluntary basis, liaison with the
Tournament of Roses Organization and the float builder, selection of float riders,
publicity, float decoration, food service for the decorators, costumes,
accommodation for float riders, photography and videography, design and sales of
merchandise relating to the float, and many other details.
The theme of the 1998 Rose Parade was "HAV'N FUN". The 1998
Parade coincided with the l OOth anniversary of the Masonic Homes of California,
the 75th Anniversary of the Shriners' Hospitals and the 125 1h Anniversary of the
Order of Eastern Star. Following the great public and media reception of our 1996
float depicting Humpty Dumpty, we decided that the 1998 float would be based on

391

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

another storybook rhyme "The Little Old Woman Who Lived in A Shoe". The
float consisted of a large shoe built in the form of a roller blade shoe with a roof
over the top from which smoke poured out as the shoe was careening down the
street headed for Pasadena. It encountered a skunk in the road and came to a halt
just in time with its front wheels spinning in the air. The title of the float was
"FANTASY ON WHEELS". As the float passed along the Parade route, music
was played to the tune of "The Little Old Lady From Pasadena".
The 35 foot float was designed and built by Phoenix Decorating Co.,
Pasadena at a cost of $80,000 for the float contract which includes the design,
rendering, construction, decoration materials, music, float driver, observer and
insurance. Additional Committee expenses include the entry fee of $1,000,
publicity and fund raising expenses, mailing, video production, photography,
costumes, office supplies and food for the decorators which collectively totaled
approximately $15,000. Thus the total cost of the 1998 float was approximately
$95,000.
The float was adorned with an assortment of seeds, leaves and more than
20,000 flowers, all carefully prepared and placed by a team of about 600 members
of the many organiz.ationscomprisingthe Family of Freemasonry who spent more
than 6000 hours decorating the float. Fortunately, the Masonic float was the 39th
unit in the Parade of l 05 units, ensuring that it would be shown on the national
television networks before these stations cut away to football games.
Riders on the float consisted of ten children and two "old women". One
of the ladies was Melissa Cronin, a tireless decorator of many Masonic floats, who
rode in the top of the shoe while seated at a steering wheel. The other "old
woman" was 99-year old Mrs. Mildred (Dolly) Burke, a resident of the Masonic
Home at Covina. All of the riders were dressed in roller blade safety helmets and
pads. Dolly Burke was believed to be the oldest person ever to ride in the Rose
Parade. She was the star of the Parade in many respects. The press and television
reporters spent many hours with her before and after the Parade. The Parade TV
commentators also spent much of the float's exposure time (approximately one
minute) talking about Dolly while the children waved to the very receptive
audience along the Parade route and the 500 million people viewing the Parade in
more than 100 countries around the world. The Family of Freemasonry was the
recipient of much positive publicity with the appearance of this float.

Hospitals, Scottish Rite clinics, York Rite hospitals, scholarships for children and
the Masonic Model Student Assistance Program. Unfortunately, commentators
did not cover these items completely.
The Committee felt that this float was one of the more successful floats
in terms of the viewing public's ability to recognize and be amused by the float
design and the publicity for Freemasonrythrough Dolly Burke's presence and her
lively comments.
Immediately after the 1998 Parade, work began on the selection of a float
design for the 1999 Parade. Because of some earlier rumors that several float
sponsors might not be invited to participate in upcoming Parades, we made a
conscious decision to enter a larger and more expensive float in the 1999 Parade
so that we would be in a position to be invited to sponsor a float in the 2000 Parade
which is expected to be an elaborate affair. The 1999 float is 55 feet in length and
is designed as a replica of the original Hunt Club horse-drawn carriage with eight
riders. The riders will be prominent people, including some Masons, who have
played important roles in the history of the Rose Parade, the city of Pasadena,
government and entertainment industries. The design has been strongly endorsed
by the President of the Tournament of Roses. The total outlay for this float will be
$132,000.
Fund raising for this program continues to be a problem as voluntary
contributions from Grand Lodges, Constituent Lodges, other organizations and
individuals have been steadily declining each year. Contributions during 1997 for
the 1998 float amounted to only $38,500. Fortunately, in 1995, Grand Master
Charles H. Alexander offered his support through the adoption of a Grand Master's
gift pin program proposed by Affmity Marketing Associates. This program was
very successful and enabled the Float Committee to fulfill its financial obligations
by drawing on some of these funds. Grand Master Allen B. Gresham continued
the pin program during his term as Grand Master and thus ensured that the
Rainbow girls would not be disappointed. We are especially grateful to Grand
Master Alexander and Grand Master Gresham for their vision and assistance in our
hour of need. Unfortunately, some problems occurred with the program for the
current year and no funds were obtained for the float program. However, by
drawing on the previously mentioned funds, we will be able to meet our 1999 float
obligations.
The future of the float program is uncertain at this point. After seven
years, it is quite apparent that the voluntary contribution method of fund raising has
run its course both in California and in other Grand Lodges and associated
organizations. We hope to be able to sponsor a float in the year 2000 to help
celebrate the beginning of a new century and, hopefully, the beginning of a turnaround in Masonic membership.

390

In the words of the nursery rhyme, the Old Woman " had so many
children, she didn't know what to do, so she fed them some broth without any
bread, then whipped them all soundly and put them to bed". We took advantage
of this wording to draft a TV script which pointed out that Masons know what to
do with children - treat them with love and care. The script then covered the
support that Masons provide to children, through the Masonic Homes, Shrine

The Float Committee has produced a video of each year's float, including
the design, construction and decorating of the float and the television coverage
during the Parade. In addition to providing a record of each float for historical
purposes, these videos serve as useful tools for informing friends and the general
public about various aspects of the Family of Freemasonry. We also furnish a
complimentary copy of each video to every Grand Lodge in North America for use
in their jurisdictions.
The Committee wishes to thank the Trustees of the Masonic Homes of
California for permission to invite some of the children and Dolly Burke to be
riders on the 1998 float. The assistance of staff members at the Covina Home in
procuring safety items for the riders, providing transportation to the Parade with
the Homes bus and arranging lunch for the group after the Parade is also greatly
appreciated.
Again, the Committee gratefully acknowledges the contributions of many
individuals and organizations in the success of the program. In addition to the
Lodges and other organizations which contributed financially, we wish to thank
members of Al Malaikah Shrine RV Club who, for several years, have stationed
their motor homes at the beginning of the Parade to keep the riders warm and
nourished prior to boarding the float, Pasadena Temple which also made
arrangements for facilities in which to hold the New Year's Eve party for the youth
decorators, Pasadena Scottish Rite for the use of their meeting facilities, Southern
California Research Lodge for assisting with the distribution of float flyers through
their regular mailings to members, members of the York Rite and Shrine who
provided food service to the decorators for more than a week and, last but not least,
the approximately 600 volunteer decorators who turned out to add their touch to
the beauty of the float. We also are indebted to Mrs. Melissa Cronin for her
untiring efforts to coordinate the youthful decorators, to Mr. and Mrs. William
LaValley for coordinating the adult decorators and to Mrs Saundra Coe for her
devoted work in handling the decorator registration and sale of float memorabilia.

The Float Committee is convinced that the continual presence of the
Family of Freemason ry in the Rose Parade is a cost-effective way to inform the
public about some aspects of Freemasonry. It is the only Masonic public relations
program in existence which reaches a potential audience of almost half a billion
people in more than 100 countries throughout the world. Through this !)oat
program, we hope to increase the awareness of the fraternity and its good works,
but we also recognize that the float program is only one part of a series of efforts
needed to attract high quality members in the future. We hope that our efforts meet
with your approval. We are always receptive to suggestions for improving our
performance and enhancing the image of the fraternity in the community.

REPORT OF THE COMMIT TEE
ON TRIAL REVIEW

To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F.& A.M ofCalifornia:
Since the 1997 Annual Communication there have been referred to your
Committee on Trial Review eleven completed trials, and one application for
restoration from expulsion. Two restorations from suspension were considered at
the Lodge level. These are reviewed by the committee and the Grand Lodge only
when exceptional circumstances are present. Our log shows eleven completed
trials, four matters disposed of before trial, seven matters pending but not
completed , one petition for restoration from expulsion and two cases in which
Lodges have restored suspended members.
Your committee has reviewed each of the Trial Records numbered 2383,
2398, 2404, 2405, 2406, 2408, 2410 and2412 and finds that in each case there was
substantial compliance with the procedural requiremen ts of our Constitution and
Ordinances, and the result is supported in the record of each case, and that there are
no miscarriages of justice.

The committee feels compelled to highlight Trial Record No. 2406
included in this report. This trial involved a Past Master of Pasadena Lodge No.
272 who was found Guilty of embezzling property and stealing funds from the
Lodge and its Temple Association, and was expelled. This was a very complicated
and difficult trial. The committee was very impressed with the well-documented
trial transcript and the outstanding conduct of the Trial Master and others
connected with conduct of the trial. A newly made Master Mason, Charles
Carmody, attended the trial. He heard of the difficulty in reporting the trial. He
volunteered to record it, and when the trial was over he volunteered to prepare the
transcript and did so. Your committee on Trial Review commends the Trial Master
and other Brothers involved in conducting the trial in Trial Record No. 2406 for
their outstanding effort on behalf of Grand Lodge.
Your committee therefore submits and moves for adoption the following
resolution:
"Resolved, that in each of Trial Records numbered 2383, 2398, 2404,
2405, 2406, 2408, 2410 and 2412 the judgment and penalty imposed be
and are ratified, affirmed and approved."
Resolution ADOPTED.
Members of this committee are lawyers, judges, and law enforcement
officials. As such they have seen in court all manner of human foibles. They
expect in Masonry to see the rare serious crime, either of violence or greed. But
it is almost as disturbing to see charges of petty bickering, of Lodge politics, or of
brother against brother by words or conduct, which result in Masonic charges,
seemingly filed as a tool for revenge. Most of these should not have been elevated
to Masonic charges. Often they have a very divisive effect upon the Lodge. Each
of us can and should do something to prevent the offended feelings, the hurt, the
jealousy, which cause some of these things to arise.
The members of this committee are grateful for the opportunity to use
their professional skill for the benefit of Masonry. We thank the many people who
participate in the task of providing Masonic justice.

395

Trial Record No. 2219
This is an application for restoration from suspension.
Because the Lodge was notified that the penalty was suspension, it
properly entertained the application of the accused for restoration and approved it.
A restoration from suspension need not be reviewed by Grand Lodge.
However, this is an unusual case.
The accused was charged and found guilty. It was recommended that he
be suspended. The Trial Review Committee in 1985 recommended to the Grand
Lodge that the penalty be raised to expulsion. The 1985 Proceedings do not
indicate the result of the ballot. The vote on the recommendation is not recorded.
The Grand Secretary's office wrote the Lodge that the penalty was fixed at
suspension. However, the Grand Secretary's log show expulsion. The Junior
Warden from Vitruvius Lodge was present in Grand Lodge for the first time. He
was quite impressed with everything, but particularly the action of Grand Lodge
concerning a matter from his home Lodge. He remembers discussion from the
floor and the vote which denied the change recommended and left the penalty at
suspension. A Trial Review Committee member for that year also re members that
Grand Lodge denied the recommendation of the committee on Trial Record No.
2219.
So that the record may be clear and unambiguous, we make this report.
The record should show that the penalty in Trial Record No. 2219, was fixed in
1985 at suspension. Thus, the action ofVitruvius Lodge No. 145 in restoring the
accused is in accord with Masonic law.
We therefore move the adoption of the following resolution:
"Resolved that the records of this Grand Lodge shall show that the
penalty in Trial Record No. 2219 was fixed in 1985 at suspension."
Resolution ADOPTED.

Trial Record No. 2330
This is an application for restoration from expulsion. The accused was
found guilty of taking Lodge funds from a refreshment box; of taking money from
an elderly Brother, now deceased, who had given him a power of attorney; and of
two counts involving his conduct with Rainbow Girls. He was tried in 1991 and
found guilty. Because of the state of the record, the 1991 Annual Communication
reversed the verdict and remanded the matter for a new trial. He was tried again

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

in 1992, was again found guilty and the 1992 Annual Communication upheld the
verdict and the penalty of expulsion.
He has now applied for restoration from his expulsion. He gave notice of
his intent to the Lodge of which he had been a member at the time of his trial and
expulsion, though he failed to include a copy of the intended application as
required by California Masonic Code Section 33 l 00. The Lodge received at least
two letters opposing restoration and heard oral objections to the restoration. The
Lodge voted 17 to 0 to disapprove of the application for restoration.

The evidence shows that the accused, while a trustee of a trust, did
transfer $I 00,000 to his own personal account from which he used monies to
purchase personal items, including an automobile for himself; further, that the
accused received interest payments payable to the trust, but deposited same into his
own personal account. The accused admitted that he made a "mistake'', but he said
that the principal, before her death, had verbally gifted the funds to him. The
accused further testified that he later returned the funds to the estate.
As a trustee, the accused owes a fiduciary duty to the Principal which was
admittedly breached by the accused, and is a very serious Masonic offense
involving moral turpitude.

396

In a letter accompanying his Application for Restoration he says:
"I have now spent six years on the outside looking in. I still see a good
organization. I very much want to be a part of Masonry now and in the
future.
I am truly sorry that I accepted the money from (Brother X) - now
deceased. I can assure you this will never happen again with him or any
other person.
As for the charges concerning the girls, there is nothing I would ever
knowingly do to hurt or embarrass one of any sex. Actions such as this
are not part of my nature."

397

We do not concur with the penalty of suspension and believe that this case
requires the greatest penalty and recommend that the penalty be raised to
expulsion.
Your committee therefore submits the following resolution:
"Resolved, that in Trial Record No. 2407 the findings of the
Commissioners be affirmed and approved except that the penalty is raised
to expulsion."
Resolution ADOPTED.

The Committee on Trial Review recommends that the Application for
Restoration in Trial Record No. 2330 be denied, and moves the adoption of the
following resolution:
"Resolved that the Application for Restoration in Trial Record No. 2330
be denied."
Resolution ADOPTED.

Trial Record No. 2407
A member of Alhambra Lodge No. 322 was charged with unmasonic
conduct in two specifications. The specificationsalleged Breach ofFiduciary Duty
and Embezzlement.
The accused was properly served with the charges and pied "Not Guilty".
A Trial Master was appointed and Commissioners duly charged with hearing the
evidence. A Trial resulted in a finding that the accused was guilty of both counts
and penalty was fixed at suspension.

Trial Record No. 2409
In Trial Record No. 2409, the accused, a Past Master, was charged with
the unlawful taking of money from three brothers whom he was coaching on their
proficiencies . In this case the accused fraudulently promised the victims that they
would double their money in less than 60 days if they invested with him.
The fraudulent solicitation claimed that a company, which would be based
in Palm Springs under the name of Chase Mortgage Company, was about to go
public. This company in fact, did not exist; therefore it could not issue any stock
certificates for anyone to purchase. Additionally neither the company, nor the
accused were registered and/or authorized to engage in the sale of securities. The
three victim brothers, along with others in the community, were defrauded by the
accused by means of buying stock in this nonexistent company.
Masonic charges were filed and the accused pied guilty, a Masonic Trial
was held and the accused was found guilty on all specifications with the penalty
set at suspension.

Trial Record No. 2411
In Trial Record No. 2411, a member of North Hollywood Lodge No. 542
was charged in the Superior Court of the State of California for the County of Los
Angeles with l) shooting at an occupied motor vehicle, and 2) assault with a
firearm . There were additional allegations regarding Count l that the charged
crime is a serious felony, that the defendant personally used a firearm, and with the
intent to do so inflicted great bodily injury. There were additional allegations
regarding Count 2 that the defendant personally used a firearm, and with the intent
to do so defendant inflicted great bodily injury. Factually, the case involved an
altercation in a parking lot which escalated to the point where the member shot
through a car window causing the driver of the vehicle to suffer both gunshot and
glass wounds as he was retreating from the scene. After a jury trial, the member
was found guilty of both counts and all special allegations. Further, after an
unsuccessful appeal to the California Appellate Court, the member was remanded
to state prison.
Masonic charges were filed. They alleged substantiallythe same offenses
as had been charged in the Superior Court. Upon being properly served with the
charges, the member pied not guilty and requested a Masonic Trial. The Trial
Commissioners found the member not guilty. In the usual case this would be the
end of the story. However, after a complete and thorough review of the entire trial
record, your Committee on Trial Review is convinced that the evidence in this case
requires a reversal. California Masonic Code Sections 330 l 0 and 33030 provide
authority in an appropriate case for reversal of a not guilty finding in a case of
gross violation of Masonic law by the Trial Commission.

399

The record reveals irregularities in the presentation of the evidence and
the order of argument allowed by the Trial Master. Further, it appears from the
record that there is a substantial likelihood the Trial Commissioners were not
properly instructed on the issue of moral turpitude and were thus inadvertently
misled in their duty. Your committee believes this was a gross violation of
Masonic law, which has caused a miscarriage of justice and requires the reversal
of this not guilty finding.
The committee therefore submits the following resolution:
"Resolved, that in Trial Record No. 2411, the findings of the Trial
Commissioners be reversed and set aside and the matter be remanded for
further proceedings and retrial with the following instructions to the Trial
Master. In any retrial of these charges, the Trial Commissioners shall be
instructed that the crimes of 1) shooting an occupied vehicle, and 2)
assault with a firearm are crimes which involve moral turpitude as a
matter of law."
Resolution ADOPTED .
Respectfully submitted,
Donald R. Fretz, Chairman
David R. Doan
Thomas C. Letcher

REPORT OF THE COMMIT TEE ON
U.S. CONSTIT UTION OBSERVA NCE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
The committee has had a very active year in terms of Constitution
Commemorations and related activities. In July, the Grand Master issued a
proclamation directing all constituent Lodges to "participate in an appropriate
program to commemorate the signing of the Constitution during the month of
September". His theme was "We the People - The Constitution, an Indelible
Document of Freedom". The Grand Master's proclamation was supplemented by
a letter from the committee chair providing and referring to materials that would
assist Lodges in their commemoration programs. A Constitution Week Planning
Booklet, which was originally prepared for the Constitution Bicentennial, was
provided each Lodge and offered ideas in planning local programs. Copies of the

401

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Si~ature Newsletter of the National Constitution Center were disseminated, which
contained information on commemorative activities. Also provided were
facsimiles of the U.S. Constitution, the Bill of Rights and the Declaration of
Independence. A Report of Activities form, sample Certificates of Recognition
and a directory of U.S. Constitution Observance Committee members were also
provided.

Worshipful Master John Gates of Georgetown Lodge No. 25 reported a
program which included patriotic music, poems, members portraying George
Washington, Benjamin Franklin, Thomas Jefferson and Abraham Lincoln.

400

Since the U.S. Congress was in the process of considering a constitutional
amendment that would protect our Flag from acts of desecration, a separate
memorandum was distributed which encouraged Lodges to display the U.S. Flag
and participate in the programs of the Citizens Flag Alliance. A sample Certificate
entitled "Show Your Colors, America" was provided, encouraging Lodges to
nominate organizations and individuals for recognition for their outstanding
citizenship and activities in displaying the U.S. Flag. A large number of Lodges,
individuals and public spirited organizations were nominated to receive and were
issued the "Show Your Colors, America" certificates.
The committee received many reports of Lodge Constitution Observance
Programs. Many of these activities were conducted strictly within the Lodges and
entailed speeches or patriotic programs. Other reported programs were more
elaborate, involving several Lodges, as well as other Masonic and non-Masonic
organizations.
Noteworthy among these programs was the program at San Bernardino
Lodge No. 178 which included a colonial style dinner, an enjoyable Masonic play
on the Constitution with participants in costume, and speeches by Senior Grand
Warden Weis (in colonial costume) and R:.W:. Alvin portraying Benjamin
Franklin. Many other members and participating groups were garbed in colonial
attire, including Past Grand Master Allen Gresham.
The Constitution Observances at the Knotts Berry Farm Independence
Hall continue to attract public attention. Again, several Lodges, the National
Sojourners, Sons of the American Revolution, representatives of the U.S. Armed
Forces and Masonic Youth Group Flag Teams participated in this elaborate
commemoration, which included comments by costumed speakers representing
delegates to the Constitution Convention. Committee members Bill Sizemore,
Gene Collins, Ron Markarian and Chris Christoff all participated in the program.
Brother David Francis Philips entertained the attendees with several patriotic
songs.

Lodges, such as Nevada No. 13, co-sponsoreda Community Constitution
Day Parade and Celebration that included a Civil War Encampment and Battles,
a "gold country duck race", outside concert, ceremonies re-enacting the signing of
the Constitution and a pancake breakfast. Participating organizations included the
49er Rotary Club, Nevada City Fire Department, Re-enactors of the American
Civil War, Shrine units and the world famous Watsonville Marching Band.
Worshipful Master Hall states, "it (the program) grows each year".
The committee continues to sponsor a booth during the Annual Grand
Lodge Sessions. Constitution Observance materials, including articles, quizzes,
examples of programs, pocket Constitutions and other related materials, are
available to Grand Session attendees. The committee is indebted to Brothers Brad
White, Roger Torrey and Russ Roberts, among others, for setting up and staffing
the booth.
As a follow-up to the very successful and popular 501h Anniversary of
World War II program, the committee distributed advance copies of informational
material and applications for Commemorative Community status for the 501h
Anniversary of the Korean War, which will be celebrated nationally during the
years 2000-2003. Participating Lodges will receive a Certificate from the U.S.
Department of Def~nse designating them as an official "Commemor~tive
Community", a specially designed 501h Anniversary flag and other educational
materials relating to the Korean War and its significance in United States history
and world events during that period.
Again, the committee salutes the many, many Lodges that marshaled their
resources to make the 1998 U.S. Constitution Observance Program a great success.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON YOUTH ORDERS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
During the 1998 Masonic Year the Youth Orders Committee has actively
engaged in a fraternal interchange with the youth orders in our jurisdiction. In
November an introductory meeting of the adult leadership of Job's Daughters,
Rainbow for Girls and the Northern and Southern Jurisdictions ofDeMolay was
held while attending the NORCAL DeMolay Convention in Sacramento. The
meeting, although brief, was productive in setting forth the committee's objectives
for the ensuing Masonic year. The annual MA YO conference with the Grand
Master, members of the Executive Committee and the youth orders adult leadership
was held in January. All in attendance contributed freely in the discussions that
centered primarily on items concerning membership and methods and programs
that would renew interest in joining organizations of the Masonic family.
In addition to the NORCAL DeMolay convention the committee chairman
and members attended the Rainbow Grand Assembly in April, Job's Daughters
Grand Bethel in June and the SOCAL DeMolay Conclave in September. As is past
years, the Youth Orders Committee presented each of the four youth groups with
$1,500 to support their leadership training programs. Throughout the year all
committeemen endeavored to attend local youth activities in their areas. These
visitations supported the committee's goal of improving the fraternal relationship
between Grand Lodge, constituent Lodges and the Youth Orders.
Two regular meetings of the committee were held. The first on March 28,
1998 and the second on May 16, 1998. The first meeting was primarily for
organization and establishing the objectives of the committee for the ensuing year.
It was emphasized for the committee members that the purpose of the committee
was to promote fraternal relations between the Youth Orders, Grand Lodge and the

405

constituent Lodges. Additionally, that a secondary role of the committee was to
identify Master Masons that would serve on Rainbow Advisory Boards, Job's
Daughters Bethel Councils and DeMolay Advisory Boards.
The May 16th meeting was spent documenting the selection criteria and
guidelines for nominating and selecting recipients of the Grand Master's Youth
Service Award. It was found that the criteria and guidelines used in previous years
were not well documented and were changed from time to time in response to
verbal inputs from various sources. The committee is continuing this task into the
1999 Masonic year and the documented criteria and guidelines will be presented
to the Executive Committee for review and approval.
To enhance the communications of the committee a Web site was created
on the Internetand linked from the Grand Lodge Web site. The Web site includes
links to the Grand Lodge home page, the Masonic Foundation, and to the Northern
and Southern Jurisdictions of DeMolay home pages. Web pages for the California
Rainbow for Girls and Job's Daughters were also established in the Web site. This
tool has proven effective as several inquiries for information related to our youth
orders were received during the year from throughout the country as well as in the
jurisdiction. Visitors to the site included a senior DeMolay from Massachusetts,
members of our youth orders asking for information regarding Masonic
scholarships and others seeking locations of our local youth groups in their
immediate area.
At this year's Annual Communication of Grand Lodge the committee set
up a booth in the exhibition hall. The committee provided handouts on the youth
orders organizations as well as answering questions from the many visitors
stopping at the booth. Additionally, a computer based color presentation was on
display during the three day period.
Your Committee on Youth Orders respectfully submits this report on its
activities for the 1998 Masonic year. We thank you for the opportunity to have
served this Grand Lodge and its elected and appointed officers, our constituent
Lodges and our Masonic Youth Orders.
Respectfully submitted,
Raymond W. Peltier, Chairman
James J. Nash, Jr.
